school-c7-science-b.title: Class 7 Science · Part B
school-c7-science-b.description: Every chapter of Class 7 Science (NCERT 2023–24 rationalised order) as its own course: nutrition, heat, acids, light, electricity and more, explained with everyday examples and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Reproduction in Plants
courses.summary: How plants make new plants: vegetative propagation, budding, fragmentation and spores; the parts of a flower, pollination and fertilisation; and how fruits and seeds form and spread.
outcomes: Learners can describe asexual reproduction in plants with examples
Learners can name the parts of a flower and distinguish unisexual and bisexual flowers
Learners can explain pollination, fertilisation and formation of fruits and seeds
Learners can explain seed dispersal by wind, water, animals and explosion

scenes.text: Grandma cuts a piece of a rose stem with a node and plants it in moist soil.
Weeks later, new leaves and roots appear.
"Potatoes do this too," she says, showing the buds on a potato's eyes.

steps.title: Modes of reproduction
steps.body:
Production of new individuals from parents is **reproduction**. Two modes:

- **Asexual**: new plants without seeds — from roots, stems, leaves, buds or spores.
- **Sexual**: new plants from **seeds**, after fusion of male and female cells.

steps.title: Vegetative propagation
steps.body:
New plants grow from **roots, stems, leaves or buds** (vegetative parts).

- **Stem cutting**: rose, champa — a cut piece with a **node** (point where a leaf attaches) is planted.
- **Potato**: a modified stem; its **eyes** (buds) grow into new plants.
- **Ginger, turmeric**: underground stems.
- **Bryophyllum** (sprout leaf plant): **buds on leaf margins** grow into plants.
- **Roots**: sweet potato, dahlia.

The young plant is called a **bud** at the node or axil before it grows.

steps.title: Advantages
steps.body:
- Plants grow faster and bear flowers/fruits earlier than from seeds.
- New plants are **identical** to the parent (same characters).
- Plants that produce few or no viable seeds can be multiplied.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: A farmer wants many potato plants exactly like his best crop. Method?

A: Cut potatoes into pieces, each with an **eye**, and plant them — vegetative propagation.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why must a stem cutting have a node?

A: Buds at the node grow into shoots and roots; without a node no new plant grows.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a potato a root — it is an underground **stem** (it has buds/eyes).
- Thinking only seeds can make new plants.

activity.prompt: Match the plant with how it is propagated.

quiz.why: Vegetative propagation grows new plants from vegetative parts such as roots, stems and leaves, not from seeds or flowers.
Bryophyllum grows small buds on the edges of its leaves. When they fall to the soil, each can grow into a new plant.

quiz.q: The "eye" of a potato is a
quiz.why: The eyes of a potato are buds. Each can grow into a new plant.
Plants grown vegetatively come from one parent only, so they are identical to it.

options: where a leaf is attached to the stem
quiz.why: A node is the point on a stem where a leaf is attached. New roots and shoots can grow from nodes in a cutting.

scenes.text: Boojho sees green slimy threads in a pond. In a few days the patch has spread over the whole pond!
His teacher says: these algae break into pieces, and each piece grows into a new one.
Bread left out gets mould from tiny spores floating in the air.

steps.title: Budding (yeast)
steps.body: **Yeast** is a single-celled organism. It produces a small bulb-like projection called a **bud**, which grows and detaches to form a new yeast cell. Sometimes a chain of buds forms.

steps.title: Fragmentation (algae)
steps.body: When water and nutrients are available, algae (e.g. **Spirogyra**) grow and multiply rapidly by **fragmentation**: an alga breaks into two or more fragments, each growing into a new individual.

steps.title: Spore formation
steps.body: Fungi (bread mould), mosses and ferns reproduce by **spores**. Spores are asexual reproductive bodies with a **hard protective coat** that withstands heat and dryness. They float in the air and, on landing in a moist place, germinate into new plants.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why does bread left in a warm, moist kitchen grow mould?

A: Mould spores in the air land on the bread; moisture and warmth help them germinate and grow.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: How can spores survive harsh conditions?

A: Their hard protective coat protects them from high temperature and low humidity until conditions improve.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ferns reproduce by seeds — they reproduce by spores.
- Confusing budding in yeast with buds of vegetative propagation in plants.

quiz.why: Yeast cells form small outgrowths called buds. The bud grows and separates as a new cell. This is budding.
Spirogyra, a green alga, breaks into pieces. Each piece grows into a new alga, which is fragmentation.
Spores are covered by a hard coat that protects them in harsh conditions until they find good soil and moisture.
Ferns reproduce by spores, which form on the underside of the leaves. Mango, rose and potato do not.
Spore formation, budding and fragmentation are asexual. Seeds form after fertilisation, which is sexual reproduction.

scenes.text: A bee visits a mustard flower to drink nectar.
Yellow dust (pollen) sticks to its legs.
At the next flower, some pollen rubs off onto the sticky top of the pistil. Pollination!

steps.title: Parts of a flower
steps.body:
- **Stamens** (male parts): each has a **filament** and an **anther**; the anther contains **pollen grains**, which produce **male gametes**.
- **Pistil** (female part): **stigma** (sticky top), **style** (stalk) and **ovary** (swollen base) containing **ovules**; each ovule has a **female gamete (egg)**.
- Sepals and petals protect and attract.

steps.title: Unisexual and bisexual
steps.body:
- **Unisexual flowers**: only stamens or only pistil — corn, papaya, cucumber.
- **Bisexual flowers**: both stamens and pistil — mustard, rose, petunia.

steps.title: Pollination
steps.body:
Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma is **pollination**.

- **Self-pollination**: to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant.
- **Cross-pollination**: to a flower of a different plant of the same kind.

Agents: **wind, water, insects**. Pollen grains have a tough protective coat to prevent drying.

steps.title: Fertilisation
steps.body: The fusion of a **male gamete** with a **female gamete (egg)** is **fertilisation**. The fertilised egg is the **zygote**, which develops into an **embryo** inside the seed.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Papaya plants are either male or female. Can a lone female papaya tree bear fruit?

A: Only if pollen from a male papaya plant reaches its flowers (cross-pollination by insects or wind). Without pollination there is no fertilisation and no seeds.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name the male and female parts in order of pollen's journey. → Anther (pollen) → stigma → style → ovary → ovule (egg).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing pollination (transfer of pollen) with fertilisation (fusion of gametes).
- Thinking all flowers have both stamens and pistil.

activity.prompt: Male part, female part, or neither?

quiz.q: Pollen grains are produced in the
quiz.why: Pollen grains are made in the anther, the top part of the stamen. The ovary is the female part and the stigma receives pollen.
Ovules are the small structures inside the ovary. Each may become a seed after fertilisation.
Papaya has separate male and female flowers, so it is unisexual. Petunia, mustard and rose have both parts in the same flower.

quiz.q: Transfer of pollen to stigma is
quiz.why: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. Fertilisation is the later joining of male and female cells.
When the male and female gametes fuse, the first cell formed is the zygote. It later grows into an embryo.
Pollen can be carried by wind, water and insects, and also by birds and other animals. So it is not limited to one agent.

scenes.text: After a walk through a field, Paheli finds spiky seeds stuck to her socks.
At home, fluffy madar seeds float out of the window.
Seeds travel by animals, wind, water — even by bursting pods!

steps.title: Fruits and seeds
steps.body: After fertilisation, the **ovary grows into a fruit** and the **ovules develop into seeds**. A seed contains an **embryo** enclosed in a protective **seed coat**. The other flower parts usually fall off. Fruits may be fleshy (mango, orange) or hard (almond, walnut).

steps.title: Why disperse?
steps.body: If all seeds fell under the parent, seedlings would compete for sunlight, water and minerals. **Dispersal** helps plants reach new habitats and reduces competition.

steps.title: Ways of dispersal
steps.body:
- **Wind**: light seeds with wings (drumstick, maple) or hairs (madar/aak, sunflower, dandelion); light grass seeds.
- **Water**: floating, fibrous fruits like **coconut**; seeds with spongy coats (lotus).
- **Animals**: spiny or hooked seeds (**Xanthium**, **Urena**) stick to animal fur; animals eat fruits and the seeds pass out unharmed.
- **Explosion**: fruits burst and jerk seeds away — **castor, balsam**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: How is coconut adapted for dispersal by water?

A: Its thick fibrous husk traps air and lets it float long distances across seas.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Classify: drumstick, Xanthium, castor, coconut. → wind; animals; explosion; water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the whole flower becomes a fruit — the **ovary** becomes the fruit.
- Mixing up winged seeds (wind) and spiny seeds (animals).

quiz.why: After fertilisation the ovary grows and becomes the fruit.
After fertilisation each ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Coconut has a light, fibrous fruit that floats. So it is carried by water, often along seashores.

quiz.q: Seeds of balsam are dispersed by
quiz.why: Balsam fruits burst open when ripe and throw the seeds out. This is dispersal by explosion.
Dispersal spreads seeds away from the parent. This reduces competition for light, water and space, and lets plants reach new places.

questions.q: Asexual reproduction in rose is by
questions.why: Rose is commonly grown from a stem cutting that has a node. The cutting grows roots and a shoot. Budding is for yeast and spores are for ferns.

questions.q: Yeast reproduces by
questions.why: Yeast makes buds that break off to form new yeast cells. This is budding.

questions.q: Male part of a flower
questions.why: The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part of a flower. The pistil, which has the ovary, is female.

questions.q: After fertilisation, the ovary becomes
questions.why: After fertilisation the ovary develops into the fruit, and the ovules inside become seeds.

questions.q: Ferns and mosses reproduce by
questions.why: Ferns and mosses do not make seeds. They reproduce by spores.

questions.q: A bisexual flower
questions.why: Mustard has both stamens and pistil in one flower, so it is bisexual. Papaya, cucumber and corn have unisexual flowers.

questions.q: Drumstick seeds are dispersed by
questions.why: Drumstick seeds have wing-like parts, so the wind carries them away.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Plants from vegetative propagation are identical to the parent. Reason (R): They come from only one parent.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: the new plants come from one parent, with no mixing of characters. R is true, and it explains why they are identical to the parent.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Pollination and fertilisation are the same. Reason (R): Both happen in flowers.
questions.why: A is false: pollination is the transfer of pollen, while fertilisation is the fusion of gametes. R is true that both happen in flowers, but it does not make them the same.

questions.q: Zygote develops into
questions.why: The zygote divides and grows into an embryo, which is the young plant inside the seed.

questions.q: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen to
options: a flower of a different plant
stigma of the same flower or same plant
questions.why: Self-pollination is when pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower, or of another flower on the same plant.

questions.q: Case: A gardener wants mangoes of exactly the same taste as his best tree, quickly. Better choice?
options: Vegetative methods from the best tree
questions.why: Vegetative methods like grafting or cutting give plants identical to the parent, with the same taste. They are also quicker than growing from seeds, which can vary.

questions.q: Case: Seeds of a plant are found far away in a river delta, inside a fibrous fruit. Likely agent of dispersal?
questions.why: A light fibrous fruit that floats is carried by water. Winged seeds travel by wind, and fur carries burs.

questions.q: Why would a pond surface get covered with algae within days?
questions.why: Algae can break into fragments quickly when conditions are good, and each fragment grows. So the pond is soon covered.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct?
questions.why: First pollination, then fertilisation forms a zygote, which grows into an embryo, and then the seed. The other orders break this chain of events.

questions.q: Spores survive unfavourable conditions because they
questions.why: A hard protective coat lets spores survive heat, dryness and cold. They grow when conditions improve.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Motion and Time
courses.summary: Slow and fast motion, speed as distance per unit time, how humans measured time from sundials to pendulums and quartz clocks, units, speedometers and odometers, and reading and drawing distance–time graphs.
outcomes: Learners can calculate speed, distance and time with correct units
Learners can distinguish uniform and non-uniform motion
Learners can describe a simple pendulum and its time period
Learners can draw and interpret distance–time graphs

scenes.text: In a race, Rani covers 100 m in 16 s; Meena covers 100 m in 18 s.
Rani took less time for the same distance — she is faster.
But how to compare a bus that went 120 km in 3 h with a car that went 150 km in 2.5 h? Use speed!

steps.title: Speed
steps.body:
**Speed = Total distance covered ÷ Total time taken.**

The SI unit of speed is **metre per second (m/s)**. Other units: km/h, km/min.

Rearranged: Distance = Speed × Time; Time = Distance ÷ Speed.

steps.title: Uniform and non-uniform motion
steps.body:
- **Uniform motion**: an object moves along a straight line at **constant speed** (covers equal distances in equal intervals).
- **Non-uniform motion**: speed keeps changing (a car in traffic).

For non-uniform motion, distance ÷ time gives the **average speed**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A bus covers 120 km in 3 h; a car covers 150 km in 2.5 h. Which is faster?

- Bus: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h
- Car: 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h
- **The car is faster.**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A train moves at 90 km/h. How far does it go in 20 minutes?

- 20 min = 1/3 h
- Distance = 90 × 1/3 = **30 km**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Salma takes 15 min from home to school by bicycle at 2 m/s. Distance?

- 15 min = 900 s
- d = 2 × 900 = **1800 m = 1.8 km**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing units: minutes with km/h. Convert first.
- Thinking a larger number always means faster — 20 m/s (72 km/h) is faster than 60 km/h.

activity.prompt: A cyclist covers 9 km in 30 minutes. Speed in km/h?

quiz.why: Speed is distance per time. With distance in metres and time in seconds, the SI unit is metre per second (m/s).

quiz.q: Speed of a car covering 180 km in 3 h
quiz.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 180 km ÷ 3 h = 60 km/h.
To change km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18. 36 × 5/18 = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: Motion with constant speed in a straight line
quiz.why: Motion at constant speed along a straight line is called uniform motion. If the speed changes it is non-uniform.

quiz.q: Time to cover 300 m at 5 m/s
quiz.why: Time = distance ÷ speed = 300 m ÷ 5 m/s = 60 s.

lessons.title: Measuring time: from sundials to pendulums

scenes.text: Long ago, the young scientist Galileo watched a lamp swinging from a church ceiling.
Timing it with his pulse, he found each swing took the same time, big or small.
This idea later led to pendulum clocks.

steps.title: Old ways of measuring time
steps.body: People used natural periodic events: a **day** (sunrise to next sunrise), a **month** (new moon to next new moon), a **year** (one revolution of Earth around the Sun). Devices: **sundials**, **water clocks**, **sand clocks (hourglasses)**. India had sundials at Jantar Mantar (e.g. in Jaipur and Delhi).

steps.title: Simple pendulum
steps.body:
A small metal ball (**bob**) hung from a rigid stand by a thread. Pulled to one side and released, it moves to and fro — **oscillatory motion**.

- One **oscillation**: from one extreme position to the other and back.
- **Time period**: time taken for one oscillation.
- For a given length of thread at a place, the time period is constant.

steps.title: Modern clocks and units
steps.body:
Most clocks today use **quartz crystals** (electric circuits with cells). Very precise atomic clocks are used for special purposes.

The basic unit of time is the **second (s)**. 60 s = 1 min; 60 min = 1 h. Symbols: s, min, h — written without 's' for plurals and without full stops.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A pendulum makes 20 oscillations in 32 s. Time period?

- T = 32 ÷ 20 = **1.6 s**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why do we time 20 oscillations and not just one?

A: One oscillation is too short to time accurately; timing many and dividing reduces the error.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting one swing (one side to the other) as one oscillation. An oscillation is a complete to-and-fro.
- Writing '20 secs.' — the correct form is '20 s'.

activity.prompt: A pendulum takes 45 s for 25 oscillations. Its time period (s)?

quiz.q: One complete to-and-fro of a pendulum is
quiz.why: One full to-and-fro movement of a pendulum is called one oscillation.
The time period of a pendulum is the time it takes to make one complete oscillation.
The basic unit of time is the second. Minutes, hours and days are made from it.

quiz.q: Galileo noticed the regular swinging of a
quiz.why: Galileo noticed that a swinging lamp took the same time for each swing. This led to the idea of the pendulum clock.
Most modern clocks and watches use quartz crystals, which vibrate at a very steady rate.

scenes.text: On a trip, Amit watches the dashboard: one needle shows 60 km/h.
Another meter shows the total kilometres the car has run.
He writes the odometer reading every 10 minutes and later draws a graph.

steps.title: Speedometer and odometer
steps.body:
- **Speedometer**: shows the speed at that moment (in km/h).
- **Odometer**: shows the total distance covered by the vehicle.

steps.title: Distance–time graph
steps.body:
Plot **time on the x-axis** and **distance on the y-axis**, with a suitable scale.

- **Uniform motion** → a **straight line** graph.
- Steeper line → higher speed.
- A **horizontal line** → object at rest (distance not changing).
- Speed from the graph = (change in distance) ÷ (change in time).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Odometer readings: 8:00 → 36540 km, 8:30 → 36560 km. Distance and speed?

- Distance = 20 km in 0.5 h
- Speed = 20 ÷ 0.5 = **40 km/h**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A distance–time graph is a straight line through (0 min, 0 km) and (40 min, 20 km). Speed?

- 20 km ÷ 40 min = 0.5 km/min = **30 km/h**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Graph: (0, 0) to (2 h, 80 km) straight, then flat until 3 h, then to (5 h, 200 km). Describe.

- 0–2 h: 40 km/h
- 2–3 h: at rest
- 3–5 h: 120 km in 2 h = 60 km/h

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping axes (time goes on the x-axis).
- Reading a flat part as 'moving slowly' — it means the object is at rest.
- Choosing a scale that squeezes the graph into a corner.

statements.s: A straight-line distance–time graph shows uniform motion.
A horizontal line means high speed.
An odometer measures speed.
A steeper line means greater speed.
Time is usually plotted on the x-axis.

quiz.why: The speedometer in a vehicle shows its speed at that moment.
The odometer shows the total distance a vehicle has covered.

quiz.q: For an object at rest, the distance–time graph is
quiz.why: An object at rest stays at the same distance, so its distance–time graph is a horizontal line.

quiz.q: Odometer: 1200 km to 1290 km in 1.5 h. Speed
quiz.why: Distance = 1290 − 1200 = 90 km. Speed = 90 ÷ 1.5 = 60 km/h.

quiz.q: On a graph, line A is steeper than line B. A is
quiz.why: On a distance–time graph, a steeper line means more distance in the same time. So A is faster.

scenes.text: The family plans a 240 km drive. Papa says they will average 60 km/h.
Time = 240 ÷ 60 = 4 h. Leaving at 7 a.m., they should reach at 11 a.m.
With a 30 min tea stop, they arrive at 11:30 a.m.

steps.title: Problem-solving steps
steps.body:
1. List the given quantities with units.
2. Convert units so they match.
3. Choose the formula (S = D/T, D = S × T, T = D/S).
4. Calculate and write the unit.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Sound travels about 340 m/s in air. Lightning is seen and thunder heard 3 s later. How far away was the lightning?

- d = 340 × 3 = **1020 m (about 1 km)**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A car travels 60 km at 30 km/h and then 60 km at 60 km/h. Average speed?

- Time 1 = 2 h; time 2 = 1 h
- Average = 120 ÷ 3 = **40 km/h** (not 45!)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging speeds directly instead of using total distance ÷ total time.
- Forgetting stops when calculating total time.

activity.prompt: A train runs at 54 km/h. What is its speed in m/s?

quiz.why: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time taken. It is not just the mean of the speeds.
1 minute = 60 s. Distance = speed × time = 15 × 60 = 900 m.

quiz.q: Time to travel 45 km at 90 km/h
quiz.why: Time = 45 km ÷ 90 km/h = 0.5 h, which is 30 minutes.
To change m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5. 5 × 18/5 = 18 km/h.

quiz.q: Thunder heard 5 s after lightning (sound 340 m/s). Distance
quiz.why: Distance = speed × time = 340 × 5 = 1700 m. The 3400 would need 10 s.

questions.q: Speed =
questions.why: Speed is the distance moved per unit time, so speed = distance ÷ time.

questions.q: SI unit of time
questions.why: The SI unit of time is the second. The hour, minute and day are other units.

questions.q: Instrument showing distance covered by a vehicle
questions.why: The odometer shows the distance covered by a vehicle. The speedometer shows its speed.

questions.q: Motion of a pendulum is
questions.why: A pendulum moves to and fro about a fixed point. That kind of motion is oscillatory.

questions.q: A car covers 150 km in 3 h. Speed
questions.why: Speed = 150 km ÷ 3 h = 50 km/h.

questions.q: 54 km/h in m/s
questions.why: Multiply by 5/18: 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s.

questions.q: A horizontal distance–time graph shows the object is
questions.why: On a distance–time graph a horizontal line means the distance does not change with time, so the object is at rest.

questions.q: Assertion (A): We time 20 oscillations to find a pendulum's time period. Reason (R): Timing many oscillations reduces measuring error.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: we time about 20 oscillations. R is true: a small timing error is shared among many oscillations, so the period is more accurate. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A car in city traffic is in uniform motion. Reason (R): Uniform motion means constant speed in a straight line.
questions.why: A is false: city traffic keeps speeding up, slowing down and turning, so it is non-uniform. R is a correct definition but does not suit the case.

questions.q: Pendulum makes 30 oscillations in 48 s. Time period
questions.why: Time period = total time ÷ number of oscillations = 48 ÷ 30 = 1.6 s.

questions.q: A bus travels at 40 km/h for 2.5 h. Distance
questions.why: Distance = speed × time = 40 × 2.5 = 100 km.

questions.q: Case: Odometer readings: 10:00 → 57321 km; 10:45 → 57366 km. Average speed?
questions.why: Distance = 57366 − 57321 = 45 km. Time = 45 min = 0.75 h. Speed = 45 ÷ 0.75 = 60 km/h.

questions.q: Case: A distance–time graph is a straight line through (0 s, 0 m) and (10 s, 50 m). Speed and distance in 30 s?
questions.why: Speed = 50 m ÷ 10 s = 5 m/s. In 30 s the distance is 5 × 30 = 150 m.

questions.q: Which device was NOT used for measuring time in the past?
questions.why: Sand clocks, water clocks and sundials were used to measure time. The odometer measures distance, not time.

questions.q: A cyclist goes 12 km at 12 km/h and returns at 6 km/h. Average speed for the round trip?
questions.why: Going takes 12 ÷ 12 = 1 h and returning takes 12 ÷ 6 = 2 h. Total distance 24 km in 3 h gives 8 km/h. It is not the simple mean of 12 and 6.

questions.q: Two cars start together. A at 72 km/h, B at 15 m/s. After 10 minutes, how far apart (same direction)?
questions.why: Car A: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. Car B: 15 m/s. The gap grows by 5 m/s, and 10 min is 600 s, so 5 × 600 = 3000 m = 3 km.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Electric Current and its Effects
courses.summary: Symbols and circuit diagrams, combining cells into a battery, the heating effect (bulbs, heaters, fuses and MCBs), the magnetic effect discovered by Oersted, electromagnets and how an electric bell works.
outcomes: Learners can draw circuit diagrams using standard symbols
Learners can explain the heating effect and its uses and dangers
Learners can explain how fuses and MCBs protect circuits
Learners can demonstrate the magnetic effect and make an electromagnet
Learners can explain how an electric bell works

story.title: The torch that would not glow

scenes.text: Rani's torch will not light. She opens it: the two cells are placed the wrong way.
She turns one around so the positive end of one touches the negative end of the other.
Click — light! Cells must be joined correctly to form a battery.

steps.title: Symbols
steps.body:
- **Electric cell**: a long thin line (positive) and a short thick line (negative)
- **Battery**: two or more cells joined
- **Bulb**: a circle with a cross or a coil inside
- **Switch** (key): open (OFF) or closed (ON)
- **Wire**: a straight line

A **circuit diagram** shows a circuit using these symbols.

steps.title: Closed and open circuits
steps.body: Current flows only in a **closed circuit** (switch ON, complete path). When the switch is OFF, the circuit is **open** and no current flows. By convention, current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the cell.

steps.title: Battery
steps.body: A battery is made by connecting the **positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next**. Cells in torches, transistors, toys are placed this way. A battery gives a larger push than one cell.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: A bulb does not glow in a closed circuit. Give possible reasons.

A: The bulb may be fused (broken filament), a connection may be loose, or the cell may be used up.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Draw a circuit with a battery of two cells, a closed switch and a bulb (in words).

A: Two cell symbols side by side (long line of one next to short line of the other) → wire → closed switch → wire → bulb → wire back to the battery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Joining cells positive-to-positive: they oppose each other.
- Thinking a switch in OFF position completes the circuit.
- Never experiment with mains electricity at home — use only cells.

activity.prompt: Match the component to its symbol description.
pairs: Long thin line and short thick line
Two or more cells joined + to −

quiz.why: Current flows only in a closed circuit, where the path is complete. An open circuit has a break, so no current flows.

quiz.q: In a battery, cells are joined
quiz.why: In a battery the positive terminal of one cell is joined to the negative terminal of the next, in series.

quiz.q: Longer line in a cell symbol is
quiz.why: In the cell symbol the longer line is the positive terminal and the shorter, thicker line is the negative.
A fused bulb has a broken filament. The circuit is broken, so no current flows and it does not glow.
Cells are safe for experiments. Mains supply, lightning and generators can give dangerous shocks.

scenes.text: Sana touches a bulb that has been on for an hour — ouch, it is hot!
Her mother's electric iron and room heater also get hot when current flows.
Current flowing through a wire produces heat: the heating effect.

steps.title: What happens
steps.body:
When electric current passes through a wire, the wire gets heated. This is the **heating effect of current**. The amount of heat depends on the material, length and thickness of the wire.

Appliances using it: room heater, electric iron, immersion heater, geyser, electric kettle, toaster, hair dryer. Their coil is called the **element**, usually made of **nichrome** (an alloy).

steps.title: Bulbs and energy saving
steps.body: In an incandescent bulb, the thin **filament** gets so hot it glows and gives light. But much electricity is wasted as heat. **CFLs and LEDs** give the same light using far less electricity. Buy appliances with the **ISI mark** — a sign of meeting safety standards.

steps.title: Fuse and MCB
steps.body: Too much current can overheat wires, melt insulation and cause fires. A **fuse** contains a wire of special material that **melts and breaks the circuit** when current exceeds a safe limit (short circuit or overloading). Today **miniature circuit breakers (MCBs)** are used; they **switch off automatically** and can be switched on again after fixing the fault.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why does a fuse protect a house?

A: When current becomes too large, the fuse wire melts and the circuit breaks, preventing overheating and fire.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why are CFLs/LEDs better than ordinary bulbs?

A: They waste less electricity as heat and give the same light, so they save energy and money.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body:
- Never replace a fuse with an ordinary wire.
- Do not plug many high-power appliances into one socket (overloading).
- Do not touch switches with wet hands.
- CFLs contain mercury vapour; dispose of them safely.

statements.s: A fuse wire melts when too much current flows.
LED bulbs waste more energy than incandescent bulbs.
Heater elements are often made of nichrome.
MCBs must be replaced each time they trip.
statements.why: They can be switched on again.

statements.s: The ISI mark shows the appliance meets safety standards.

quiz.q: The coil in a heater is called the
quiz.why: The coil of wire in a heater that gets hot is called the heating element. The thin wire in a bulb is the filament.
An electric iron works on the heating effect of current. A compass and magnet relate to the magnetic effect.
A fuse has a thin wire that melts if the current is too high. This breaks the circuit and protects appliances and wiring.
MCB stands for miniature circuit breaker. It switches off automatically when the current is too high, and can be switched on again.
CFLs and LEDs give more light for less electric energy, since less is wasted as heat than in ordinary bulbs.

scenes.text: Boojho places a compass near a wire connected to a cell and a switch.
He presses the switch — the needle swings! Off — it returns.
A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet. Oersted discovered this in 1820.

steps.title: Magnetic effect
steps.body: When current flows through a wire, the wire behaves like a **magnet** and deflects a nearby compass needle. This is the **magnetic effect of electric current**, first observed by **Hans Christian Oersted**.

steps.title: Electromagnet
steps.body:
Wind insulated wire around an **iron nail** to make a coil; connect it to a cell through a switch. When current flows, the nail attracts pins and iron filings; when current stops, it loses most magnetism. This temporary magnet is an **electromagnet**.

Electromagnets can be made very strong and are used in cranes to lift heavy iron scrap, in electric bells, loudspeakers and toys. Doctors use small electromagnets to remove tiny iron pieces from the eye.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?

A: Use more turns of wire in the coil, or use more cells (larger current), or use a soft iron core.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why are electromagnets used in scrap yards rather than permanent magnets?

A: They can be switched off to drop the scrap where needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying an electromagnet stays magnetic after the current stops — it loses its magnetism.
- Using bare wire for the coil; it must be insulated so current flows round the coil.

activity.prompt: Make an electromagnet (with an adult, using only cells):
items: Take a large iron nail and about 1 m of insulated copper wire
Wind the wire tightly around the nail in one direction
Scrape the insulation off both ends of the wire
Connect the ends to a cell through a switch
Switch on and bring pins near the nail tip
Switch off and watch the pins drop
Disconnect the cell after use (it heats and drains)

quiz.q: Who discovered the magnetic effect of current?
quiz.why: Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle. This showed its magnetic effect.

quiz.q: A compass needle near a wire deflects when
quiz.why: A current produces a magnetic field around the wire, so the compass needle deflects only when current flows.

options: a coil around an iron core with current
quiz.why: An electromagnet is a coil of wire wound on an iron core. It behaves like a magnet when current passes.
An electromagnet is a temporary magnet. It works only while current flows, and loses magnetism when current stops.

quiz.q: Used in cranes to lift scrap
quiz.why: Cranes use strong electromagnets to lift scrap iron. The magnet can be switched on to pick up and off to drop it.

scenes.text: The school bell rings at the end of the period.
Inside the cover: a coil, an iron strip with a hammer, a gong and a contact screw.
An electromagnet switches itself on and off many times a second.

steps.title: Parts
steps.body: Coil of wire wound on an iron piece (electromagnet), an **iron strip (armature)** with a **hammer**, a **gong**, and a **contact screw** touching the strip to complete the circuit.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body:
1. Press the switch: current flows through the coil; it becomes an electromagnet.
2. It pulls the iron strip; the hammer strikes the gong.
3. As the strip moves, it **loses contact with the screw** — the circuit breaks, the coil stops being a magnet.
4. The strip springs back, touches the screw again, the circuit completes, and the cycle repeats rapidly — the bell rings continuously.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: What would happen if the contact screw always touched the strip even when attracted?

A: The coil would stay magnetised, the hammer would stay pressed on the gong, and the bell would ring only once (a single 'clunk').

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Is the heating effect or magnetic effect used in a bell? → **Magnetic effect** (electromagnet).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the hammer is moved by a motor; the electromagnet does it.
- Forgetting the role of the contact screw in breaking and making the circuit.

activity.prompt: Order the working of an electric bell.
items: Switch is pressed and current flows in the coil
Coil becomes an electromagnet and attracts the iron strip
Hammer strikes the gong
Strip loses contact with the screw; circuit breaks
Coil stops being a magnet; strip springs back
Contact is made again and the cycle repeats

quiz.why: An electric bell works on the magnetic effect of current: an electromagnet pulls the iron strip, so the hammer hits the gong.

quiz.q: The part struck by the hammer
quiz.why: The hammer strikes the gong, which is a metal bowl, and makes the ringing sound.

quiz.q: Circuit breaks in a bell when
options: strip moves away from contact screw
quiz.why: When the electromagnet pulls the strip, it moves away from the contact screw and breaks the circuit. The magnet turns off, and the strip springs back, so it vibrates.

quiz.q: The coil in a bell is wound on
quiz.why: The coil is wound on an iron core so that it becomes a strong electromagnet when current flows.

quiz.q: Without the contact screw breaking the circuit, the bell would
quiz.why: If the circuit did not break, the electromagnet would keep the strip pulled. The hammer would hit once and stay pressed instead of ringing again and again.

questions.q: Device that breaks a circuit when current is too high
questions.why: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit if the current gets too high. This protects appliances from damage and fire.

questions.q: In a cell symbol, the longer line is
questions.why: The longer line in the symbol of a cell is its positive terminal.

questions.q: Current-carrying wire deflects a
questions.why: A wire carrying current makes a magnetic field and deflects a compass needle. Paper, wood and glass are not affected.

questions.q: Coil of a heater is the
questions.why: The coil that heats up in a heater is called the element.

questions.q: Combination of two or more cells
questions.why: Two or more cells joined together make a battery.

questions.q: An electromagnet is
questions.why: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet. It acts as a magnet only while current flows.

questions.q: Electric bell uses
questions.why: An electric bell uses an electromagnet. It pulls an iron strip with the hammer on it to hit the gong.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A fuse must not be replaced by a copper wire. Reason (R): Copper wire will not melt at the safe current limit, so it gives no protection.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: a copper wire must not replace a fuse. R is true: copper has a high melting point, so it does not melt when current is too high and gives no protection. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): An electromagnet attracts pins even after current is switched off. Reason (R): Iron is magnetic.
questions.why: A is false: an electromagnet loses its magnetism once the current is off, so it drops the pins. R is true that iron is magnetic, but it does not support A.

questions.q: Which is NOT based on the heating effect?
questions.why: Iron, toaster and geyser use the heating effect of current. The electric bell works on the magnetic effect.

questions.q: To increase the strength of an electromagnet
questions.why: More turns of wire give a stronger magnetic field, so a stronger electromagnet. A wooden core or less current would weaken it.

questions.q: Case: A student's torch has two cells but only one glows the bulb dimly. She finds both cells placed with positive terminals touching. Fix?
questions.why: Cells must be joined positive to negative, so the + of one touches the − of the next. Two touching positives work against each other.

questions.q: Case: In a house, the MCB trips whenever a heater, geyser and iron run together on one line. Most likely reason?
questions.why: Many high-power appliances on one line draw too much current. This is overloading, so the MCB trips to prevent overheating.

questions.q: Why do incandescent bulbs waste electricity?
questions.why: In an incandescent bulb the filament becomes very hot, and much of the electric energy is lost as heat, not light.

questions.q: In a circuit with a cell, a switch and a bulb, the bulb glows but a nearby compass also deflects. This shows
questions.why: The glowing bulb shows the heating effect and the deflected compass shows the magnetic effect. So both happen in the same circuit.

questions.q: An electric bell rings continuously only because
options: the contact screw repeatedly breaks and makes the circuit
questions.why: In the bell the circuit keeps breaking at the contact screw and making again. This makes the hammer hit the gong again and again.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Light
courses.summary: Light travels in straight lines; reflection and images in plane mirrors (including left–right inversion); concave and convex mirrors and lenses, the images they form and their uses; and how white sunlight splits into seven colours.
outcomes: Learners can describe the image formed by a plane mirror
Learners can distinguish concave and convex mirrors and their uses
Learners can distinguish convex and concave lenses and their images
Learners can explain dispersion of white light and the rainbow

lessons.title: Straight lines, reflection and plane mirrors

scenes.text: Paheli sees an ambulance with the word written as ƎƆИA⅃UBMA on its front.
In her rear-view mirror it reads correctly — AMBULANCE!
Mirrors swap left and right; the word is written reversed so drivers ahead read it properly.

steps.title: Light travels in a straight line
steps.body: Look at a candle through a straight pipe: you can see it. Bend the pipe: you cannot. This shows **light travels along straight lines**.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.body: When light falls on a shiny, smooth surface like a **mirror**, it bounces back in a definite direction. This is **reflection**. A mirror changes the direction of light falling on it.

steps.title: Image in a plane mirror
steps.body:
- **Erect** (upright)
- **Same size** as the object
- As far **behind** the mirror as the object is **in front** of it
- **Virtual** (cannot be obtained on a screen)
- **Laterally inverted**: left appears right and right appears left

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Ravi stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is his image from him?

- Image is 2 m behind the mirror
- Distance from Ravi = 2 + 2 = **4 m**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: You raise your right hand in front of a mirror. Which hand does your image raise?

A: It appears to raise its **left** hand — lateral inversion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the image is 'on the mirror surface' — it is behind the mirror.
- Thinking a plane mirror image can be caught on a screen.

statements.s: A plane mirror image is erect.
The image is larger than the object.
A plane mirror image can be obtained on a screen.
Left and right appear swapped in a plane mirror.
Light travels in curved paths in air.

quiz.q: Object 3 m in front of a plane mirror; image distance from mirror
quiz.why: In a plane mirror the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. So the image is 3 m from the mirror.

quiz.q: Bouncing back of light from a surface
quiz.why: Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface. Refraction is bending, and dispersion is splitting into colours.

quiz.q: Image in a plane mirror is
quiz.why: The image in a plane mirror is virtual (cannot be caught on a screen) and erect (upright).

quiz.q: Why is AMBULANCE written in reverse?
options: so drivers read it correctly in rear-view mirrors
quiz.why: A mirror swaps left and right (lateral inversion). Writing AMBULANCE reversed lets drivers read it correctly in the rear-view mirror.
You can see the candle only when the pipe is straight. This shows light travels in straight lines.

scenes.text: Boojho looks into the inner side of a shiny spoon: his face is upside down when far, big when close!
On the outer side, his face is always upright but small.
The spoon is a curved mirror — concave inside, convex outside.

steps.title: Two kinds
steps.body:
A spherical mirror's reflecting surface is curved, like part of a hollow sphere.

- **Concave mirror**: reflecting surface curves **inward** (like the inside of a spoon).
- **Convex mirror**: reflecting surface bulges **outward** (back of a spoon).

steps.title: Images
steps.body:
- **Concave**: an object close to it gives an **erect, magnified, virtual** image. An object far away gives a **real, inverted** image that can be obtained on a screen; its size depends on distance.
- **Convex**: image is always **erect, diminished (smaller), virtual** — and it shows a **wider area**.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Concave**: doctors examining eyes, ears, nose, throat; dentists to see enlarged teeth; reflectors in **torches, headlights** of cars and scooters; shaving mirrors.
- **Convex**: **side/rear-view mirrors** of vehicles (wide view of traffic behind); at sharp road bends; in shops for security.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why are convex mirrors used as side mirrors in vehicles?

A: They always form erect, smaller images and show a much wider area of traffic behind.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Sunlight is focused by a concave mirror onto a paper; the paper starts burning. Why?

A: The concave mirror converges sunlight to a point, concentrating heat. (Do not try this without an adult — it can start a fire and never look at the Sun.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying convex mirrors can form real images on a screen — they cannot.
- Mixing up which side of a spoon is concave.

activity.prompt: Match the use to the mirror.
pairs: Mirror at a sharp hill-road bend

quiz.q: Inside of a shiny spoon acts as a
quiz.why: The inside of a shiny spoon curves inward, so it acts like a concave mirror. The outside bulges out like a convex mirror.

quiz.q: Image in a convex mirror is always
quiz.why: A convex mirror always gives an erect, smaller (diminished) and virtual image.

quiz.q: Which mirror can form a real image on a screen?
quiz.why: Only a concave mirror can form a real image that can be caught on a screen. Plane and convex mirrors give virtual images.
Headlights use concave mirrors as reflectors. A bulb at the right point sends a strong beam ahead.

quiz.q: Wider field of view is given by
quiz.why: A convex mirror gives a wider field of view, since it shows a larger area in a small image.

scenes.text: Grandpa reads tiny print on a medicine strip with a magnifying glass.
The glass is thicker in the middle than at the edges.
It is a convex lens; it makes the letters look bigger.

steps.title: Lenses
steps.body:
A lens is a piece of transparent glass (or plastic) with curved surfaces. Light passes **through** a lens (it does not reflect it).

- **Convex lens**: **thicker in the middle** than at the edges; **converging** — bends light rays inward.
- **Concave lens**: **thinner in the middle**; **diverging** — spreads rays outward.

steps.title: Images
steps.body:
- **Convex lens**: near object → **erect, magnified, virtual** image (magnifying glass). Distant object → **real, inverted** image on a screen (size depends on distance).
- **Concave lens**: image is always **erect, smaller, virtual**.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body: Spectacles, telescopes, microscopes, cameras, magnifying glasses, projectors. Our **eye** contains a convex lens.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How can you tell a convex lens from a concave one by touch? → Convex is thicker at the centre; concave is thinner at the centre.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: A lens forms an image of a distant tree upside down on a screen. Which lens? → **Convex** (only it forms real images).

steps.title: Safety and mistakes
steps.body:
- **Never look at the Sun or a bright light directly or through a lens or mirror** — it can damage the eyes.
- Do not leave a convex lens in sunlight on paper or dry leaves; it can start a fire.
- Mixing up mirrors (reflect) and lenses (let light pass through).

items.text: Can form a real image on a screen

quiz.why: A magnifying glass is a convex lens, thicker in the middle. It makes objects look bigger when held close.
A concave lens is thinner at the middle and spreads light rays out, so it is diverging.

quiz.q: Image formed by a concave lens is
quiz.why: A concave lens always gives an erect, virtual and smaller image.
The eye has a convex lens that focuses light onto the retina.
Lenses let light pass through and bend it. Mirrors reflect it.

scenes.text: After a shower, with the Sun behind her, Paheli sees a rainbow.
Seven colours in a curve — red on the outside, violet inside.
In class, a glass prism shows the same colours from a beam of sunlight.

steps.title: Dispersion
steps.body: White light (sunlight) is a mixture of **seven colours**: **violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red** (VIBGYOR). A **prism** splits white light into these colours. Splitting of light into its colours is **dispersion**.

steps.title: Rainbow
steps.body: A **rainbow** is seen after rain when the Sun is behind you: tiny water drops in the air act like prisms and split sunlight into colours. Rainbows show the same seven colours.

steps.title: Newton's disc
steps.body: A disc divided into seven sectors painted with the rainbow colours. When spun fast, it looks nearly **white**, showing that the seven colours together make white light.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why does a CD's surface show colours in sunlight? → Its surface splits white light into colours (like a prism).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: When can you see a rainbow? → After rain, when the Sun is low in the sky behind you and water drops are in front of you.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the prism 'adds colour' to light — the colours were already in white light.
- Getting the order wrong — remember VIBGYOR.

activity.prompt: Arrange the colours of white light in order (VIBGYOR).
items: Violet
Indigo
Blue
Green
Yellow
Orange
Red

quiz.q: Number of colours in white light
quiz.why: White light is made of 7 colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR).

quiz.q: Splitting of white light into colours
quiz.why: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours, as a prism does.
On a quickly spinning Newton's disc the colours blend, and the disc looks white or whitish.
A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through water droplets. They split it into colours, like tiny prisms.

quiz.q: To see a rainbow, the Sun should be
quiz.why: To see a rainbow the Sun must be behind you, and the water droplets in front of you.

questions.q: Light travels in
questions.why: Light travels in straight lines. That is why we get sharp shadows.

questions.q: Plane mirror image is
questions.why: A plane mirror image is erect. It is also virtual and the same size, but swapped left to right.

questions.q: Vehicle side mirrors are
questions.why: Side mirrors of vehicles are convex. They give a wider field of view of the road behind.

questions.q: Number of rainbow colours
questions.why: A rainbow shows 7 colours in order: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red.

questions.q: Magnifying glass uses a
questions.why: A magnifying glass is a convex lens, which makes an enlarged image of a close object.

questions.q: Lateral inversion means
questions.why: Lateral inversion means the left and right sides appear swapped in a mirror. It is not upside down.

questions.q: Real image can be formed by
questions.why: A concave mirror can form a real image that can be caught on a screen. Plane and convex mirrors give only virtual images, and a concave lens as well.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Dentists use concave mirrors. Reason (R): An object close to a concave mirror gives an enlarged erect image.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: dentists use concave mirrors. R is true: a close object gives an enlarged, erect image, so the teeth look bigger. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A concave lens can form an image on a screen. Reason (R): A concave lens is thinner at the centre.
questions.why: A is false: a concave lens always gives a virtual image, which cannot be caught on a screen. R is true: it is thinner at the centre, but it does not support A.

questions.q: A girl stands 1.5 m from a plane mirror and walks 0.5 m towards it. Distance between her and her image now
questions.why: After walking, she is 1.5 − 0.5 = 1 m from the mirror. Her image is 1 m behind it, so the distance between them is 1 + 1 = 2 m.

questions.q: Which forms a wider view of traffic?
questions.why: A convex mirror gives a wider field of view, so it is used to see a larger part of the traffic behind.

questions.q: Case: A student holds a lens over a page and the letters look bigger and upright. Then at arm's length the window looks upside down through it. The lens is
questions.why: Close up it magnifies and gives an upright image. A distant object appears inverted. This is how a convex lens behaves.

questions.q: Case: A shopkeeper fixes a curved mirror at a corner to watch the whole shop. Type of mirror?
questions.why: A convex mirror shows a wide area, so a shopkeeper can watch the whole shop in it.

questions.q: Which colour is at the top (outside) of a rainbow?
questions.why: In a rainbow the red band is on the outer (top) edge, and violet is on the inner edge.

questions.q: An object is placed far from a concave mirror and the screen shows a small image. The image is
questions.why: A concave mirror forms a small, real and inverted image of a distant object, and it can be caught on a screen.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to look at the Sun through a lens?
options: Lens concentrates light and can damage the eye
questions.why: A lens can focus sunlight into a tiny bright spot. Looking at the Sun through it concentrates harmful light and heat onto the eye and can damage the retina.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Forests: Our Lifeline
courses.summary: What a forest is made of, its layers and living partners, food chains and decomposers, how forests give oxygen, rain, soil and products, and what happens when they disappear.
outcomes: Learners can describe the layers and components of a forest
Learners can build food chains and explain the role of decomposers and humus
Learners can explain why forests are called green lungs and how they help rain and soil
Learners can explain the effects of deforestation and ways to conserve forests

lessons.title: Inside a forest: layers and life

story.title: A walk with a forest guard

scenes.text: On a school trip, a forest guard leads the class into the forest.
Tall trees form a roof of branches high above — the canopy.
Below are shrubs, herbs, climbers, deer, insects, birds, mushrooms… a whole world!

steps.title: What a forest is
steps.body: A **forest** is a system of plants, animals and micro-organisms living together. Trees are its main plants (sal, teak, semal, sheesham, neem, palash, fig, khair, amla, bamboo, kachnar…). Animals include boar, bison, jackal, porcupine, elephant, deer, birds, insects.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
- **Crown**: branchy part of a tree above the stem.
- **Canopy**: the roof formed by branches of tall trees.
- **Understorey**: shrubs and smaller trees below.
- **Herbs** and ground plants form the lowest layer.

Different layers get different amounts of sunlight, so different plants and animals live in each layer.

steps.title: A forest keeps renewing
steps.body: Seeds germinate, young trees grow, old ones fall and decay. A forest is **dynamic** — always growing and changing.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do the lowest layers of a forest stay dark and cool?

A: The dense canopy blocks much of the sunlight.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name the layers from top to bottom. → Canopy (tall tree crowns) → understorey (shrubs, short trees) → herbs and the forest floor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a forest is just a group of trees — it includes animals, micro-organisms, soil and water.
- Confusing crown (one tree's branches) with canopy (roof formed by many crowns).

activity.prompt: Arrange forest layers from top to bottom.
items: Canopy of tall trees
Understorey of shrubs and small trees
Herbs and ground plants
Forest floor with dead leaves and humus

quiz.q: Roof formed by branches of tall trees
quiz.why: The canopy is the roof formed by the spreading branches of tall trees. The crown is the branchy part of one tree.

quiz.q: Branchy part of a tree above the stem
quiz.why: The crown is the branchy part of a tree above the stem. The canopy is the layer formed by many crowns together.
A forest is a whole system of plants, animals and micro-organisms that depend on each other, not only trees.
The canopy blocks most sunlight, so the forest floor gets the least light. That is why shade-loving plants grow there.
A forest is dynamic because it keeps growing, changing and renewing itself as plants grow, die and decay and new ones appear.

scenes.text: Grass is eaten by a deer; the deer is hunted by a tiger.
When the tiger dies, beetles, fungi and bacteria break its body down.
Nutrients go back to the soil, and grass grows again. Nothing goes waste in a forest!

steps.title: Food chains
steps.body:
Plants are **producers**; animals are **consumers** (herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat other animals).

- Grass → insects → frog → snake → eagle
- Grass → deer → tiger

Many food chains link to form a **food web**. Each organism depends on others.

steps.title: Decomposers and humus
steps.body: Micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi) and small animals that convert dead plants and animals into a dark-coloured substance called **humus** are **decomposers**. Humus makes soil fertile and holds water. Dead leaves on the forest floor decompose quickly in warm, moist conditions.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Make a food chain with these: snake, grass, eagle, insect, frog. → **Grass → insect → frog → snake → eagle**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: What happens if all decomposers vanish?

A: Dead bodies and leaves would pile up, nutrients would not return to soil, and plants would not get enough nutrients.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting a food chain with an animal — it starts with a producer (plant).
- Thinking decomposers are harmful — they recycle nutrients.

items: Grass
Insect
Frog
Snake
Eagle

quiz.why: Plants are producers, as they make food from sunlight. So every food chain begins with them, and herbivores and carnivores come after.
Humus is the dark, fertile substance formed when decomposers break down dead plants and animals.
Fungi and bacteria are decomposers. They break down dead plants and animals into simpler substances.
A deer feeds on plants, so it is a herbivore. A carnivore eats other animals.

quiz.q: Many interlinked food chains form a
quiz.why: Many food chains linked together in a forest form a food web.

lessons.title: Forests as green lungs: air, rain and soil

scenes.text: In a village near a forest, the river runs clear even in monsoon.
Downstream, where the forest was cut, the river turns muddy and floods.
Tree roots hold the soil; forests also help bring rain.

steps.title: Green lungs
steps.body: Plants release **oxygen** in photosynthesis and use **carbon dioxide**. Animals and plants use oxygen for respiration. Forests help **maintain the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide** in the air, so they are called **green lungs**.

steps.title: Rain and climate
steps.body: Trees release water vapour by **transpiration**, which helps form clouds and bring **rain**. Forests also keep the area cooler and moderate the climate.

steps.title: Soil and water
steps.body:
- Tree roots **bind soil** and prevent **soil erosion**.
- The forest floor and humus act like a **sponge**, soaking rainwater, which seeps into the ground and recharges groundwater.
- This reduces **floods** and keeps rivers flowing steadily.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why are floods more common in areas where forests have been cut?

A: Without trees and humus, rainwater runs off quickly instead of soaking in, and carries soil with it.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do forests help in rain? → Transpiration adds water vapour to the air, which helps cloud formation and rainfall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking forests only provide wood — they also provide air balance, water, soil protection and homes for wildlife.
- Believing rain depends only on oceans — local forests contribute water vapour too.

statements.s: Forests are called green lungs.
Tree roots increase soil erosion.
Forests help recharge groundwater.
Transpiration from trees can help bring rain.
Cutting forests reduces floods.

quiz.q: Forests are called green lungs because they
quiz.why: Forests take in CO₂ and release oxygen in photosynthesis, which helps balance these gases in the air. So they are called green lungs.
Roots bind the soil and hold it in place. So they prevent soil erosion by wind and water.
The forest floor, with its humus and leaf litter, soaks up rain like a sponge and releases it slowly.

quiz.q: Water vapour from leaves is released by
quiz.why: Plants lose water vapour from their leaves by transpiration. In a forest this adds a lot of moisture to the air.
Without trees, rain washes the soil away and floods become more likely. Deforestation therefore leads to more floods and soil erosion.

scenes.text: Tibu lives in a village near a forest. His family collects honey, tendu leaves, fruits and medicinal herbs.
A plan to clear part of the forest for a factory worries the village.
The villagers meet the officials: they want to protect the forest that protects them.

steps.title: What forests give
steps.body:
- Wood (timber, firewood), bamboo, paper
- **Gum, resin, honey, lac, sealing wax**, catechu, katha
- **Medicinal plants**, spices, fruits, fodder
- Homes (habitat) for wild animals; livelihood for forest dwellers and many communities

steps.title: Dangers
steps.body: **Deforestation** (cutting forests for farms, buildings, roads, industries) causes loss of wildlife, soil erosion, floods, less rain locally, higher CO₂ in the air and harm to forest-dwelling people.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body:
- Plant trees and protect young saplings
- Use paper wisely, recycle, reduce wood use
- Protected areas: national parks and wildlife sanctuaries
- Respect the rights and knowledge of forest communities, who often protect forests best
- Prevent forest fires

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Give two reasons why forest-dwelling communities depend on forests.

A: (1) Food, fuel and medicines; (2) livelihood from honey, leaves, bamboo and other forest products.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How does saving paper help forests? → Less paper means fewer trees cut for wood pulp.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking planting trees anywhere fully replaces an old forest — natural forests have complex layers and species that take decades to develop.
- Forgetting the human side: forest communities are part of the forest.

items: Plant or water a sapling
Use both sides of notebook pages
Send old newspapers for recycling
Learn the names of 5 trees in my area
Avoid wasting wooden pencils
Tell my family why forests matter

quiz.why: Honey is a forest product. Glass, plastic and steel are made in factories.
Deforestation means cutting down or clearing forests on a large scale.
Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks are protected areas where wild animals and plants are kept safe.
Paper is made from wood pulp. Saving paper means fewer trees need to be cut.

quiz.q: Forest dwellers depend on forests for
quiz.why: People living in forests get food, fuel, medicines and a livelihood from them. Forests also give them shelter.

questions.q: Roof of tall tree branches in a forest
questions.why: The roof formed by the branches of tall trees is the canopy.

questions.q: Dark fertile substance from decomposed matter
questions.why: Humus is the dark, fertile substance made when dead plants and animals decompose.

questions.q: A food chain starts with
questions.why: A food chain starts with plants, the producers, which make food. Animals and decomposers come later.

questions.q: Forests are called
questions.why: Forests are called green lungs because they take in CO₂ and give out oxygen, helping balance these gases.

questions.q: Decomposers include
questions.why: Bacteria and fungi break down dead matter, and they are the decomposers. Grass is a producer, and deer and lions are consumers.

questions.q: Tree roots help prevent
questions.why: Tree roots hold the soil together, so rain and wind cannot easily wash it away. They prevent soil erosion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a forest product?
questions.why: Lac, honey and gum are collected from forests. Plastic is made in factories from chemicals, so it is not a forest product.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Forests reduce floods. Reason (R): Humus and forest floor soak up rainwater.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: forests reduce floods. R is true: humus and the forest floor soak up rainwater like a sponge, so less runs off. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A food chain can start with a tiger. Reason (R): Tigers are carnivores.
questions.why: A is false: a food chain starts with a producer, which is a plant. R is true that tigers are carnivores, but that is why they come at the end.

questions.q: Correct food chain
questions.why: In a food chain, energy goes from producer to herbivore to carnivore. So grass is eaten by deer, and deer by tiger. The arrows point to the eater.

questions.q: Forest helps in rainfall mainly by
questions.why: Trees release water vapour by transpiration, which adds moisture to the air and helps form clouds and rain.

questions.q: Case: A hill slope was cleared of trees. Next monsoon, the stream below became muddy. Reason?
options: Soil washed down due to no roots binding it
questions.why: With the trees gone, no roots bind the soil. Monsoon rain washes it down the slope into the stream, making it muddy.

questions.q: Case: If all the deer in a forest were hunted, what would happen to tigers and grass?
questions.why: Tigers eat deer, so they would lose food and decline. With fewer deer to eat it, the grass may grow too much.

questions.q: Why are decomposers called the cleaning agents of the forest?
options: They break down dead matter and recycle nutrients
questions.why: Decomposers break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil. This clears the forest of dead matter and recycles nutrients.

questions.q: Increasing deforestation leads to more CO₂ in the air because
options: fewer trees absorb CO₂ in photosynthesis
questions.why: Trees take in CO₂ for photosynthesis. With fewer trees, less CO₂ is removed from the air, so more stays in it.

questions.q: Which layer of a forest would shade-loving herbs prefer?
questions.why: Shade-loving herbs need little light. The forest floor and lower layers get the least sunlight, so they grow there.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Wastewater Story
courses.summary: What sewage contains, how the sewerage network carries it, step-by-step treatment in a wastewater treatment plant, what we should never pour down the drain, and sanitation solutions where there are no sewers.
outcomes: Learners can describe what sewage is and what it contains
Learners can explain each stage of a wastewater treatment plant
Learners can practise good housekeeping to reduce pollution of wastewater
Learners can describe sanitation options and their link to health

story.title: Where does the bath water go?

scenes.text: After her bath, Paheli watches the water swirl down the drain.
"Where does it go? Does it come back to our tap?"
Her teacher shows a map of underground pipes leading to a treatment plant outside the city.

steps.title: Our lifeline
steps.body: Clean water is essential, yet many people lack access to safe water. **World Water Day** is observed on **22 March** each year to draw attention to this. Cleaning water before it re-enters water bodies is called **sewage treatment** or wastewater treatment.

steps.title: What sewage is
steps.body:
**Sewage** is wastewater released by homes, industries, hospitals, offices and other users; it also includes rainwater that runs down streets carrying harmful substances. It is a complex mixture:

- **Organic impurities**: human faeces, animal waste, oil, urea (urine), pesticides, herbicides, fruit and vegetable waste
- **Inorganic impurities**: nitrates, phosphates, metals
- **Nutrients**: phosphorus, nitrogen
- **Bacteria**: e.g. those causing cholera and typhoid
- **Other microbes**: e.g. those causing dysentery

steps.title: Sewerage
steps.body: A network of big and small pipes called **sewers** forming the **sewerage** carries sewage from where it is produced to the point of disposal (treatment plant). **Manholes** are placed at intervals (about 50–60 m) and at junctions so workers can access the sewers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Name two organic and two inorganic impurities in sewage.

A: Organic: human faeces, food waste. Inorganic: nitrates, phosphates (or metals).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: What is the difference between sewage and sewerage?

A: Sewage is the wastewater itself; sewerage is the network of pipes that carries it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking wastewater is 'just dirty water' — it carries disease-causing microbes and chemicals.
- Mixing up sewage (liquid) and sewer (pipe).

quiz.why: World Water Day is observed every year on 22 March. It reminds us to save and protect water.
Sewage is the dirty wastewater from homes, industries, hospitals and other places. It needs treatment before it is released.
Sewerage is the network of pipes that carries sewage. Sewage is the waste itself, and sludge is the solid settled part.
Nitrates are inorganic impurities in sewage. Faeces, food waste and urea come from living things, so they are organic.

options: access sewers for cleaning and repair
quiz.why: Manholes let workers go down to inspect, clean and repair the sewer pipes.

story.title: A visit to the treatment plant

scenes.text: The class visits a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP).
First, big screens catch rags, sticks, plastic bags and cans.
At the end of a long journey, the water leaving the plant is clear enough to be released into a river.

steps.title: Physical stages
steps.body:
1. **Bar screens**: remove large objects — rags, sticks, cans, plastic packets, napkins.
2. **Grit and sand removal tank**: wastewater flows slowly so sand, grit and pebbles settle.
3. **Primary clarifier (large settling tank)**: solids like faeces settle at the bottom as **sludge**, scraped out by a scraper; a **skimmer** removes floating **oil and grease**. The water left is **clarified water**.

steps.title: Biological stage
steps.body:
4. **Aeration tank**: air is pumped into the clarified water to help **aerobic bacteria** grow. They consume human waste, food waste, soaps and other unwanted matter.
5. After several hours, the microbes settle as **activated sludge** (about 97% water). Water is removed by sand drying beds or machines; the dried sludge is used as **manure**.
6. Treated water has very low levels of organic material and suspended matter. It is discharged into a sea, river or ground. Sometimes it is **disinfected with chlorine and ozone** first.

steps.title: Sludge and biogas
steps.body: Sludge from the settling tank is transferred to a separate tank where **anaerobic bacteria** decompose it, producing **biogas**, which can be used as fuel or to produce electricity.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Arrange: aeration tank, bar screen, primary clarifier, grit chamber. → **Bar screen → grit and sand removal → primary clarifier → aeration tank**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why is air bubbled through the clarified water?

A: To support aerobic bacteria that consume the remaining organic waste.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking treatment makes water fit to drink directly — it is made safe to release; drinking water needs further purification.
- Mixing aerobic bacteria (aeration tank) with anaerobic bacteria (biogas from sludge).

activity.prompt: Order the stages of wastewater treatment.
items: Bar screens remove large objects
Grit and sand removal tank
Primary clarifier: sludge settles, skimmer removes oil
Aeration tank: aerobic bacteria digest waste
Activated sludge settles and is removed
Treated water disinfected and released

quiz.why: Bar screens are the first step in treatment. They remove large objects such as rags, sticks and plastic.

quiz.q: Floating oil and grease are removed by a
quiz.why: A skimmer removes floating oil and grease from the top of the water. A bar screen takes out large objects.
Air is pumped into the water so that aerobic bacteria, which need oxygen, can grow and break down the waste.
Activated sludge is mostly water, about 97%. The rest is solid matter that settles out.

quiz.q: Biogas is produced from sludge by
quiz.why: Anaerobic bacteria break down sludge without oxygen. This gives biogas, which can be used as fuel.

quiz.q: Treated water may be disinfected with
quiz.why: After treatment the water can be disinfected with chlorine or ozone, which kill the germs that remain.

lessons.title: Better housekeeping: what not to pour down the drain

scenes.text: Every day, Mother poured leftover frying oil into the kitchen sink.
One morning the drain was completely blocked!
The plumber explained: oil hardens in pipes. Wipe it with paper and throw it in the dustbin.

steps.title: Keep out of drains
steps.body:
- **Cooking oil and fats**: harden and block pipes; in open drains they clog soil pores and reduce filtering.
- **Chemicals** (paints, solvents, insecticides, motor oil, medicines): kill the useful microbes that purify water.
- **Solid wastes**: tea leaves, food remains, cotton, soft toys, sanitary towels — block drains and stop oxygen flowing, hampering treatment.

Throw them in the dustbin or give them for proper disposal.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Less pollution at the source means easier, cheaper treatment and cleaner rivers. **Reduce, reuse, recycle**: use wastewater from washing vegetables to water plants.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why should medicines not be flushed?

A: They kill helpful microbes in treatment plants and can pollute rivers.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How can a family reduce wastewater pollution? → Wipe greasy pans before washing, put food scraps in a compost bin, store old paint for safe disposal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking hot water carries oil safely away — it cools and sticks further down the pipe.
- Flushing wet wipes or cotton because they 'disappear' — they block sewers.

quiz.why: Cooking oil and fat cool and harden inside the pipes. They stick and build up, blocking the drains.
Chemicals like paint kill the useful microbes that clean the water. This makes treatment harder.
Tea leaves are solid waste and would block pipes. They belong in the dustbin or compost, not the sink or toilet.

quiz.q: Water used for washing vegetables can be
quiz.why: Water used to wash vegetables is fairly clean. It can be reused to water plants, which saves water.
Wet wipes do not break down easily and clog sewers. They should go in the dustbin.

scenes.text: Ramnagar village has no sewer pipes. People used to defecate in the open.
Every monsoon, cholera and diarrhoea spread from contaminated water.
With toilets connected to septic tanks and composting pits, illness fell sharply.

steps.title: Open defecation and health
steps.body: Untreated human excreta pollutes soil and water, including groundwater. It is a major cause of diseases like **cholera, typhoid, polio, meningitis, hepatitis and dysentery**. Proper sanitation is essential for public health.

steps.title: Low-cost onsite sanitation
steps.body:
Where there is no sewerage:

- **Septic tanks**: for places without sewers (hospitals, isolated buildings, small groups of houses).
- **Chemical toilets**: e.g. in trains, buses and events.
- **Composting pits**.
- **Vermi-processing toilets**: human excreta is treated by **earthworms**, producing high-quality manure (vermi cakes); the design has been tried in India.
- Some plants link toilets to **biogas plants**, producing energy from excreta.

steps.title: Sanitation in public places
steps.body: Fairs, railway stations, bus depots, airports and hospitals produce large amounts of waste. Proper disposal and clean toilets are essential to prevent epidemics. **We must not litter, spit or urinate in public places.** Planting **eucalyptus trees** along sewage ponds is suggested because they absorb surplus wastewater rapidly and release pure water vapour into the air.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How do vermi-processing toilets work? → Earthworms feed on and break down human waste, turning it into manure.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why should a railway station keep toilets clean and drains covered?

A: Thousands of people pass daily; dirty toilets and open waste spread disease quickly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking open defecation affects only the person — it pollutes water for the whole community.
- Believing sanitation is only the government's job; each of us must use toilets, keep surroundings clean and wash hands with soap.

items: I always use a toilet and flush/clean it
I wash my hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating
I never throw solid waste into drains
I do not litter or spit in public places
I keep drinking water covered
I report open drains or overflowing sewers to adults/authorities

quiz.q: Diseases spread by poor sanitation include
quiz.why: Poor sanitation lets germs reach drinking water, causing water-borne diseases like cholera and typhoid. Myopia, sunburn and fractures are not caused by it.

quiz.q: Toilets in which earthworms treat excreta
quiz.why: Vermi-processing toilets use earthworms to break down excreta. They are a low-cost way to treat waste on site.
Eucalyptus trees take up a lot of water, so planting them near sewage ponds helps absorb the extra water.
Septic tanks treat waste on site, so they are useful where there is no sewer network.
Untreated excreta can seep into the soil and pollute groundwater, which people may then drink or use, spreading disease.

questions.q: Wastewater from homes and industries is called
questions.why: Wastewater from homes and industries is called sewage. Sewerage is the pipe system, and sludge is the settled solid part.

questions.q: First step in a WWTP
questions.why: Bar screens come first in a treatment plant. They take out large objects before the later steps.

questions.q: World Water Day
questions.why: World Water Day is on 22 March each year.

questions.q: Gas produced from sludge
questions.why: When anaerobic bacteria break down sludge, they give out biogas. It can be used as fuel.

questions.q: Skimmer removes
questions.why: A skimmer takes off oil and grease that float on top of the water. Heavier solids settle instead.

questions.q: Aerobic bacteria are encouraged in the
questions.why: The aeration tank has air pumped in, so aerobic bacteria can grow there. They digest the waste.

questions.q: Dried sludge is used as
