questions.why: Banda Bahadur was a Sikh leader, not a Maratha. Churaman was a Jat, Murshid Quli Khan ruled Bengal and Asaf Jah founded Hyderabad.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Environment (Geography)
courses.summary: What the environment is, its natural components — lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere — ecosystems, the human environment, and how human needs and technology have changed our surroundings.
outcomes: Learners can name and describe the four domains of the natural environment
Learners can explain what an ecosystem is with examples
Learners can distinguish natural, human-made and human environments
Learners can explain how humans modify the environment and why balance matters

scenes.text: At a lakeside picnic, Riya notices rocks, water, the breeze and birds.
Her father says: "Land, water, air and living things — together they make our environment."
Each part depends on the others.

steps.title: What is environment?
steps.body: **Environment** is everything around us — the place, people, things and nature that surround a living organism. It is a combination of **natural** (land, water, air, plants, animals) and **human-made** (buildings, roads, parks, bridges, industries) things.

steps.title: Four domains
steps.body:
- **Lithosphere**: the solid crust or hard top layer of the Earth — rocks and minerals, covered by a thin layer of soil. Landforms: mountains, plateaus, plains, valleys. It gives forests, grasslands, agricultural land, human settlements and minerals.
- **Hydrosphere**: domain of water — rivers, lakes, seas, oceans, estuaries.
- **Atmosphere**: thin layer of air surrounding the Earth, held by gravity; protects us from the harmful rays and scorching heat of the Sun.
- **Biosphere**: the narrow zone where land, water and air interact and life exists — the plant kingdom and the animal kingdom.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classify: a mountain, a river, oxygen, a tiger → lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why is the biosphere described as a narrow zone? → Life exists only where land, water and air meet and support each other — a thin layer near the Earth's surface.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the atmosphere is only oxygen; it is a mixture of gases.
- Forgetting humans are part of the biosphere.

quiz.why: The lithosphere is the solid crust of the Earth, made of rocks and soil.
The hydrosphere is the domain of water, including oceans, rivers and lakes.
The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and life exists.

quiz.q: The atmosphere is held around the Earth by
quiz.why: The Earth's gravity holds the atmosphere around it, so air does not escape into space.
A bridge is built by people, so it is human-made. A forest, mountain and river are natural.

scenes.text: In a small pond, fish eat insects, frogs eat insects, herons eat fish and frogs.
Water plants make food using sunlight; bacteria break down dead matter.
The pond is an ecosystem — living things and their surroundings working together.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: All plants, animals and human beings depend on their immediate surroundings and are often interrelated. A system formed by the interaction of all living organisms with each other and with the physical and chemical factors of the environment is an **ecosystem**.

steps.title: Examples and sizes
steps.body: Ecosystems can be large or small: a pond, a forest, a desert, grassland, an ocean, even a fish tank. In each, producers (plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi) depend on one another and on sunlight, water, soil and air.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Give one example of interdependence in a forest ecosystem. → Trees give food and shelter to birds; birds disperse seeds of trees.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What happens to a pond ecosystem if its water dries up? → Fish and water plants die; frogs and birds lose food and must move; the whole system collapses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an ecosystem must be large — a pond is an ecosystem.
- Forgetting non-living parts (water, soil, sunlight).

statements.s: A pond can be an ecosystem.
Ecosystems include only living things.
Organisms in an ecosystem depend on each other.
A desert has no ecosystem.

options: interaction of organisms with each other and their surroundings
quiz.why: An ecosystem is a community of living things that interact with each other and with their non-living surroundings.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an ecosystem?
quiz.why: A forest is an example of an ecosystem. Plants, animals and the soil and water there interact.
Bacteria and fungi are decomposers. They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
Sunlight, water and soil are non-living parts of an ecosystem. Plants and animals are living.
Ecosystems can be as large as a forest or as small as a pond or an aquarium.

scenes.text: Early humans lived in caves and depended on nature for food, shelter and clothing.
Later they learned to grow crops, domesticate animals and live in villages.
Today we build cities, roads and factories — changing the environment more than ever.

steps.title: Human environment
steps.body: Human beings interact with the environment and modify it according to their needs. Early humans adapted to nature. With time they learned new skills: grow crops, domesticate animals, lead a settled life; invented the wheel; practised barter; trade and commerce developed. The **Industrial Revolution** enabled large-scale production. Transportation became faster; the **information revolution** made communication easier and speedier across the world. Human-made environment: buildings, parks, bridges, roads, industries, monuments.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Rapid modification led to problems — pollution of air, water and land, deforestation, climate change. A **perfect balance** between the natural and human environment is needed. **World Environment Day** is observed on **5 June**. Humans must learn to live in harmony with the environment.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Give two examples of human-made environment and two ways it has affected nature. → Roads and factories; they have caused air pollution and loss of forests.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How did the information revolution change human life? → Communication became faster and the world more connected.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all change is bad — the aim is balance, not stopping development.
- Mixing Environment Day (5 June) and Water Day (22 March).

activity.prompt: Ways I can help the environment this week:
items: Switch off lights and fans when leaving a room
Carry a cloth bag instead of plastic
Save water while brushing
Plant or care for a plant
Segregate wet and dry waste at home
Walk or cycle short distances

quiz.why: World Environment Day is celebrated on 5 June.
The Industrial Revolution brought machines and factories, so goods could be made on a large scale.
Early humans lived by hunting and gathering. They depended on nature and adapted to it.
Roads and buildings are made by humans, so they belong to the human-made environment.

quiz.q: The goal for humans and environment
quiz.why: We should aim for balance and harmony between human needs and the environment. Unlimited use of nature harms both.

scenes.text: Teacher asks the class to list everything they see on a walk around the school.
Lists include trees, birds, a pond, a road, a mobile tower, a park and a bridge.
Back in class, they sort each item into natural, human-made and human environment.

steps.title: Three kinds
steps.body:
- **Natural environment**: land, water, air, plants, animals.
- **Human-made environment**: things built by people — buildings, roads, bridges, parks, industries, monuments.
- **Human environment**: people as individuals, families, communities, with their religion, education and economic activities.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classify: river, temple, family, bridge, forest, school community → natural, human-made, human, human-made, natural, human.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How is a park both natural and human-made? → Its plants and soil are natural, but humans designed and built the park.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Treating 'human environment' and 'human-made environment' as the same: one is people and their activities, the other is things they build.

quiz.q: A bridge is part of the
quiz.why: A bridge is built by humans, so it is part of the human-made environment.

quiz.q: Communities and their activities are the
quiz.why: Communities and their activities form the human environment.
A forest is part of the natural environment, since people did not make it.
A monument is built by people, so it is human-made. Wind, sea and mountains are natural.

quiz.q: People with their education and religion form the
quiz.why: People and their education, religion and activities make up the human environment.

questions.q: Environment includes
questions.why: The environment includes both natural and human-made surroundings, not just one kind.

questions.q: Lithosphere is
questions.why: The lithosphere is the solid crust of the Earth, made of rocks and soil.

questions.q: World Environment Day
questions.why: World Environment Day is on 5 June each year.

questions.q: Ecosystem example
questions.why: A pond is an ecosystem, as living things in it interact with each other, the water and the light. A chair, computer or car is not.

questions.q: Atmosphere protects us from
options: harmful rays and scorching heat of the Sun
questions.why: The atmosphere shields us from the harmful rays and the scorching heat of the Sun.

questions.q: Biosphere is
options: narrow zone where land, water and air interact
questions.why: The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and interact to support life.

questions.q: Which is a natural component?
questions.why: A river is a natural part of the environment. Roads, bridges and factories are built by people.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A pond is an ecosystem. Reason (R): Organisms in a pond interact with each other and with water, light and soil.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: a pond is an ecosystem. R is true: its organisms interact with each other and with water, light and soil. That is the meaning of an ecosystem, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Human-made environment never affects the natural environment. Reason (R): Humans build roads and factories.
questions.why: A is false: roads and factories do affect nature, for example by clearing land and causing pollution. R is true that humans build them, but that does not support A.

questions.q: Which domain gives us minerals?
questions.why: The lithosphere is the Earth's solid crust, made of rocks and minerals, so it gives us minerals.

questions.q: Barter system means
questions.why: In the barter system people exchange goods or services directly, without using money.

questions.q: Case: A city cut its trees for a highway; summers became hotter and floods worse. What is missing?
options: Balance between human and natural environment
questions.why: Cutting the trees upset the natural environment and led to heat and floods. What was missing was a balance between development and nature.

questions.q: Case: A student sorts "hill, sea, wind, deer". Which domain is NOT represented?
questions.why: A hill is in the lithosphere, the sea in the hydrosphere, wind in the atmosphere and a deer in the biosphere. So all four domains are present.

questions.q: The information revolution mainly changed
questions.why: The information revolution changed how we communicate, making it faster through computers, the internet and phones.

questions.q: Why must decomposers be part of every ecosystem?
options: They recycle nutrients from dead matter
questions.why: Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. Without them, nutrients would not be recycled.

questions.q: Which shows interaction of all four domains?
options: A farmer growing crops using soil, rain, air and plants
questions.why: A farmer uses soil (lithosphere), rain (hydrosphere), air (atmosphere) and plants (biosphere). So all four domains interact in his work.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Inside Our Earth (Geography)
courses.summary: The layers of the Earth — crust, mantle and core — the three kinds of rocks and how they form, the rock cycle, and the minerals and uses of rocks.
outcomes: Learners can describe the layers of the Earth with their thickness and materials
Learners can distinguish igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks with examples
Learners can explain the rock cycle
Learners can describe uses of rocks and minerals

scenes.text: Peel an onion — layer under layer. The Earth is built in layers too.
The deepest mine in the world reaches only about 4 km; the Earth's centre is about 6000 km down.
Scientists study earthquakes and volcanoes to learn about the interior.

steps.title: Crust
steps.body:
The uppermost layer, the **crust**, is the thinnest. About **35 km** on continental masses and only **5 km** on the ocean floors.

- Continental crust: mainly **silica and alumina** → called **sial** (si = silica, al = alumina).
- Oceanic crust: mainly **silica and magnesium** → **sima** (si = silica, ma = magnesium).

steps.title: Mantle and core
steps.body:
- **Mantle**: just beneath the crust, extending to a depth of about **2900 km**.
- **Core**: innermost layer, radius about **3500 km**, mainly **nickel and iron** → **nife** (ni = nickel, fe = ferrous/iron). The central core has very high temperature and pressure.

steps.title: How deep have we gone?
steps.body: To reach the centre of the Earth (about 6000 km below the ocean floor) is impossible today; the deepest mine (in South Africa) is about 4 km deep, and oil drilling has gone about 6 km.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is the crust called sial on continents but sima under oceans? → Continental crust is rich in silica and alumina; oceanic crust in silica and magnesium.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Arrange the layers by depth from the surface. → Crust (~35 km on continents) → mantle (to ~2900 km) → core (radius ~3500 km).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping sial and sima.
- Thinking the crust is the thickest layer — it is the thinnest.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Layer below the crust, to ~2900 km

quiz.why: Continental crust is about 35 km thick on average. Oceanic crust is only about 5 km thick.

quiz.q: The core is made mainly of
quiz.why: The Earth's core is made mainly of nickel and iron. It is sometimes called nife.
The mantle lies below the crust and extends to about 2900 km deep.
The crust is the thinnest layer, about 5 to 35 km. The mantle and core are much thicker.
Oceanic crust is thinner than continental crust, only about 5 km thick.

scenes.text: Arjun collects three rocks: a speckled granite, a layered sandstone and a shiny marble.
His teacher explains: one formed from molten lava, one from layers of sand, one changed by heat and pressure.
Every rock tells the story of how it was made.

steps.title: Rocks and minerals
steps.body: Any natural mass of mineral matter that makes up the Earth's crust is a **rock**. Rocks can be of different colour, size and texture. There are three major types.

steps.title: Igneous rocks
steps.body:
When molten **magma** cools, it becomes solid — **igneous rocks** (primary rocks).

- **Extrusive igneous**: molten lava comes onto the surface and cools rapidly → very fine grains. **Basalt** (Deccan plateau is made of basalt).
- **Intrusive igneous**: molten magma cools deep inside the crust slowly → large grains. **Granite** (used for grinding stones).

steps.title: Sedimentary and metamorphic
steps.body:
- **Sedimentary rocks**: rocks roll down, crack, break into small fragments (**sediments**); these are transported and deposited by wind, water etc. Loose sediments get compressed and hardened in layers. Example: **sandstone** (from grains of sand). They may contain **fossils** of plants, animals and micro-organisms.
- **Metamorphic rocks**: igneous and sedimentary rocks change into metamorphic rocks under **great heat and pressure**. **Clay → slate**, **limestone → marble**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why does granite have large grains and basalt fine grains? → Granite cools slowly deep inside the Earth; basalt cools quickly on the surface.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Classify: marble, basalt, sandstone, slate, granite → metamorphic, igneous (extrusive), sedimentary, metamorphic, igneous (intrusive).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling marble sedimentary — it is metamorphic (from limestone).
- Thinking fossils are found in igneous rocks; they are mostly in sedimentary rocks.

quiz.why: Igneous rocks form when molten magma or lava cools and hardens. They are called primary rocks.
The Deccan plateau is made mainly of basalt, from lava that flowed out and cooled long ago.
Heat and pressure change limestone into marble. This process is called metamorphism.
Clay changes to slate under heat and pressure, so slate is a metamorphic rock.
Fossils are mostly found in sedimentary rocks, because soft layers of sediment can bury remains. Igneous rocks form from hot lava, which destroys remains.

lessons.title: The rock cycle, minerals and uses

scenes.text: Lava cools into basalt. Rain and wind wear it into sand.
Rivers carry the sand to the sea where it hardens into sandstone.
Deep inside, heat turns it into new rock, which may melt into magma again.

steps.title: Rock cycle
steps.body: Rocks change from one type to another in a cycle: molten magma cools → **igneous** rocks; broken into particles → **sedimentary** rocks; under heat and pressure → **metamorphic** rocks; under great heat and pressure, metamorphic rocks may melt into magma again. This transformation of one type of rock into another under certain conditions in a cyclic manner is the **rock cycle**.

steps.title: Minerals and uses
steps.body:
Rocks are made of **minerals** — naturally occurring substances with certain physical properties and definite chemical composition. Minerals are important: some are used as fuels — **coal, natural gas, petroleum**; others in industries — **iron, aluminium, gold, uranium**; in medicine, fertilisers etc.

Rocks are useful for roads, houses and buildings; stones are used in games (seven stones/pithoo, hopscotch, five stones).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Trace a path in the rock cycle from igneous to metamorphic. → Igneous → weathered into sediments → sedimentary rock → heat and pressure → metamorphic.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name two minerals used as fuel and two used in industry. → Coal, petroleum; iron, aluminium.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the rock cycle has only one direction — rocks can change in several ways.
- Confusing rocks (mixtures) with minerals (definite composition).

activity.prompt: Arrange one path of the rock cycle.
items: Magma cools to form igneous rock
Rock is broken into sediments
Sediments are compressed into sedimentary rock
Heat and pressure form metamorphic rock
Rock melts into magma again

options: transformation of rocks from one type to another
quiz.why: The rock cycle is the process by which rocks change from one type to another. For example, igneous rock can become sedimentary or metamorphic and then melt into magma.
A mineral is a natural substance with a definite chemical composition and set properties.
Coal is a mineral fuel, used to produce energy. Iron and gold are metals used otherwise.
Rocks are made up of one or more minerals.

quiz.q: Metamorphic rocks can melt to form
quiz.why: Metamorphic rocks may melt to form magma, which can cool and form new igneous rocks. This continues the cycle.

lessons.title: Practice: rocks around us and diagrams in words

scenes.text: The kitchen counter is granite, the floor is marble, and the old school roof uses slate.
The temple steps are sandstone.
Can you name the type of each and how it formed?

steps.title: Diagram of the Earth in words
steps.body: Draw three circles one inside the other: the outermost thin ring is the **crust** (sial on continents, sima below oceans), the thick middle ring is the **mantle** (to about 2900 km), and the centre is the **core** (radius about 3500 km, nife). Label thickness and composition.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Granite counter → igneous (intrusive). Marble floor → metamorphic (from limestone). Slate roof → metamorphic (from clay). Sandstone steps → sedimentary.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Which rock would you expect to find fossils in? → Sedimentary rock such as limestone or sandstone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Labelling the core as 'sima'.
- Saying all hard rocks are igneous.

activity.prompt: Match the object to the rock and its type.

quiz.q: The Taj Mahal is made of
quiz.why: The Taj Mahal is made of white marble, a metamorphic rock.

quiz.q: Red Fort is built mainly of
quiz.why: The Red Fort is built mainly of red sandstone, a sedimentary rock.
The mantle is the middle layer of the Earth, between the crust and the core.
Fossils are commonly found in sedimentary rocks, which form in layers from sediments.
Granite is very hard, so it is used for grinding stones and kitchen counters. Chalk, glass and paper are made from other materials.

questions.q: Outermost layer of the Earth
questions.why: The crust is the outermost layer of the Earth. Below it are the mantle and then the core.

questions.q: Core is mainly
questions.why: The core is mainly nickel and iron, which is why it is called nife.

questions.q: Granite is an
questions.why: Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep inside the Earth, so it is an intrusive igneous rock. It has large crystals.

questions.q: Marble is formed from
questions.why: Marble forms from limestone when it is changed by heat and pressure (metamorphism).

questions.q: Sima stands for
questions.why: Sima stands for silica and magnesium. It is the main material of the oceanic crust.

questions.q: Sedimentary rocks form from
questions.why: Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sediments are pressed and cemented together over a long time.

questions.q: Radius of the core (approx.)
questions.why: The core has a radius of about 3500 km. The mantle is about 2900 km thick.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Basalt has fine grains. Reason (R): Lava cools rapidly on the surface.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: basalt has fine grains. R is true: lava cools rapidly on the surface, so crystals have no time to grow big. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The crust is the thickest layer of the Earth. Reason (R): It forms the ocean floor and continents.
questions.why: A is false: the crust is the thinnest layer, not the thickest. R is true that it forms the continents and the ocean floor.

questions.q: Slate forms from
questions.why: Slate forms from clay, changed by heat and pressure. It is a metamorphic rock.

questions.q: Fossils help us learn about
questions.why: Fossils are the remains of plants and animals of the past, so they tell us about past life.

questions.q: Case: A geologist finds a layered rock with shells of sea creatures high in the Himalayas. The rock is likely
questions.why: Layers and fossils point to a sedimentary rock. Layers of sediment buried the sea creatures long ago, and the rock was later lifted high.

questions.q: Case: A rock cooled deep underground and was later exposed by erosion. It has large crystals. Likely
questions.why: Rock that cooled slowly underground has large crystals, which suggests an intrusive igneous rock like granite. Basalt cools quickly on the surface and has fine grains.

questions.q: Why can't we drill to the Earth's centre?
options: Extreme heat and pressure; it is about 6000 km deep
questions.why: The Earth's centre is about 6000 km deep, and the heat and pressure rise greatly with depth. The deepest mines go only a few kilometres.

questions.q: Which sequence is a possible rock cycle path?
questions.why: Sedimentary rock can change to metamorphic rock, which can melt to magma, and magma cools to igneous rock. This is a possible path in the rock cycle. The others include air, water and the core, which are not rock types.

questions.q: Which layer is described as "nife" and why?
questions.why: Nife stands for nickel and iron, the main substances of the core.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Our Changing Earth (Geography)
courses.summary: Moving lithospheric plates, earthquakes and volcanoes, and the landforms created by rivers, sea waves, glaciers and wind through weathering and erosion — with earthquake safety tips.
outcomes: Learners can explain endogenic and exogenic forces and plate movement
Learners can describe earthquakes, their measurement and safety measures
Learners can describe landforms made by rivers, sea waves, ice and wind
Learners can distinguish weathering and erosion

scenes.text: During class, the desks begin to rattle and the fan swings.
The teacher calls: "Drop, cover, hold!" Everyone ducks under their desks.
Later they learn that the ground shook because huge plates of rock moved deep below.

steps.title: Lithospheric plates and forces
steps.body:
The lithosphere is broken into a number of plates called **lithospheric plates**, which move around very slowly — just a few millimetres each year — because of the movement of molten magma inside the Earth.

- **Endogenic forces**: act in the interior of the Earth (cause earthquakes, volcanoes).
- **Exogenic forces**: work on the surface (weathering, erosion, deposition).

steps.title: Earthquakes
steps.body: When lithospheric plates move, the surface vibrates — an **earthquake**. The place in the crust where the movement starts is the **focus**; the place on the surface above the focus is the **epicentre**. Vibrations travel outwards from the epicentre as waves; greatest damage is usually closest to the epicentre. Earthquakes are measured with a **seismograph**; magnitude on the **Richter scale** (2.0 or less – little felt; above 5.0 – damage from falling objects; 6.0 or more – very strong; 7.0 and above – major earthquake). Common predictions include animal behaviour.

steps.title: Volcanoes
steps.body: A **volcano** is a vent (opening) in the Earth's crust through which molten material (lava, ash, gases) erupts suddenly.

steps.title: Earthquake safety
steps.body:
- Indoors: **drop, cover and hold** under a sturdy table; stay away from windows, mirrors, heavy furniture.
- Outdoors: move to an open area away from buildings, trees, power lines.
- Do not use lifts. Afterwards, check for injuries; call **112** in emergencies.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Distinguish focus and epicentre. → Focus: place inside the crust where movement starts. Epicentre: point on the surface directly above the focus.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking plates move fast; they move only millimetres a year.
- Running outside during shaking from a high floor — it is safer to drop, cover and hold.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Starting point of an earthquake inside the crust
Point on the surface above the focus
Force acting on the Earth's surface
Vent through which molten material erupts

quiz.why: Earthquakes are measured on the Richter scale, which gives their magnitude.

quiz.q: Point on the surface above the focus
quiz.why: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus, where the earthquake starts underground.
The plates move very slowly, only a few millimetres a year.
Forces working inside the Earth are called endogenic forces. Forces on the surface are exogenic.

quiz.q: During an earthquake indoors, you should
quiz.why: Indoors during an earthquake, drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on. Stay away from windows, and do not use the lift.

scenes.text: High in the mountains a river rushes down steep slopes, cutting deep valleys.
Where it falls over a hard rock edge, it forms a waterfall.
Down in the plains it winds in loops, floods its banks and finally splits into many streams near the sea.

steps.title: Weathering and erosion
steps.body:
- **Weathering**: breaking up of rocks on the Earth's surface.
- **Erosion**: wearing away of the landscape by agents like **water, wind and ice**. The eroded material is carried away and **deposited** elsewhere. These processes create various landforms.

steps.title: River landforms
steps.body:
- **Waterfall**: river falls over a steep hard rock or a steep valley side. **Angel Falls of Venezuela** is the highest waterfall in the world.
- **Meanders**: as the river enters the plain, it twists and turns forming large bends.
- **Ox-bow lake**: erosion and deposition cut off a meander loop, forming a lake.
- **Floodplains**: when a river overflows, it deposits fine soil and sediments on the banks — fertile flat land.
- **Levees**: raised banks formed by deposition.
- **Distributaries and delta**: near the sea the river splits into many streams (distributaries); the mouth gets a deposit called a **delta**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How is an ox-bow lake formed? → A meander loop grows; erosion and deposition at its ends cut it off from the main river, leaving a curved lake.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why are floodplains good for farming? → Floods deposit fertile soil and sediment on them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing weathering (breaking of rocks in place) and erosion (wearing away and carrying).
- Thinking a delta forms in the mountains — it forms at the river mouth.

activity.prompt: Arrange river landforms from the mountains to the sea.
items: V-shaped valley and waterfall in the hills
Meanders in the plains
Ox-bow lake from a cut-off meander
Floodplains and levees
Distributaries and delta at the mouth

quiz.why: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest waterfall.
Large bends in a river's course are called meanders.
When a meander gets cut off from the main river, it becomes an ox-bow lake.
During floods a river deposits sediment along its banks, building raised banks called levees.

quiz.q: Breaking up of rocks on the surface
quiz.why: Weathering is the breaking up of rocks on the Earth's surface. Erosion carries the material away.

lessons.title: Work of sea waves, ice and wind

scenes.text: On a rocky coast, waves have carved caves, arches and lonely pillars of rock.
In the Himalayas, slow rivers of ice grind valleys and leave piles of rocks.
In the desert, the wind has shaped a rock like a giant mushroom.

steps.title: Sea waves
steps.body: Waves strike rocks continuously; cracks develop and become larger, forming hollow **sea caves**. As cavities become bigger, only the roof remains — **sea arches**. Further erosion breaks the roof and only walls are left — **stacks**. The steep rocky coast rising almost vertically above sea water is a **sea cliff**. Waves deposit sediments along shores, forming **beaches**.

steps.title: Ice (glaciers)
steps.body: **Glaciers** are 'rivers' of ice which erode the landscape by bulldozing soil and stones to expose solid rock below; they carve out deep hollows that fill with water and become beautiful lakes in the mountains. Material carried by the glacier — rocks big and small, sand and silt — gets deposited, forming **glacial moraines**.

steps.title: Wind
steps.body: Wind is an active agent of erosion and deposition in deserts. It erodes the lower section of rocks more than the upper part, forming **mushroom rocks** (narrow base, wider top). When wind blows, it lifts and transports sand; when it stops, sand falls and gets deposited in low hill-like structures — **sand dunes**. When grains of sand are very fine and light, wind carries them over long distances; deposited over large areas they form **loess** (large deposits are found in **China**).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Arrange the sequence of coastal erosion. → Sea cave → sea arch → stack.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do mushroom rocks have a narrow base? → Wind carries sand close to the ground, which erodes the lower part more than the top.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing stacks (erosion) with beaches (deposition).
- Mixing moraines (glacier) and loess (wind).

quiz.q: When a sea arch's roof collapses, what remains is a
quiz.why: When the roof of a sea arch collapses, the pillar of rock left standing in the sea is a stack.
Rocks and soil deposited by a glacier are called moraines.
Wind erosion in deserts shapes rocks into mushroom forms, called mushroom rocks.

quiz.q: Large deposits of loess are found in
quiz.why: Loess, a fine wind-blown deposit, is found in large amounts in China.
Sea waves deposit sand and pebbles along the shore, forming beaches.

scenes.text: Teacher shows photos: a rock pillar in the sea, a curved lake beside a river, a heap of rocks at a glacier's end, a dune.
For each, students name the landform and the agent that made it.

steps.title: Quick guide
steps.body:
- Rivers: waterfall, meander, ox-bow lake, floodplain, levee, delta
- Sea waves: sea cave, arch, stack, cliff, beach
- Glaciers: glacial lakes, moraines
- Wind: mushroom rock, sand dune, loess

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A curved lake next to a winding river → **ox-bow lake**, made by the river (erosion + deposition).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A pillar of rock standing in the sea near the coast → **stack**, made by sea waves after an arch collapsed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every hill of sand a 'mountain' — sand hills are dunes.
- Thinking moraines are made by rivers.

quiz.q: A lake left by a cut-off river bend
quiz.why: A meander that gets cut off from the river leaves an ox-bow lake.
A stack is a pillar of rock left standing in the sea after waves wear away the rest.

quiz.q: Heap of rocks deposited by a glacier
quiz.why: A moraine is a heap of rocks and soil deposited by a glacier.
Loess is fine, wind-blown dust that settles as deposits.
Waves erode rock at the coast and leave a steep rocky face, called a sea cliff.

questions.q: Instrument that records earthquakes
questions.why: A seismograph records the waves of an earthquake. A barometer measures air pressure.

questions.q: Mushroom rocks are made by
questions.why: Wind erosion in deserts wears rocks into mushroom shapes. So mushroom rocks are made by wind.

questions.q: Highest waterfall
questions.why: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the highest waterfall in the world.

questions.q: Point inside the crust where an earthquake begins
questions.why: The focus is the point inside the crust where the earthquake starts. The epicentre is the point above it on the surface.

questions.q: Wearing away of land by water, wind, ice
questions.why: Erosion is the wearing away of land by running water, wind or ice. Weathering is the breaking of rock in place.

questions.q: Ox-bow lakes form in
questions.why: Ox-bow lakes form on plains where a river forms meanders that are later cut off.

questions.q: Earthquake of magnitude 7 or more is
questions.why: On the Richter scale an earthquake of magnitude 7 or more is major and can cause heavy damage.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Floodplains are fertile. Reason (R): Rivers deposit fine soil during floods.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: floodplains are fertile. R is true: rivers deposit fine soil during floods, which adds nutrients. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Weathering and erosion are the same. Reason (R): Both are exogenic processes.
questions.why: A is false: weathering breaks rock down in place, whereas erosion carries it away. R is true that both are exogenic processes, but this does not make them the same.

questions.q: Correct order of coastal erosion
questions.why: Waves first carve a cave in a cliff. The cave widens into an arch, and when the arch's roof falls, a stack is left.

questions.q: Delta forms at the
questions.why: A delta forms at the mouth of a river, where the river slows down, drops its sediment and splits into branches before entering the sea.

questions.q: Case: A village near a river floods every year but has rich crops. The village is likely on a
questions.why: Floods leave fine, fertile silt on the land beside a river. So a village that floods yearly but has rich crops is likely on a floodplain.

questions.q: Case: During an earthquake, Ravi is on the 5th floor. Best action?
options: Drop under a sturdy table and hold on
questions.why: In an earthquake, drop down, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. Lifts, balconies and windows are dangerous.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: A glacier carries and deposits rocks and soil as moraines. Levees come from rivers, loess from wind and stacks from sea waves, so the other pairs are mismatched.

questions.q: Why are earthquakes most damaging near the epicentre?
options: Waves are strongest closest to it
questions.why: Earthquake waves lose energy as they spread out. So the shaking is strongest, and damage greatest, closest to the epicentre.

questions.q: Lithospheric plates move because of
options: movement of molten magma inside the Earth
questions.why: The lithospheric plates float on hot, molten magma in the mantle, and the slow movement of this magma makes them move. This is an endogenic cause.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Air (Geography)
courses.summary: The composition and layers of the atmosphere, weather and climate, temperature and insolation, air pressure and winds, moisture, humidity and kinds of rainfall.
outcomes: Learners can state the composition of air and the role of each gas
Learners can describe the five layers of the atmosphere
Learners can distinguish weather and climate and explain temperature and pressure
Learners can classify winds and types of rainfall

scenes.text: Astronaut photos show Earth wrapped in a thin blue haze.
That haze is the atmosphere — the air that lets us breathe and keeps us warm.
Mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of other gases.

steps.title: Gases in air
steps.body:
Our Earth is surrounded by a huge blanket of air called the **atmosphere**. Air is a mixture of many gases:

- **Nitrogen ≈ 78%**
- **Oxygen ≈ 21%**
- **Argon ≈ 0.93%**
- **Carbon dioxide ≈ 0.03%**
- Others (helium, ozone, hydrogen, etc.) in tiny amounts

Air also contains water vapour and dust particles.

steps.title: Role of the gases
steps.body:
- **Nitrogen**: plants need it but cannot take it directly from air; bacteria in soil and roots of some plants change it into a usable form.
- **Oxygen**: breathed by humans and animals; plants produce it in photosynthesis.
- **Carbon dioxide**: plants use it to make food; it absorbs heat radiated by the Earth, keeping the planet warm. But burning fuels adds more CO₂, increasing heat in the atmosphere — the **greenhouse effect** — leading to **global warming**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is CO₂ important even though it is only about 0.03% of air? → Plants need it for photosynthesis, and it keeps the Earth warm by absorbing heat.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do plants get nitrogen? → Bacteria in soil and in roots of some plants convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying oxygen is the most abundant gas — it is nitrogen.
- Thinking the greenhouse effect is always bad — some is needed to keep Earth warm; extra CO₂ causes global warming.

activity.prompt: Match the gas to its share or role.
pairs: Small amount; absorbs harmful UV rays

quiz.why: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air. Oxygen is about 21%, and the rest is argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
Oxygen is about 21% of the air. Nitrogen is the largest part at 78%.

quiz.q: Gas used by plants to make food
quiz.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide and use it in photosynthesis to make food. Argon and helium are not used.
More CO₂ traps more heat in the air, which is the greenhouse effect. This leads to global warming.
Plants cannot use nitrogen directly from the air. Bacteria in the soil and root nodules change it into a form plants can take up, called nitrogen fixation.

scenes.text: A jet plane cruises above the clouds where the air is calm.
Higher up, meteors burn up as streaks of light.
Even higher, radio waves bounce off a charged layer back to Earth.

steps.title: Five layers
steps.body:
Starting from the Earth's surface:

1. **Troposphere** (average height ~13 km): most important layer — air we breathe; almost all weather (rain, fog, hailstorms) occurs here.
2. **Stratosphere** (up to ~50 km): almost free from clouds and weather, so ideal for **flying aeroplanes**; contains the **ozone layer**, which protects us from harmful UV rays.
3. **Mesosphere** (up to ~80 km): **meteorites burn up** here on entering from space.
4. **Thermosphere** (80–400 km): temperature rises very rapidly with height; the **ionosphere** is part of it — helps radio transmission (radio waves sent from Earth are reflected back).
5. **Exosphere**: uppermost layer with very thin air; light gases like helium and hydrogen float into space from here.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why do aeroplanes fly in the stratosphere? → It is almost free from clouds and weather disturbances.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: In which layer do we live and where does weather occur? → **Troposphere**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the ozone layer in the troposphere — it is in the stratosphere.
- Mixing mesosphere (meteors burn) and thermosphere (ionosphere).

activity.prompt: Arrange the layers from the Earth's surface upward.
items: Troposphere
Stratosphere
Mesosphere
Thermosphere
Exosphere

quiz.why: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere. Clouds, rain and weather occur there.
The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere. It absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun.
Meteorites burn up in the mesosphere as they fall towards Earth, because friction with air heats them.
The ionosphere reflects radio waves back to Earth, which helps radio transmission.
The troposphere is on average about 13 km high. It is thicker near the equator and thinner at the poles.

scenes.text: "It is raining in Mumbai today" — that is weather.
"Mumbai gets heavy rain every monsoon" — that is climate.
Weather can change hour by hour; climate is the average over many years.

steps.title: Weather and climate
steps.body: **Weather** is the hour-to-hour, day-to-day condition of the atmosphere; it can change dramatically. The average weather condition of a place over a long period is its **climate**. Elements: temperature, pressure, wind, moisture, rainfall.

steps.title: Temperature and insolation
steps.body: The degree of hotness and coldness of air is **temperature**. It changes between day and night and from season to season. An important factor is **insolation** — incoming solar energy intercepted by the Earth. Insolation decreases from the **equator towards the poles**, so temperature too. Temperatures in cities are higher than in villages (concrete and metal absorb heat; less vegetation).

steps.title: Air pressure
steps.body:
**Air pressure** is the pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface. It is highest at sea level and **decreases with height**. Horizontally, it depends on temperature:

- Where temperature is **high**, air heats up and rises → **low pressure** → cloudy skies and wet weather.
- Where temperature is **low**, air is cold and heavy, it sinks → **high pressure** → clear and sunny skies.

**Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure areas.**

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why do mountaineers carry oxygen cylinders? → Air pressure and the amount of oxygen decrease with height, making breathing difficult.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: An area has low pressure. Expect what weather? → Rising air, cloudy and wet weather.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping weather (short-term) and climate (long-term).
- Thinking air moves from low to high pressure — it moves from high to low.

items.text: It is foggy this morning in Delhi
Rajasthan is generally hot and dry
Kerala receives heavy rain every year
Polar regions are cold throughout the year

quiz.q: Average weather over a long time
quiz.why: Climate is the average weather of a place over a long time, usually 30 years or more. Weather is the day-to-day state.

options: incoming solar energy received by Earth
quiz.why: Insolation is the incoming solar radiation, the Sun's energy received by the Earth.
Air pressure is highest at sea level, because there is the most air above pressing down. It falls as we go higher.
Air always moves from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure. This movement is wind.
Low pressure means air rises. As it rises it cools and forms clouds, so low pressure brings cloudy, wet weather.

scenes.text: In May, a hot, dry wind called the loo blows across the plains of north India.
In June the monsoon winds arrive from the sea, bringing rain.
Winds carry moisture; when moist air rises and cools, it rains.

steps.title: Winds
steps.body:
The movement of air from high pressure to low pressure is **wind**.

- **Permanent winds**: blow constantly in a particular direction throughout the year — **trade winds, westerlies, easterlies**.
- **Seasonal winds**: change direction with seasons — **monsoon** winds in India.
- **Local winds**: blow only during a particular period of the day or year in a small area — land and sea breezes; the hot, dry **loo** of the northern plains of India.

steps.title: Moisture and humidity
steps.body: When water evaporates from land and water bodies, it becomes water vapour. **Moisture** in the air at any time is **humidity**. When air is full of water vapour, it is humid; on a humid day, clothes take longer to dry and sweat does not evaporate easily. When water vapour rises, it cools and condenses into tiny droplets — **clouds**. When droplets become too heavy, they fall as **precipitation** (rain, snow, sleet).

steps.title: Types of rainfall
steps.body:
- **Convectional rainfall**: heated air rises, cools and forms clouds — common in hot, equatorial regions (afternoon rain).
- **Orographic (relief) rainfall**: moist air is forced to rise along a mountain; the windward side gets heavy rain, the other side (rain-shadow) stays dry.
- **Cyclonic rainfall**: associated with cyclones.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why does the windward side of the Western Ghats get heavy rain and the leeward side less? → Moist monsoon winds rise along the slope, cool and shed rain (orographic); descending air on the other side is dry.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Classify the monsoon: permanent, seasonal or local? → **Seasonal**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the loo a permanent wind — it is local.
- Thinking humidity is the same as rainfall.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its example or meaning.
pairs: Local hot, dry wind of northern India
Rain as moist air rises over mountains
Heated air rises, cools and rains

quiz.why: The loo is a hot, dry wind of the northern plains in summer. It blows over a small area, so it is a local wind.
Monsoon winds change direction with the seasons, so they are seasonal winds. Trade winds and westerlies are permanent.

quiz.q: Moisture in the air at any time
quiz.why: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air at a given time.

quiz.q: Rain on the windward side of mountains
quiz.why: When moist air rises over mountains and cools, it gives rain on the windward side. This is relief or orographic rainfall.

quiz.q: Clothes take longer to dry when
quiz.why: When the air already holds a lot of moisture, water evaporates slowly from clothes. So wet clothes take longer to dry.

questions.q: Nitrogen in air (approx.)
questions.why: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air. Oxygen is about 21%.

questions.q: Layer for flying aeroplanes
questions.why: Aeroplanes fly in the stratosphere because it is calm there, with little cloud or weather. The troposphere has storms and clouds.

questions.q: Day-to-day condition of the atmosphere
questions.why: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere in a place. Climate is the long-term average.

questions.q: Air moves from
questions.why: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure. This movement is what we call wind.

questions.q: Ionosphere is part of the
questions.why: The ionosphere lies inside the thermosphere, where gases are electrically charged.

questions.q: Insolation decreases from
questions.why: Insolation is greatest at the equator, where the Sun's rays fall nearly straight. It decreases towards the poles, where rays are slanted.

questions.q: Westerlies are
questions.why: Westerlies are permanent winds that blow all year in the same direction. Monsoons are seasonal and the loo is a local wind.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mountain tops have low air pressure. Reason (R): Air pressure decreases with height.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: mountain tops have low air pressure. R is true: pressure drops with height as there is less air above. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Weather of a place stays the same for years. Reason (R): Climate is the long-term average of weather.
questions.why: A is false: weather changes day by day and even hour by hour. R is true that climate is the long-term average of weather.

questions.q: Greenhouse effect is mainly caused by increase in
questions.why: Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, so an increase causes the greenhouse effect to grow.

questions.q: Meteors burn in the
questions.why: Meteors burn up in the mesosphere due to friction with the air. This is why most never reach the ground.

questions.q: Case: A town on the leeward side of a mountain gets very little rain while the other side is green. Why?
options: It lies in the rain-shadow area
questions.why: The leeward side of a mountain gets little rain because the air has lost its moisture on the windward side. This dry region is a rain-shadow area.

questions.q: Case: In an equatorial town, mornings are sunny but there is heavy rain every afternoon. Type of rainfall?
questions.why: Strong morning heating makes warm, moist air rise, cool and form clouds, giving heavy rain in the afternoon. This is convectional rainfall.

questions.q: Why are cities warmer than nearby villages?
options: Concrete and metal absorb heat; less vegetation
questions.why: Concrete, metal and tarmac absorb and keep heat, and cities have less vegetation to cool the air. So cities are warmer, an effect called the urban heat island.

questions.q: An area of high temperature usually has
questions.why: Where it is hot, air warms and rises, which gives low pressure. High pressure with sinking air goes with cooler areas.

questions.q: Which correctly matches the layer and feature?
options: Exosphere – light gases escape to space
questions.why: In the exosphere, the top layer, gases are very thin and the lightest ones escape into space. Ozone is in the stratosphere, meteors burn in the mesosphere and radio waves reflect from the ionosphere.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Water (Geography)
courses.summary: The water cycle, how water is distributed on Earth, why oceans are salty, and the movements of ocean water — waves, tides (spring and neap) and warm and cold ocean currents — including tsunamis.
outcomes: Learners can explain the water cycle and the distribution of water on Earth
Learners can explain salinity and give examples
Learners can describe waves, tides (spring and neap) and tsunamis
Learners can distinguish warm and cold ocean currents and their effects

lessons.title: The water cycle and distribution of water

scenes.text: After rain, a puddle in the school yard disappears by afternoon.
The water evaporated, rose and may join a cloud.
Some day it may fall again as rain on a mountain far away.

steps.title: The water cycle
steps.body: The Sun's heat causes **evaporation** of water into vapour. On cooling, the vapour **condenses** to form clouds, and falls as **precipitation** (rain, snow, sleet) on land or sea. The process by which water continually changes its form and circulates between oceans, atmosphere and land is the **water cycle**. Fresh water is obtained from rain, rivers, lakes, springs and glaciers.

steps.title: How water is distributed
steps.body:
About three-fourths of the Earth's surface is covered with water, but most of it is in oceans and is salty:

- **Oceans: 97.3%**
- Ice caps: 2.0%
- Groundwater: 0.68%
- Freshwater lakes: 0.009%
- Inland seas and salt lakes: 0.009%
- Atmosphere: 0.0019%
- Rivers: 0.0001%

So very little is usable fresh water. **World Water Day** is celebrated on **22 March**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is fresh water precious though Earth is mostly covered with water? → About 97.3% is salty ocean water and 2% is locked in ice caps; very little fresh water is easily available.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name the three main processes of the water cycle. → Evaporation, condensation, precipitation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking rivers hold a lot of water — they have only about 0.0001% of the Earth's water.
- Forgetting groundwater, which is a large share of usable fresh water.

items: Sun heats water in oceans and lakes
Water evaporates into vapour
Vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds
Water falls as precipitation
Water flows back to rivers, oceans or seeps underground

quiz.q: Percentage of Earth's water in oceans
quiz.why: About 97.3% of Earth's water is in the oceans, and it is salty. Only a small part is fresh.

quiz.q: Water vapour cooling to form clouds
quiz.why: Condensation is when water vapour cools and turns into tiny droplets, which form clouds. Evaporation is the reverse.

quiz.q: Rain, snow and sleet are forms of
quiz.why: Rain, snow and sleet are different forms in which water falls from clouds. Together they are called precipitation.
World Water Day is celebrated on 22 March.
Most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, about 2% of all water. Lakes and rivers hold far less.

scenes.text: Tourists at the Dead Sea float effortlessly — they cannot sink!
Its water is extremely salty — about ten times saltier than the ocean.
Salty water is denser, so it pushes up more on swimmers.

steps.title: Salinity
steps.body: Ocean water is salty because it contains large amounts of dissolved salts, mostly **sodium chloride** (common salt). **Salinity** is the amount of salt in grams present in 1 litre of water. The oceans have an average salinity of about **35 grams per litre**.

steps.title: Extreme example
steps.body: The **Dead Sea** in West Asia has a salinity of about **340 grams per litre**. Swimmers can float in it because the salt makes it dense.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: If 2 litres of ocean water are evaporated, how much salt is left? → 2 × 35 = **70 g** (approximately).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why can people float easily in the Dead Sea? → Very high salinity makes the water dense.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking salinity is measured in percent here — in Class 7 it is grams per litre.
- Thinking all seas have the same salinity.

activity.prompt: Average ocean salinity is 35 g per litre. How much salt (g) in 5 litres of ocean water?

quiz.why: The average salinity of ocean water is about 35 grams of salt per litre.
The main salt in sea water is sodium chloride, which is common salt.
The Dead Sea is extremely salty, about 340 g of salt per litre. That is nearly ten times the ocean average.

options: grams of salt per litre of water
quiz.why: Salinity is the amount of salt in water, measured in grams of salt per litre.

quiz.q: People float in the Dead Sea because
quiz.why: Dead Sea water has so much salt that it is very dense, and a person floats easily on it.

scenes.text: At Mumbai's harbour, a fisherman waits for high tide to sail his boat out.
On full-moon nights the tide rises especially high.
The Moon's pull causes the sea to rise and fall twice a day.

steps.title: Waves
steps.body: When water on the ocean surface rises and falls alternately, these are **waves**. They are formed by wind blowing across the water; strong winds make bigger waves; storms produce huge waves that can cause destruction. **Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions or underwater landslides** can shift large amounts of water, creating huge tidal waves called **tsunami** (sometimes as high as 15 m). The **Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004** caused huge loss of life and property along coasts including the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Tides
steps.body:
The rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water **twice a day** is a **tide**. **High tide**: water covers much of the shore; **low tide**: water recedes. Tides are caused by the strong gravitational pull of the **Moon** (and the Sun) on the Earth's surface.

- **Spring tides**: at **full moon and new moon**, the Sun, Moon and Earth are in the same line → highest tides.
- **Neap tides**: when the Moon is in its **first and last quarter**, the pulls of Sun and Moon act at right angles → low tides.

steps.title: Uses of tides
steps.body: High tides help navigation by raising the water level close to shores, helping ships arrive at harbours; they help fishing; they can be used to generate electricity.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why are tides highest at full moon? → Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line; their pulls add up → spring tide.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What causes a tsunami? → Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions or underwater landslides that displace a lot of ocean water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking spring tides happen only in spring — the name has nothing to do with the season.
- Thinking tsunamis are caused by wind.

items.text: Sun, Moon, Earth in a line
Sun and Moon pull at right angles

quiz.why: Most places have two high tides and two low tides a day, so tides happen twice daily.
Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller pull from the Sun.
Spring tides occur at full moon and new moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line. Their pulls add up and tides are highest.
The Indian Ocean tsunami took place on 26 December 2004.
A tsunami comes from sudden movement of the sea floor, usually an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption, which pushes a huge amount of water.

scenes.text: Near Newfoundland, ships often sail through thick fog.
Here a warm current meets a cold current.
The meeting place is also one of the world's richest fishing grounds.

steps.title: What currents are
steps.body:
**Ocean currents** are streams of water flowing constantly on the ocean surface in definite directions. They may be warm or cold.

- **Warm currents** originate near the **equator** and move towards the poles. Example: **Gulf Stream**.
- **Cold currents** carry water from **polar or higher latitudes** towards tropical or lower latitudes. Example: **Labrador Current**.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
- Areas where warm and cold currents meet provide the **best fishing grounds** in the world — e.g. seas around Japan and the east coast of North America.
- Areas where they meet also experience **foggy weather**, making navigation difficult.
- Warm currents raise the temperature of coastal areas; cold currents lower it.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Name a warm and a cold current. → Gulf Stream (warm); Labrador Current (cold).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why is the area near Newfoundland good for fishing but foggy? → The warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current; plankton grows (fish food) and the mixing of warm and cold air creates fog.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking currents and waves are the same — currents are steady streams; waves are up-and-down movements.
- Thinking warm currents flow from the poles.

statements.s: Warm currents start near the equator.
The Labrador Current is warm.
Meeting of warm and cold currents creates good fishing grounds.
Ocean currents flow in random directions.
Fog is common where warm and cold currents meet.

quiz.why: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the tropics towards higher latitudes, so it is a warm current.
Cold currents carry cold water from polar regions towards lower latitudes.
Where warm and cold currents meet, plankton grows well and fish gather, so these are the best fishing grounds.
The Labrador Current is a cold current. The Gulf Stream, Kuroshio and North Atlantic Drift are warm.

quiz.q: Streams of water flowing on the ocean surface in definite directions
quiz.why: Ocean currents are streams of water flowing in definite directions on the ocean surface. Waves, tides and tsunamis are different movements.

questions.q: Process by which water changes to vapour
questions.why: Evaporation is when water turns into vapour, usually by heating. Condensation is the opposite.

questions.q: Percentage of Earth's water in oceans
questions.why: About 97.3% of Earth's water is in the oceans.

questions.q: Rise and fall of ocean water twice a day
questions.why: The rise and fall of ocean water, about twice a day, is called a tide.

questions.q: Gulf Stream is
questions.why: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current.

questions.q: Average salinity of oceans
questions.why: Ocean water has on average about 35 g of salt per litre.

questions.q: Neap tides occur during
questions.why: Neap tides occur at the first and last quarter of the Moon, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles. Their pulls partly cancel, so tides are lower.

questions.q: Tsunami is caused by
questions.why: A tsunami is caused by sudden movement of the sea floor, such as an undersea earthquake. Evaporation, tides and wind do not cause it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Spring tides are higher than neap tides. Reason (R): At spring tides the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: spring tides are higher than neap tides. R is true: at spring tides the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line, so their pulls add together. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Rivers hold most of the Earth's fresh water. Reason (R): Rivers flow throughout the year.
questions.why: A is false: most fresh water is in ice caps and glaciers. R is false too: many rivers dry up or shrink in the dry season.

questions.q: How much salt in 4 L of ocean water (35 g/L)?
questions.why: Salt = volume × salinity = 4 L × 35 g/L = 140 g.

questions.q: Labrador Current is
questions.why: The Labrador Current is a cold current, flowing from the Arctic towards the south along the coast of North America.

questions.q: Case: Fishermen near the east coast of North America find huge catches but frequent fog. Why?
options: Warm and cold currents meet there
questions.why: The warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current off eastern North America. Plankton and fish are plentiful there, but the mixing also brings fog.

questions.q: Case: A port allows large ships to enter only at certain hours each day. Which ocean movement helps?
questions.why: A high tide raises the water level, so large ships can enter the harbour. At low tide the water may be too shallow.

questions.q: Why are we told to save water when Earth is a "blue planet"?
options: Very little of Earth's water is usable fresh water
questions.why: Although most of the Earth is covered by water, almost all of it is salty or frozen. Only a tiny share is fresh water we can use, so it must be saved.

questions.q: Which order of the water cycle is correct?
questions.why: Water evaporates, then condenses into clouds, and then falls as precipitation. That is the right order of the water cycle.

questions.q: Which is NOT a use of tides?
questions.why: Tides help fishing, bring ships into harbours, and can generate electricity. They do not cause earthquakes.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Human Environment Interactions: The Tropical and the Subtropical Region (Geography)
courses.summary: Life in the hot, wet Amazon basin near the equator and in the subtropical Ganga–Brahmaputra basin: climate, rainforests, wildlife, people, farming, cities and the threats both regions face.
outcomes: Learners can locate the Amazon and Ganga–Brahmaputra basins and describe their climate
Learners can describe rainforest vegetation, wildlife and the lives of people in the Amazon
Learners can describe agriculture, wildlife, settlements and tourism in the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin
Learners can explain human impact such as deforestation and compare the two regions
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: The Amazon basin: climate and rainforest

story.title: A boat on the world's greatest river

scenes.text: A boat drifts along the Amazon, near the equator in South America.
Trees rise like a green wall on both banks; the canopy blocks the sky.
Macaws screech, monkeys swing, and somewhere a jaguar watches.

steps.title: Location and river
steps.body: The **Amazon basin** lies in the **equatorial region** (about 10°N–10°S) in **South America**. The **Amazon river** flows from the mountains in the west to the **Atlantic Ocean** in the east. The place where a river flows into another body of water is its **mouth**. Numerous tributaries join the Amazon to form the basin, which drains parts of Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia and a small part of Venezuela.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Hot and wet throughout the year — the equator passes through it. Both days and nights are almost equally hot and humid; the skin feels sticky. It rains almost every day, often without warning. Days are very hot, nights are a little cooler, but humidity stays high.

steps.title: Rainforest and wildlife
steps.body: Due to heavy rain, thick forests grow — **tropical rainforests**. The thick canopy of leaves and branches does not allow sunlight to reach the floor, which stays dark and damp; only shade-tolerant plants grow there. Orchids and bromeliads grow as plant parasites. The forest is rich in fauna: birds like **toucans, hummingbirds, birds of paradise** with brilliantly coloured plumage and oversized bills; animals like **monkeys, sloths, ant-eating tapirs**; reptiles and snakes like crocodiles, pythons, **anacondas and boa constrictors**; the flesh-eating **piranha** fish; and thousands of insects.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is the forest floor of the Amazon dark? → The dense canopy of tall trees blocks sunlight.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name four animals of the Amazon rainforest. → Toucan, sloth, anaconda, piranha.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the Amazon in Africa — it is in South America.
- Thinking the Amazon flows into the Pacific; it flows into the Atlantic.

statements.s: The Amazon river flows into the Atlantic Ocean.
The Amazon basin has a cold, dry climate.
The rainforest floor gets a lot of sunlight.
Piranhas are flesh-eating fish of the Amazon.
The equator passes through the Amazon basin.

quiz.why: The Amazon basin lies in South America, mainly in Brazil.
The Amazon basin is close to the equator, so it is hot and wet through the year.
The Amazon flows eastwards and empties into the Atlantic Ocean.

quiz.q: Bird with an oversized bill in the rainforest
quiz.why: The toucan is a rainforest bird with a very large bill.
The Amazon rainforest is home to large snakes such as the anaconda and the boa constrictor.

lessons.title: People of the Amazon and change

scenes.text: In a small village, families grow manioc in a forest clearing.
When the soil loses fertility, they move and clear a new patch — slash and burn.
Today, roads and ranches are cutting into the forest at an alarming pace.

steps.title: Life of the people
steps.body: People grow most of their food in small areas after clearing some trees — **slash and burn agriculture**. Men hunt and fish along rivers; women take care of crops. They mainly grow **tapioca, pineapple and sweet potato**. Staple food is **manioc (cassava)**, which grows under the ground like a potato. They also eat queen ants and egg sacs. **Cash crops** like coffee, maize and cocoa are also grown. Some live in thatched houses shaped like beehives; others in large apartment-like houses called **'Maloca'** with a steeply slanting roof.

steps.title: Change and threats
steps.body: Life of the Amazon is changing slowly. Earlier, the heart of the forest was accessible only by river. In 1970 the **Trans-Amazon highway** made all parts reachable; aircraft and helicopters are also used. As a result the indigenous population was pushed out of the areas where they lived. Developmental activities are destroying the rainforest; a large part of it has already been lost, with topsoil washed away by heavy rain and the lush forest turning into barren land in places.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Explain slash and burn agriculture. → Trees are cut and burnt to clear land for crops; after a few years the soil loses fertility and people move to a new patch.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How did the Trans-Amazon highway affect the region? → It opened the forest to outsiders, leading to deforestation and displacement of indigenous people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling manioc a fruit; it is a root crop.
- Thinking deforestation affects only trees — it affects soil, rainfall, wildlife and people.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Clearing forest patches by cutting and burning for farming
Large apartment-like house with slanting roof
Road built in 1970 opening up the forest
Where it flows into another body of water

quiz.why: Manioc (cassava) is the staple food of many people in the Amazon basin. It is a root crop made into flour.

quiz.q: Slash and burn is a type of
quiz.why: Slash and burn is a farming method. Trees are cut and burnt, and crops grown on the cleared land.

quiz.q: The Trans-Amazon highway was built in
quiz.why: The Trans-Amazon highway was built in 1970. It opened the forest to settlers and ranchers.
A maloca is a large house in the Amazon forest in which many families of a community live together.
Clearing the forest for roads, farms and ranches is deforestation, and it is the major threat to the Amazon and its people.

story.title: From the mountains to the Sundarbans

scenes.text: Rivers fed by Himalayan glaciers flow down to the plains of north and east India.
Farmers grow rice in flooded fields, jute along the rivers, tea on the hill slopes of Assam.
Near the sea lies the mangrove delta of the Sundarbans, home of the Royal Bengal tiger.

steps.title: The basin
steps.body: The tributaries of the **Ganga** (Ghaghara, Son, Chambal, Gandak, Kosi) and of the **Brahmaputra** drain it. The basin lies in the **subtropical region** between about 10°N and 30°N. The plains, the mountains, the foothills and the **Sundarbans delta** are its main features. **Ox-bow lakes** dot the plain. The area is dominated by **monsoon** climate: rain from mid-June to mid-September; summers hot, winters cool.

steps.title: Agriculture and vegetation
steps.body: The plains have fertile soil. **Rice** is the main crop (needs plenty of water); other crops are wheat, maize, sorghum, gram and millets; cash crops **sugarcane and jute**. **Banana** plantations in some areas; **tea** in West Bengal and Assam; silk from silkworms in Bihar and Assam. Terraced farming on mountains and hills. Vegetation varies with landform: tropical deciduous trees (teak, sal, peepal) in the plains; bamboo groves in the Brahmaputra plains; **mangroves** in the delta; coniferous trees (pine, deodar, fir) in the cooler hills of Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.

steps.title: Wildlife
steps.body: Elephants, tigers, deer and monkeys; the one-horned **rhinoceros** in the Brahmaputra plains; crocodiles and alligators in the delta; freshwater **dolphin** (locally **Susu**) in the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers — its presence shows the health of the river; it is endangered due to pollution. Fish such as rohu, catla and hilsa; **fish and rice** form the staple diet of the region. The **Royal Bengal tiger** lives in the Sundarbans.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is rice the main crop of the Ganga–Brahmaputra plains? → Fertile alluvial soil and plentiful water from monsoon rain and rivers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the basin 'tropical rainforest' like the Amazon — it is subtropical with a monsoon climate.
- Thinking dolphins live only in seas; the Ganga river dolphin is freshwater.

quiz.q: The Ganga–Brahmaputra basin lies in the
quiz.why: The Ganga–Brahmaputra basin lies in the subtropical region, roughly between 10°N and 30°N.
Rice is the main crop of the Ganga–Brahmaputra plains. Manioc, coffee and cocoa belong to other regions.
The Sundarbans is the mangrove forest in the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta.

quiz.q: Ganga river dolphin is locally called
quiz.why: The Ganga river dolphin is locally called susu. Rohu, catla and hilsa are fish.

quiz.q: One-horned rhinoceros is found in the
quiz.why: The one-horned rhinoceros lives in the Brahmaputra plains of Assam.

lessons.title: Settlements, cities and tourism; comparing the two regions

scenes.text: Cities like Kanpur, Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata line the rivers.
Tourists visit the ghats of Varanasi, the Taj Mahal on the Yamuna, and the Sundarbans.
How is this crowded, farmed basin different from the thinly populated Amazon?

steps.title: Settlements and transport
steps.body: The mountain areas with steep slopes have **inhospitable terrain**, so few people live there. The **plains** provide the most suitable land for human habitation: flat, fertile, well-watered — so **population density is very high**. Cities along the Ganga include **Allahabad (Prayagraj), Kanpur, Varanasi, Lucknow, Patna and Kolkata**; wastewater from them is often released untreated into rivers, polluting them. All four types of transport are well developed: roads, railways, waterways (along rivers, especially in the delta), and airways.

steps.title: Tourism
steps.body: Tourism is important: the **Taj Mahal** on the Yamuna at Agra, Allahabad at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, Buddhist stupas in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, **Lucknow** (Imambara), Assam (Kaziranga, Manas wildlife sanctuaries), Arunachal Pradesh (a distinct tribal culture). Sundarbans delta for wildlife.

steps.title: Comparing the regions
steps.body:
- **Amazon**: equatorial; hot and wet all year; dense rainforest; thinly populated; slash-and-burn farming; threats: deforestation.
- **Ganga–Brahmaputra**: subtropical; monsoon; fertile plains intensively farmed; very densely populated; threats: river pollution, floods, pressure on land.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is the population dense in the Ganga plains but thin in the Amazon? → The plains are flat, fertile and good for farming and transport; the Amazon is covered with thick rainforest, hard to clear and farm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the pollution problem from cities' untreated wastewater.
- Thinking both regions have the same climate.

quiz.q: Most suitable land for habitation in the basin
quiz.why: The plains are flat and fertile, with water, so they are best for living and farming. Mountains, glaciers and deep forest are hard to live in.

quiz.q: City at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna
quiz.why: Allahabad (Prayagraj) stands where the Ganga and the Yamuna meet.

quiz.q: A major problem caused by cities along the Ganga
quiz.why: Many cities along the Ganga let untreated wastewater flow into the river, which pollutes it.

quiz.q: Which basin is more densely populated?
quiz.why: The Ganga–Brahmaputra basin is much more densely populated than the Amazon, as it has fertile plains and a long history of farming.
Kaziranga in Assam is a wildlife sanctuary known for one-horned rhinoceroses. Hemis is in Ladakh, Gir in Gujarat and the Sundarbans in West Bengal.

questions.q: The Amazon basin lies near the
questions.why: The Amazon basin lies near the equator, so it has a hot, wet climate.

questions.q: Staple food in the Amazon
questions.why: Manioc (cassava) is the staple food in the Amazon region.

questions.q: Royal Bengal tiger lives in the
questions.why: The Sundarbans delta is the home of the Royal Bengal tiger.

questions.q: Main crop of the Ganga plains
questions.why: Rice is the main crop of the Ganga plains, which are warm and wet in the monsoon.

questions.q: Climate of the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin
questions.why: The Ganga–Brahmaputra basin has a monsoon climate, with a rainy season and a dry season.

questions.q: Slash and burn is practised in the
questions.why: Slash and burn farming is done by people of the Amazon basin, who clear small patches of forest.

questions.q: Tea is grown in
questions.why: Tea is grown on the hill slopes of Assam and West Bengal, where there is plenty of rain and the water drains away.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Population is dense in the Ganga plains. Reason (R): The plains are flat, fertile and well-watered.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: the Ganga plains are densely populated. R is true: they are flat, fertile and well-watered, which supports farming and many people. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The rainforest floor is brightly lit. Reason (R): Tall trees form a thick canopy.
questions.why: A is false: the rainforest floor is dark. R is true: tall trees form a thick canopy, which blocks most of the light.

questions.q: Trans-Amazon highway was built in
questions.why: The Trans-Amazon highway was built in 1970.

questions.q: Presence of river dolphins indicates
questions.why: River dolphins need clean water. Their presence is a sign of a healthy river, and their decline is a sign of pollution.

questions.q: Case: A traveller sees mangroves, crocodiles and a striped big cat on a delta. Where?
questions.why: Mangroves, crocodiles and the Royal Bengal tiger on a delta point to the Sundarbans.

questions.q: Case: Indigenous families lose their homes after a big road opens the forest to ranchers. Which region?
questions.why: The Trans-Amazon highway opened the Amazon forest to ranchers and settlers. This cost indigenous families their homes.

questions.q: Which is a common threat in BOTH regions?
options: Human activities damaging forests and rivers
questions.why: In both regions, human activities such as cutting forests and polluting rivers threaten nature. Volcanoes, dunes and snowstorms are not common to both.

questions.q: Arrange from source to sea in the Ganga basin: delta, plains, mountains
questions.why: A river starts in the mountains, flows across the plains and ends in a delta at the sea. So the order is mountains, plains, delta.

questions.q: Why does the Amazon basin have thick forests while the Ganga plains are largely farmed?
options: Constant heavy rain and less clearing in the Amazon; dense population cleared the Ganga plains for farming long ago
