questions.why: The Amazon has heavy rain all year and was less cleared, so its forests remain thick. The Ganga plains have long been settled by dense populations, and the land was cleared for farming.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Life in the Deserts (Geography)
courses.summary: The hot desert of the Sahara and the cold desert of Ladakh: their location, climate, plants, animals, people, ways of life and how they are changing.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish hot and cold deserts with examples
Learners can describe the Sahara's climate, flora, fauna and people
Learners can describe Ladakh's climate, flora, fauna and people
Learners can explain how modern changes affect desert life
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

story.title: A sea of sand… and more

scenes.text: Most people imagine the Sahara as endless sand dunes.
But it also has gravel plains and rocky plateaus with bare rock surfaces.
Days are scorching hot; nights can be freezing cold.

steps.title: Deserts
steps.body: Deserts are areas of very **low rainfall**, scanty vegetation and extreme temperatures. They can be **hot** or **cold**.

steps.title: The Sahara
steps.body: The **Sahara** in **North Africa** is the **world's largest (hot) desert**, covering about **8.54 million sq km**. It touches **eleven countries**: Algeria, Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, Sudan, Tunisia and Western Sahara. Besides sand dunes, it has **gravel plains and elevated plateaus with bare rocky surfaces**; some rocks are more than 2500 m high. Under the sand lie oil and other minerals. The Sahara once was a lush green plain — cave paintings show rivers with crocodiles.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: **Very hot and dry**; a short rainy season; the sky is cloudless and clear. Moisture evaporates faster than it accumulates. **Days are unbelievably hot** — temperatures can rise above 50 °C — heating the sand and bare rocks, which radiate heat. **Nights may be freezing cold**, with temperatures dropping to nearly zero degrees.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why are desert nights so cold? → There are no clouds and little moisture; the sand and rocks lose heat quickly after sunset.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name four countries touched by the Sahara. → Egypt, Libya, Algeria, Chad (any four of the eleven).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Sahara is only sand; there are large rocky and gravel areas.
- Thinking deserts are always hot — cold deserts exist (Ladakh).

statements.s: The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert.
The Sahara is only sand dunes.
statements.why: Also gravel plains and rocky plateaus.

statements.s: Nights in the Sahara can be freezing cold.
The Sahara touches eleven countries.
The Sahara receives heavy rain every day.

quiz.why: The Sahara is in North Africa. It is the largest hot desert in the world.
The Sahara covers about 8.54 million sq km, the largest hot desert in the world.

options: very hot and dry, with cold nights
quiz.why: Deserts are very hot by day and cold at night, as clear skies let heat escape. They are also dry.
Beneath the Sahara sands are minerals, oil and gas, which are being used.

quiz.q: Cave paintings show the Sahara was once
quiz.why: Cave paintings show animals and people, which suggests the Sahara was once a green region with rivers and grass, before the climate changed.

scenes.text: After a long journey across the desert, a caravan reaches an oasis.
Water rises from underground; date palms grow around it.
Bedouin families set up tents and water their camels.

steps.title: Flora and fauna
steps.body: Vegetation: **cactus, date palms and acacia**. In some places there are **oases** — green islands with date palms surrounding them. Animals: **camels, hyenas, jackals, foxes, scorpions**, many varieties of snakes and lizards.

steps.title: People
steps.body: The Sahara is inhabited by various groups pursuing different activities. **Bedouins and Tuaregs** are nomadic tribes rearing livestock — goats, sheep, camels and horses — which give milk, hides (for belts, slippers, water bottles) and hair (for mats, carpets, clothes, blankets). They wear heavy robes to protect themselves from dust storms and hot winds. The oasis in the Sahara and the **Nile valley in Egypt** support settled populations; since water is available, people grow **date palms**, crops such as **rice, wheat, barley and beans**, and **Egyptian cotton** (famous worldwide).

steps.title: Changing life
steps.body: Discovery of **oil** — in Algeria, Libya and Egypt — is transforming the Sahara. Other minerals of importance: **iron, phosphorus, manganese and uranium**. Glass and steel buildings dot the skyline; nomadic herders take to city life to find jobs in oil and gas operations.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why do desert nomads wear heavy robes? → To protect themselves from dust storms and hot winds.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What is an oasis? → A fertile green area in a desert where underground water reaches the surface; date palms grow around it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking no farming is possible in the Sahara — oases and the Nile valley are farmed.
- Confusing Bedouins/Tuaregs (Sahara) with Ladakhis.

pairs: Famous crop of the Nile valley
Mineral transforming the Sahara (Algeria, Libya, Egypt)

quiz.why: The nomadic tribes of the Sahara are the Bedouins and the Tuaregs.
Date palms grow around desert oases where there is water. Their fruit is a food and trade item.
The camel, which can go long without water, is the animal of the desert.
Oil and natural gas have been found in the Sahara, in countries like Algeria, Libya and Egypt.

quiz.q: Why do nomads keep camels, goats and sheep?
quiz.why: Desert nomads keep camels, goats and sheep for milk, meat, hides and hair, which they use for clothing and tents.

scenes.text: High in the Great Himalayas, Ladakh lies in the rain shadow of the mountains.
Winters are bitterly cold; the air is thin and dry; sunlight is fierce.
Prayer flags flutter outside monasteries perched on hills.

steps.title: Location and land
steps.body: **Ladakh**, now a Union Territory of India, is a **cold desert** lying in the Great Himalayas, to the east of Jammu and Kashmir. The Karakoram Range in the north and the Zanskar mountains in the south enclose it. Several rivers flow through it, the **Indus** being the most important; they form deep valleys and gorges. Several glaciers are found here, e.g. the Gangri glacier. Ladakh is also called **Khapa-chan**, meaning **snow land**. Its altitude varies from about 3000 m in Kargil to more than 8000 m in the Karakoram.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Due to its high altitude, the climate is **extremely cold and dry**. The air is so thin that the heat of the sun can be felt intensely. Day temperatures in summer are just above zero, and night temperatures well below **−30 °C**; in winter it gets freezing cold, with temperatures below −40 °C for most of the time. As it lies in the **rain shadow** of the Himalayas, there is little rainfall (as low as 10 cm every year). The area experiences freezing winds and burning hot sunlight: if you sit in the sun with your feet in the shade, you may suffer both sunstroke and frostbite!

steps.title: Flora and fauna
steps.body: Due to high aridity, vegetation is sparse: scanty patches of grass and shrubs for animals to graze; groves of **willows and poplars** in valleys; fruit trees like apples, apricots and walnuts bloom in the summer. Birds: robins, redstarts, Tibetan snowcock, raven, hoopoe — many migratory. Animals: **wild goats, wild sheep, yak** and special dogs. Yak milk is used to make cheese and butter; hair of sheep and goat is used to make woollens. The **chiru (Tibetan antelope)** is endangered — hunted for its wool, **shahtoosh**, which is light and extremely warm.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is Ladakh a desert even though it has snow? → It gets very little rainfall (rain shadow) and has sparse vegetation; it is a cold desert.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a desert must be hot.
- Mixing chiru (antelope, shahtoosh) with yak.

quiz.why: Ladakh is a cold desert, in the rain shadow of the Himalayas. It is dry and freezing in winter.
The Indus is the most important river of Ladakh.
Khapa-chan, the Ladakhi name for the region, means snow land.

quiz.q: Ladakh gets little rain because it is in the
quiz.why: The Himalayas block the monsoon clouds, so Ladakh lies in a rain shadow and gets very little rain.
Shahtoosh is a very fine wool from the Tibetan antelope, the chiru. The animal is endangered and hunting it is banned.

lessons.title: People of Ladakh and changing ways

scenes.text: In the short summer, Ladakhi families grow barley, potatoes, peas, beans and turnips.
Winters are long; people celebrate festivals and stay warm indoors.
Tourists arrive by road and air to see monasteries, trek and raft.

steps.title: People and culture
steps.body: People are either **Muslims or Buddhists**. Several Buddhist **monasteries (gompas)** dot the landscape with traditional prayer flags: famous ones are **Hemis, Thiksey, Shey and Lamayuru**. In summer people work in fields growing **barley, potatoes, peas, beans and turnip**; winters are long, and people keep busy with festivities and ceremonies. Women are hard-working: they work in the house and fields and also manage small businesses and shops. **Leh**, the capital of Ladakh, is well connected by road and air; the **Manali–Leh highway** crosses some of the highest passes in the world.

steps.title: Tourism and change
steps.body: Tourism is a major activity: tourists from within India and abroad visit the gompas, trek to meadows and glaciers, and watch ceremonies and festivities. Life is undergoing change due to modernisation, but people have learnt over centuries to live in balance and harmony with nature. Due to scarcity of resources like water and fuel, they are used with reverence and care; nothing is discarded or wasted.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Name three monasteries of Ladakh. → Hemis, Thiksey, Shey (also Lamayuru).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do Ladakhis live in harmony with nature? → They use scarce water and fuel carefully and waste nothing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking farming is impossible in Ladakh — crops are grown in the short summer.
- Thinking Leh is isolated — it is connected by road and air.

activity.prompt: If I visit a desert region, I will:
items: Carry water and use it carefully
Protect myself from the sun and cold with proper clothing
Respect local customs and monasteries
Not litter — carry my waste back
Never buy products made from endangered animals (like shahtoosh)
Learn a few words of the local language

quiz.why: Leh is the capital of Ladakh.
Hemis is a famous monastery (gompa) of Ladakh.
The summer in Ladakh is short, so crops that grow quickly, like barley, potatoes and peas, are grown.

quiz.q: Ladakh is connected to Manali by
quiz.why: The Manali–Leh highway links Ladakh with Manali. It is open only for part of the year, because of snow.

quiz.q: Main religions of the people of Ladakh
quiz.why: Most people in Ladakh are Buddhists or Muslims.

questions.q: Largest hot desert
questions.why: The Sahara, in North Africa, is the largest hot desert in the world.

questions.q: Ladakh is a
questions.why: Ladakh is a cold desert, as it is high up and very dry with cold winters.

questions.q: A green fertile area in a desert
questions.why: An oasis is a green, fertile spot in a desert where water is found.

questions.q: Capital of Ladakh
questions.why: Leh is the capital of Ladakh.

questions.q: Nomads of the Sahara
questions.why: The Bedouins and Tuaregs are the nomads of the Sahara.

questions.q: Main river of Ladakh
questions.why: The Indus is the main river of Ladakh.

questions.q: Famous Egyptian crop
questions.why: Egypt is famous for its cotton, called Egyptian cotton, grown along the Nile.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ladakh receives very little rain. Reason (R): It lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: Ladakh gets very little rain. R is true: it lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, which stop moist monsoon winds. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Farming is impossible anywhere in the Sahara. Reason (R): The Sahara is very dry.
questions.why: A is false: farming is possible in oases and along the Nile, even in the Sahara. R is true that the Sahara is very dry.

questions.q: Shahtoosh is obtained from
questions.why: Shahtoosh wool comes from the chiru, the Tibetan antelope.

questions.q: Desert nights are cold because
options: clear skies let heat escape quickly
questions.why: Desert skies are clear and dry, so the heat gathered by day escapes quickly after sunset. That makes the nights cold.

questions.q: Case: A traveller suffers sunburn and frostbite on the same afternoon. Where is he likely?
questions.why: Ladakh is high up, so the air is thin and the Sun's rays are strong. The air is also cold, so one can get sunburn and frostbite on the same day.

questions.q: Case: Herders in North Africa leave camel-rearing to work in oil and gas fields. This shows
questions.why: Herders now work in oil and gas fields. This shows how desert life has changed with modern developments.

questions.q: Which pair is NOT correct?
questions.why: The yak lives in cold Ladakh, not the Sahara. Date palms grow in oases, the Tuaregs are Saharan nomads, and Hemis is in Ladakh.

questions.q: Compare: in both the Sahara and Ladakh, people adapt by
options: using scarce water carefully and suitable clothing
questions.why: In both deserts water is scarce, so people use it carefully. They also wear clothes suited to the climate, loose and light in the Sahara, and warm woollen in Ladakh.

questions.q: Which minerals are found in the Sahara besides oil?
questions.why: Besides oil, the Sahara has minerals such as iron, phosphorus, manganese and uranium.

courses.title: Ch 1 · On Equality (Civics)
courses.summary: Equality as a core value of Indian democracy: the equal right to vote, unequal treatment and its effect on dignity, what the Constitution says, how governments promote equality, and lessons from the civil rights struggle in the USA.
outcomes: Learners can explain universal adult franchise and equal voting rights
Learners can identify unequal treatment based on caste, religion, gender or economic status and its effect on dignity
Learners can state constitutional provisions for equality
Learners can describe government measures like the midday meal scheme and compare with the US civil rights movement

scenes.text: On election day, a cleaner, a factory owner, a teacher and a farmer stand in the same queue.
Each gets an ink mark and one vote — no more, no less.
In a democracy, every adult citizen's vote has equal value.

steps.title: Universal adult franchise
steps.body: In India, **all adults (18 years and above)**, regardless of religion, caste, education, gender, or whether rich or poor, have the right to vote. This is **universal adult franchise**, an important aspect of all democracies. It rests on the idea of **equality** — every adult has one vote, and each vote has equal value.

steps.title: Political equality is not everything
steps.body: Having an equal right to vote does not automatically mean people are treated equally in other ways. Many poor people lack basic facilities; people still face discrimination due to caste, religion, gender and economic background.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: A wealthy businessman says his vote should count more because he pays more taxes. Is he right? → No. Under universal adult franchise, every adult citizen has one vote of equal value.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What is the minimum age to vote in India? → **18 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only educated or property-owning people can vote — every adult citizen can.
- Assuming equal voting means all inequalities have ended.

statements.s: Every adult citizen of India can vote.
A rich person gets more votes than a poor person.
The voting age in India is 18.
Equal voting rights mean there is no discrimination at all.
statements.why: Discrimination still exists in daily life.

options: all adults have the right to vote
quiz.why: Universal adult franchise means that all adult citizens have the right to vote, whatever their caste, religion, sex or wealth.
In India the voting age is 18 years.
Every vote counts the same, whether the voter is rich or poor. This is a form of equality.

quiz.q: Universal adult franchise is based on the idea of
quiz.why: Universal adult franchise rests on the idea that all people are equal, so each has one vote.

quiz.q: Who cannot be stopped from voting because of their religion?
quiz.why: No adult citizen can be stopped from voting because of religion. Everyone has the equal right to vote.

scenes.text: A family looking for a flat is told "We don't rent to people like you" because of their religion.
A student is made to sit separately because of her caste.
Such treatment hurts people's dignity — their sense of self-respect.

steps.title: Forms of inequality
steps.body: People are often treated unequally because of their **religion, caste, gender, disability or economic background**. The caste system in India has long denied 'lower' castes equal treatment; Dalits faced exclusion, and many experiences are recorded in writings like **Omprakash Valmiki's** autobiography *Joothan*, describing discrimination he faced in school.

steps.title: Dignity
steps.body: When people are treated unequally, their **dignity** is violated — they feel humiliated and their self-respect is hurt. Recognising the dignity of every person is at the heart of equality.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: A shopkeeper refuses to serve a customer because he is from a 'lower' caste. Which value is violated? → **Equality** and the customer's **dignity**; it is also against the law.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name four grounds on which people may face discrimination. → Religion, caste, gender, economic status (also disability).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking discrimination is only physical harm — insults and exclusion also violate dignity.
- Thinking inequality is natural and cannot change.

a.text: In your class, some students refuse to share a bench with a new classmate because of her caste. What do you do?

choices.label: Sit with her and invite others to join
choices.feedback: You stand up for equality and dignity.

choices.label: Ignore it — it's not my business

c.text: She looks hurt and alone. Do you want to reconsider?

choices.label: Yes, sit with her and talk to the teacher

b.text: The teacher thanks you and explains to the class that the Constitution forbids caste discrimination.

choices.label: Suggest a class discussion on equality

d.text: The class makes a "Respect for All" chart. Equality grows through small daily actions.

quiz.why: Dignity means self-respect, the feeling that one is of worth and should be treated with respect.
Joothan is the autobiography of Omprakash Valmiki, a Dalit writer. It describes the caste discrimination he faced.

quiz.q: Treating someone unequally because of caste is
quiz.why: Treating people unequally because of their caste is discrimination.
Unequal treatment makes people feel humiliated and hurts their dignity.

quiz.q: Which is a ground of discrimination?
quiz.why: Discrimination can be on grounds like religion, caste, sex or race. Shoe size, hobby and colour preference are not grounds for it.

lessons.title: Equality in the Constitution and government action

scenes.text: At noon, all children in a government school sit together for a cooked midday meal.
More poor children now come to school and stay — and they learn better when not hungry.
Children of all castes and religions eat together.

steps.title: The Constitution
steps.body:
The Indian Constitution recognises **every person as equal**. Every individual — male or female, of any caste, religion, tribe, educational or economic background — is equal.

- Every person is **equal before the law**.
- **No person can be discriminated against** on the basis of religion, race, caste, place of birth or sex.
- Everyone has access to **all public places** — playgrounds, hotels, shops, markets; wells, bathing ghats.
- **Untouchability has been abolished**.

steps.title: How governments act
steps.body: Governments implement equality through **laws** (e.g. against discrimination) and **programmes/schemes**. The **Midday Meal Scheme** provides cooked lunch in government elementary schools. It was introduced first in **Tamil Nadu**; in **2001** the **Supreme Court** asked all state governments to begin it. Effects: more poor children enrolled and attended; children of all castes eat together; reduced hunger helped concentration. (There were cases where some parents objected to Dalit cooks — showing prejudice persists and must be challenged.)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: State two provisions of the Constitution on equality. → Every person is equal before the law; no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, place of birth or sex.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How did the midday meal promote equality? → It increased enrolment of poor children and made children of all castes share a meal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking laws alone end inequality — attitudes must also change.
- Mixing the year: the Supreme Court direction on midday meals was in 2001.

items: Share my lunch table with anyone
Speak up if someone is insulted for caste, religion or gender
Use respectful words for every person and job
Include classmates with disabilities in games
Learn about the Constitution's equality rights

quiz.q: According to the Constitution, every person is
quiz.why: The Constitution says every person is equal before the law. Wealth, caste or birth gives no special place.
Untouchability has been abolished by the Constitution of India, and it is a punishable offence.

quiz.q: Midday meal scheme was first introduced in
quiz.why: The midday meal scheme was first introduced in Tamil Nadu and later spread to other states.

quiz.q: The Supreme Court directed all states to start midday meals in
quiz.why: In 2001 the Supreme Court directed all state governments to start midday meals in schools.

quiz.q: Equal access to public places includes
quiz.why: All people have equal access to public places such as wells, shops and playgrounds, not just temples or offices.

lessons.title: Equality elsewhere: the US civil rights movement

scenes.text: On 1 December 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama (USA), an African-American woman named Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white man.
Her refusal sparked a huge movement for equal rights.
In 1964 the USA passed the Civil Rights Act.

steps.title: The struggle
steps.body: In the USA, African-Americans (descendants of enslaved Africans) were treated unequally and denied equality through laws (segregation) until the 1960s — in transport, schools, theatres, restaurants. **Rosa Parks**' refusal (1955) led to the **Civil Rights Movement**. The **Civil Rights Act of 1964** prohibited discrimination on the basis of race, religion or national origin and stated that all schools would be open to African-American children.

steps.title: Lessons for us
steps.body: Equality is a struggle in many democracies. Laws are essential, but people must also change attitudes and keep raising their voices. Persons with disabilities, women and minorities still face challenges everywhere.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do? → Prohibited discrimination on the basis of race, religion or national origin; opened schools to African-American children.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why is Rosa Parks remembered? → Her refusal to give up her bus seat in 1955 sparked the Civil Rights Movement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking inequality is only India's problem.
- Mixing 1955 (Rosa Parks) and 1964 (Civil Rights Act).

events.text: Indian Constitution comes into force with equality rights
Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat
Supreme Court directs midday meals in all states

quiz.q: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat in
quiz.why: Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white man in Montgomery, USA, in 1955.
The US Civil Rights Act was passed in 1964, after years of struggle.

quiz.q: Civil Rights Act prohibited discrimination on the basis of
quiz.why: The Civil Rights Act banned discrimination on the basis of race, religion and national origin, among other grounds.

quiz.q: The movement for equal rights of African-Americans is called
quiz.why: The struggle for equal rights of African-Americans in the USA is called the Civil Rights Movement.

options: equality needs laws and changes in attitudes
quiz.why: These struggles show that laws are needed but not enough. Attitudes must also change for equality to become real.

questions.q: Minimum voting age in India
questions.why: The minimum voting age in India is 18 years.

questions.q: Universal adult franchise is based on
questions.why: Universal adult franchise is based on equality, since every adult has one vote of equal value.

questions.q: Untouchability in India is
questions.why: The Constitution of India abolished untouchability, and practising it is punishable.

questions.q: Rosa Parks was from
questions.why: Rosa Parks was an African-American woman from the USA. Her protest took place in Montgomery, Alabama.

questions.q: Midday meals began first in
questions.why: The midday meal scheme started first in Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Dignity refers to
questions.why: Dignity means self-respect, which is hurt by unequal treatment.

questions.q: Joothan describes
options: caste discrimination faced by its author
questions.why: Joothan is the story of the caste discrimination faced by its author, Omprakash Valmiki.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Equal right to vote does not end all inequality. Reason (R): People still face discrimination due to caste, religion and gender.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: the vote is equal, but inequality has not ended. R is true: people still face discrimination by caste, religion and gender. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The midday meal scheme reduced caste prejudice completely. Reason (R): Children of all castes eat together.
questions.why: A is false: the scheme helped, but caste prejudice has not completely disappeared. R is true that children of all castes eat together, but this has not removed prejudice completely.

questions.q: Which is NOT a ground of discrimination banned by the Constitution?
questions.why: The Constitution bans discrimination by caste, sex, religion and similar grounds. Selecting by merit in an exam is not discrimination.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act (1964) opened
questions.why: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 opened schools to all African-American children and ended segregation in many public places.

questions.q: Case: A hotel refuses entry to a family because of their religion. Under the Constitution this is
options: not allowed — everyone has access to public places
allowed if the hotel is small
questions.why: The Constitution gives everyone access to public places such as hotels, shops and wells. Refusing entry because of religion is discrimination and is not allowed.

questions.q: Case: After midday meals started, more girls from poor families attended school. This shows
questions.why: The midday meal brought more poor girls to school. This shows a government scheme can promote equality.

questions.q: Why is dignity linked with equality?
options: Unequal treatment humiliates people and hurts their self-respect
questions.why: Unequal treatment humiliates people and hurts their self-respect, so dignity and equality are closely linked.

questions.q: Arrange: Civil Rights Act; Rosa Parks protest; Indian Constitution; Supreme Court midday meal order
options: Constitution (1950) → Rosa Parks (1955) → Civil Rights Act (1964) → midday meal order (2001)
questions.why: The Indian Constitution came into force in 1950, Rosa Parks's protest was in 1955, the Civil Rights Act was in 1964, and the Supreme Court midday meal order was in 2001.

questions.q: Which best describes how equality is achieved?
options: Laws, government programmes and change in people's attitudes together
questions.why: Equality needs laws, government programmes and changes in people's attitudes working together. No single one is enough.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Role of the Government in Health (Civics)
courses.summary: What good health needs, public and private health care in India, inequality in access to health care, the government's responsibility (with a landmark court case), and what we can learn from Kerala and Costa Rica.
outcomes: Learners can explain what health means beyond the absence of illness
Learners can compare public and private health services
Learners can explain why access to health care is unequal
Learners can explain the government's duty to protect life and give examples of better public health
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: What is health? Health care in India

scenes.text: In a village, children fall ill every monsoon from dirty water.
Medicines help for a while, but the illness keeps coming back.
When clean drinking water and toilets arrive, illness drops sharply.

steps.title: Meaning of health
steps.body: Health means our ability to remain free of illness and injuries, but it also depends on **clean water, a pollution-free environment, adequate food** and freedom from mental strain. People who live in dirty, crowded conditions with poor food and water fall ill more often.

steps.title: The Indian situation
steps.body: India has positives: a large number of doctors, clinics and hospitals; much experience in public health; one of the largest producers of medicines in the world; a growing number of patients from abroad come for treatment (**medical tourism**). But problems remain: most doctors settle in urban areas, so rural people travel long distances; many die of preventable diseases like TB, malaria, diarrhoea; many poor people cannot afford good food or care.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is clean drinking water part of health? → Many diseases like diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid spread through dirty water.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Give one positive and one problem of health care in India. → Positive: India produces a lot of medicine. Problem: doctors are concentrated in cities, rural areas lack care.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking health = hospitals only; prevention (water, sanitation, food) matters most.
- Assuming more hospitals automatically means everyone gets care.

activity.prompt: Helps health directly or is a problem?

options: clean water, food, environment and care
quiz.why: Health depends on many things, such as clean water, food, a clean environment and medical care, not medicine alone.

quiz.q: Patients coming from abroad for treatment is called
quiz.why: People who travel to another country for medical treatment are called medical tourists, so the practice is medical tourism.
Diarrhoea and cholera spread through dirty water. They are water-borne diseases.

quiz.q: A problem of Indian health care
quiz.why: Most doctors and good hospitals are in cities. Rural areas, where most people live, have far fewer.

quiz.q: India is one of the largest producers of
quiz.why: India is one of the largest producers of medicines in the world.

scenes.text: Ravi breaks his arm. At the government hospital, treatment is free or very cheap but the queue is long.
At a private hospital nearby, he is seen quickly, but the bill is huge.
Who can afford which? This is a big question for health in India.

steps.title: Public health services
steps.body:
A chain of health centres and hospitals run by the **government**:

- Village level: health centres with a nurse and village health worker
- **Primary Health Centres (PHCs)**: cover many villages
- District level: **District Hospital**
- Cities: large government hospitals and specialised hospitals

Called 'public' because the government provides health care for all, **free or at low cost**, so that even the poor can seek treatment. It also takes action to prevent diseases like TB, malaria, jaundice, cholera, diarrhoea, chikungunya.

steps.title: Private health services
steps.body: Doctors, clinics, nursing homes, large corporate hospitals and laboratories owned by **individuals or companies**. People pay for every service; they charge high fees. Private facilities are often concentrated in urban areas. Sometimes **unnecessary tests, medicines or procedures** are prescribed. In India, private services are growing, while public services are not growing as fast.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why are government hospitals called public? → They are run by the government for everyone and are free or low-cost, paid for by taxes.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Give two problems with private health care. → High costs that the poor cannot afford; sometimes unnecessary tests or medicines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking public hospitals are free because they cost nothing to run — they are funded by our taxes.
- Thinking private always means better.

quiz.why: Primary Health Centres are run by the government, so they are public health services.

quiz.q: Public health services are funded by
quiz.why: Public health services are paid for with taxes collected by the government.
Private health services charge fees for every service, such as tests and treatment.
Private care aims at profit, and some may prescribe unnecessary tests or costly treatment.

quiz.q: The aim of public health care
options: care for all, free or low-cost
quiz.why: Public health care aims to give care to all, free or at low cost, including the poor.

lessons.title: Health care and inequality; the government's duty

scenes.text: In 1992, a man named Hakim Sheikh fell from a train in West Bengal and suffered serious head injuries.
He was taken to several government hospitals, but each refused, saying they had no bed or facility.
He finally got treatment at a private hospital and went to court. The court's judgement became a landmark.

steps.title: Inequality in access
steps.body:
- Only about 20% of the population can afford the medicines they need during an illness; even many 'non-poor' people get into debt due to medical expenses.
- Women are often not taken to a doctor promptly; their health concerns are neglected.
- Many tribal areas have few health centres, and they do not run properly.

Poor people: they live in conditions without basic amenities, fall ill more often, and must spend a large part of their income on treatment.

steps.title: The government's responsibility
steps.body: In a democracy, the government must work for people's welfare, including health. In the **Hakim Sheikh** case, the court said that failure of a government hospital to provide timely medical treatment to a person in need violates the person's **right to life** under **Article 21** of the Constitution; it ordered the state to pay compensation and directed that steps be taken so that emergency treatment is provided. Primary health centres and hospitals must be equipped to deal with emergencies.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What did the court say in the Hakim Sheikh case? → Not providing timely emergency treatment in a government hospital violates the right to life (Article 21).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do many families fall into debt during illness? → Private treatment and medicines are expensive and public facilities are inadequate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking health is only a private matter — it is the government's duty too.
- Forgetting that women and tribal communities face extra barriers.

activity.prompt: Questions people ask about health and rights:

items.q: Is health care a right in India?
items.a: Courts have read the right to life (Article 21) as including the duty of government to provide emergency medical treatment. Governments also run public hospitals for all.

items.q: What should I do in a medical emergency?
items.a: Call 112 (all emergencies) or go to the nearest hospital. Government hospitals must provide emergency care.
Many are bought privately; government schemes and generic medicine shops can lower costs. Ask a doctor about generic options.
Not necessarily. Quality varies. Public hospitals often have skilled doctors; overcrowding is the main problem.

quiz.why: The Hakim Sheikh case happened in 1992. He was refused treatment in several hospitals after a fall from a train.

quiz.q: Right to life is in Article
quiz.why: The right to life is in Article 21 of the Constitution. The court read it as including the right to health care.

quiz.q: In the Hakim Sheikh case, the court held that
options: denying timely emergency treatment violates the right to life
quiz.why: The court held that denying timely emergency treatment violates the right to life. Hospitals have a duty to treat in emergencies.

quiz.q: Who often faces neglect in getting health care?
quiz.why: Women and tribal communities often face neglect in getting health care.
112 is the all-in-one emergency number in India.

lessons.title: Better models: Kerala and Costa Rica

scenes.text: Costa Rica decided long ago not to have an army.
It spends that money on health, education and basic needs.
It is one of the healthiest countries in Latin America.

steps.title: Kerala
steps.body: In **1996**, the Kerala government made major changes: **40% of the entire state budget** was given to **panchayats**, which could plan and provide for their own requirements. Villages planned water, food, women's development and education — water supply schemes were checked, schools and anganwadis ensured. Health centres were improved. Despite these efforts, problems like shortage of medicines and insufficient hospital beds remained.

steps.title: Costa Rica
steps.body: **Costa Rica** is considered one of the healthiest countries in South America (Latin America). An important reason is the **Costa Rican Constitution**: several years ago the country took a very important decision **not to have an army**. This helped it spend the money the army would have used on health, education and other basic needs. The government provides basic services and amenities: safe drinking water, sanitation, nutrition, housing, and health education.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How did Kerala improve health in 1996? → It gave 40% of the state budget to panchayats to plan water, food, health and education locally.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What lesson does Costa Rica teach? → Spending on basic needs like water, sanitation, nutrition and health education improves public health.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Kerala solved all health problems — shortages remained.
- Thinking Costa Rica is in Africa; it is in Central America (Latin America).

pairs: No army; spends on health and basic needs
Public health service for a group of villages
Foreign patients coming to India for treatment

quiz.q: Kerala gave what share of its budget to panchayats in 1996?
quiz.why: In 1996 Kerala gave 40% of its state budget to panchayats for local planning.

quiz.q: Costa Rica decided not to have
quiz.why: Costa Rica decided not to have an army. It could then spend on other needs.
Costa Rica spends on health, education and other basic needs of its people.

options: local planning can improve health and services
quiz.why: Kerala's experience shows that planning by local bodies can improve health and services.

options: water, sanitation, nutrition and care for all
quiz.why: Health improves most when people get safe water, sanitation, nutrition and care for all, not just medicines or clinics.

questions.q: Health means
options: freedom from illness and a good environment, food and water
questions.why: Health is more than being free from illness. It also needs a good environment, food, water and care.

questions.q: PHCs are part of
questions.why: PHCs are run by the government, so they are part of public health services.

questions.q: Right to life is Article
questions.why: Article 21 gives the right to life, and the courts have said this includes health care.

questions.q: Costa Rica has no
questions.why: Costa Rica has no army and uses the money on health, education and other needs.

questions.q: Private health services
questions.why: Private health services charge fees for their services.

questions.q: Kerala's 1996 reform gave budget to
questions.why: In 1996 Kerala gave 40% of its budget to panchayats so they could plan locally.

questions.q: Medical tourism means
options: foreigners coming to India for treatment
questions.why: Medical tourism means foreigners coming to India to get treatment, as it is often cheaper.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Public health services are free or low-cost. Reason (R): They are funded by taxes paid by people.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: public services are free or low-cost. R is true: taxes paid by people fund them. That is why they can be free or cheap, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Private hospitals are spread evenly across rural India. Reason (R): Private hospitals charge high fees.
questions.why: A is false: private hospitals are mostly in cities and towns, not spread evenly across rural areas. R is true: they charge high fees.

questions.q: Which is a reason the poor fall ill more often?
options: lack of clean water, food and sanitation
questions.why: The poor often live without clean water, enough food and sanitation, so they fall ill more often.

questions.q: The Hakim Sheikh judgement was about
questions.why: The Hakim Sheikh judgement said that government hospitals must give emergency treatment, as it is part of the right to life.

questions.q: Case: A woman in a village has fever for a week but her family delays taking her to a doctor. This shows
questions.why: Delaying care for a woman's week-long fever shows how women's health is often neglected in families.

questions.q: Case: A private clinic orders many costly tests for a minor cold. Possible problem?
questions.why: Ordering many costly tests for a minor cold may be done to earn more money. That is a known problem of some private health care.

questions.q: Which measure would most reduce diarrhoea in a village?
options: a big private hospital in the city
questions.why: Diarrhoea comes from dirty water and poor sanitation. So clean drinking water and toilets prevent it best.

questions.q: Why is health care a government responsibility in a democracy?
options: The government must ensure welfare and protect the right to life of all
questions.why: In a democracy the government must look after people's welfare and protect the right to life of all. Health care is part of it.

questions.q: What do Kerala and Costa Rica both show?
options: Investing in basic needs and local planning improves health
questions.why: Kerala and Costa Rica both show that spending on basic needs and local planning improves health.

courses.title: Ch 3 · How the State Government Works (Civics)
courses.summary: How a state government is formed: MLAs and constituencies, majority and opposition, the Governor and Chief Minister, debates in the Legislative Assembly, and how ministers and departments work, including law-making and responding to public problems.
outcomes: Learners can explain who an MLA is and how they are elected
Learners can explain majority, ruling party and opposition
Learners can distinguish the roles of Governor, Chief Minister and ministers
Learners can describe how the Legislative Assembly and government departments work
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Posters fill the town: candidates from different parties ask for votes for the Legislative Assembly.
The candidate with the most votes in the constituency becomes its MLA.
She will now represent the people in the state's Legislative Assembly.

steps.title: Constituencies and MLAs
steps.body: Every state has a **Legislative Assembly**. Each state is divided into areas called **constituencies**. From each constituency, people elect one representative — the **Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA)**. MLAs belong to different political parties (or may be independent).

steps.title: Majority and opposition
steps.body: A political party whose MLAs win **more than half** the number of constituencies in a state is said to be in a **majority**. The party in majority is the **ruling party**; all other members are the **opposition**. Example: if a state has 224 MLAs, a party needs at least **113** to have a majority. Sometimes no single party wins a majority; parties join to form a **coalition** government.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A state has 70 constituencies. Party A wins 38, B 25, others 7. Who forms the government? → A has more than half (36 needed), so **Party A** is the ruling party; others are the opposition.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What does MLA stand for? → **Member of the Legislative Assembly**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the party with the most votes overall automatically rules — it must win a majority of seats (constituencies).
- Confusing MLA (state) with MP (Parliament, national).

activity.prompt: A state assembly has 288 seats. Minimum seats needed for a majority?

quiz.why: MLA stands for Member of the Legislative Assembly, a person elected to the state Assembly.

quiz.q: Areas from which MLAs are elected
quiz.why: A state is divided into constituencies, and each elects one MLA.

quiz.q: A party with more than half the seats has a
quiz.why: A party that has more than half the seats has a majority and can form the government.

quiz.q: MLAs not in the ruling party form the
quiz.why: MLAs who are not part of the ruling party form the opposition. They question and check the government.

quiz.q: A government of several parties together
quiz.why: When several parties join to form a government, it is called a coalition.

scenes.text: After the election, the Governor invites the leader of the majority party to form the government.
The leader is sworn in as Chief Minister; other MLAs become ministers.
Each minister will head a department — health, education, public works…

steps.title: Who is who
steps.body:
- **Governor**: appointed by the **Central Government** to represent it in the state; formally invites the majority leader to form the government; in some situations acts on constitutional duties.
- **Chief Minister**: leader of the ruling party's MLAs (or the coalition); head of the state government.
- **Ministers**: MLAs chosen by the Chief Minister to head different departments (health, education, public works, agriculture…).
- Ministers are responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

steps.title: Executive and legislature
steps.body: The Chief Minister and ministers are responsible for **running the government** (executive work) — they are also MLAs. The **Legislative Assembly** (all MLAs) debates, makes laws and holds the government accountable.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Who appoints the Governor? → The **Central Government** (formally the President of India).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How is the Chief Minister chosen? → MLAs of the majority party elect their leader, who is invited by the Governor to become Chief Minister.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Governor is elected by the people — the Governor is appointed.
- Thinking ministers are not MLAs — they are usually MLAs.

activity.prompt: Match the office with its role.
pairs: Appointed by the Centre; represents it in the state
MLAs not in the ruling party; question the government

quiz.why: The Governor is appointed by the Central Government (formally the President). The people do not elect the Governor.
The Chief Minister is the head of the state government. The Governor is the formal head of the state.
Ministers are usually chosen from MLAs of the ruling party or coalition.

quiz.q: Who invites the majority leader to form the government?
quiz.why: The Governor invites the leader of the majority party to form the government.

quiz.q: A minister in charge of hospitals is the
quiz.why: The minister in charge of hospitals and health matters is the Health Minister.

scenes.text: In a hot summer, many districts face a severe water shortage; diarrhoea cases rise.
Newspapers report long queues at tankers. MLAs raise questions in the Assembly.
The opposition demands action; the Health Minister replies with the government's plans.

steps.title: How the Assembly works
steps.body: In the Legislative Assembly, MLAs — both ruling party and opposition — **express opinions and ask questions** related to issues (such as a water crisis, health, schools). The concerned **minister answers**, and the Assembly discusses what steps should be taken. Decisions are then taken by the Chief Minister and ministers and **implemented** by government departments. Debates are also how **laws** are discussed and passed (or rejected).

steps.title: Accountability
steps.body: Through questions and debates, the government is **held accountable**. MLAs, opposition parties and the media all play a role. Ordinary people can also participate by writing to officials or MLAs and by **press conferences** organised by different groups, which are reported in the media.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What can an opposition MLA do about a water crisis? → Raise questions in the Assembly, demand answers from the minister, visit affected areas and inform the media.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why are debates important? → They let representatives raise people's problems and make the government explain and act.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the opposition has no role — it questions and checks the government.
- Thinking the Assembly itself runs departments; ministers and officials implement decisions.

activity.prompt: Arrange how a public problem is handled.
items: People face a problem (e.g. water shortage)
Media and MLAs raise it
Questions and debate in the Legislative Assembly
Minister replies; government decides on steps
Departments implement the decision
People and media check whether it worked

quiz.q: In the Assembly, questions are answered by the
quiz.why: In the Assembly, questions are answered by the minister in charge of that matter.
Opposition MLAs question the government, debate its actions and check how it works.
Government departments carry out the decisions of the government.
Press conferences let leaders bring issues to the public's attention through the media.

options: making it answer for its actions
giving it full freedom without questions
quiz.why: Holding the government accountable means making it answer for its actions and decisions.

lessons.title: Making laws and the work of government

scenes.text: After many accidents, the state wants a law to make helmets compulsory for two-wheeler riders.
MLAs debate the bill in the Assembly; some suggest changes.
After voting, it becomes a law; departments then enforce it.

steps.title: Law-making
steps.body: MLAs gathered in the Legislative Assembly discuss and **make new laws** for the state on subjects such as health, police, agriculture, local government. A proposed law (bill) is debated, sometimes amended, and passed by majority vote. After the Governor's assent, it becomes law.

steps.title: Working of the government
steps.body: Apart from the Legislative Assembly, the **government** (Chief Minister and ministers) and its **departments** do the work: building hospitals, running schools, supplying water, maintaining roads. Officials (secretaries, district collectors) carry out the work. People can visit officials and MLAs, write letters, and use the media to make demands.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Name two subjects on which a state government can make laws. → Police and public health (also agriculture, local government).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: After a law is passed, who makes sure it is followed? → Government departments and officials (e.g. police, transport department).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only the Chief Minister makes laws — the whole Assembly debates and votes.
- Thinking laws once passed cannot be changed — they can be amended.

statements.s: MLAs make laws for the state in the Legislative Assembly.
Laws are passed without any debate.
Government departments implement laws and decisions.
People cannot contact their MLA.
statements.why: They can meet or write to MLAs.

statements.s: Laws can be amended later.

quiz.q: A proposed law is called a
quiz.why: A proposed law, before it is passed, is called a bill.

quiz.q: State laws are made in the
quiz.why: State laws are made by the Legislative Assembly, the state legislature.
State laws are carried out by government departments and their officials.

quiz.q: Subject on which a state can make laws
quiz.why: Police is a state subject, so state governments can make laws on it. Defence, foreign affairs and currency are Union subjects.

quiz.q: People can influence the government by
options: writing to officials, meeting MLAs, using media
quiz.why: People can take part by writing to officials, meeting their MLAs and using the media. Staying silent does not help.

questions.q: MLA is elected from a
questions.why: An MLA is elected from a constituency, an area of the state.

questions.q: Head of state government
questions.why: The Chief Minister heads the state government. The Governor is the formal head of the state.

questions.q: The Governor is appointed by the
questions.why: The Governor is appointed by the Central Government, not elected.

questions.q: Party with more than half the seats
questions.why: A party with more than half the seats has a majority.

questions.q: A state with 140 seats needs ___ for a majority
questions.why: A majority means more than half. Half of 140 is 70, so at least 71 seats are needed.

questions.q: The opposition's role
questions.why: The opposition questions the government and checks its work.

questions.q: Laws in the state are discussed in the
questions.why: Laws of the state are discussed and passed in the Legislative Assembly.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ministers are answerable to the Legislative Assembly. Reason (R): MLAs can ask questions and debate government actions.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: ministers answer to the Assembly. R is true: MLAs ask questions and debate government actions. That is how they hold ministers accountable, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Governor is elected by MLAs. Reason (R): The Governor represents the Central Government.
questions.why: A is false: the Governor is not elected by MLAs but appointed by the Central Government. R is true: the Governor represents the Centre in the state.

questions.q: A government formed by several parties is
questions.why: A government formed by several parties together is a coalition. The opposition sits outside the government.

questions.q: MLA and MP differ because
options: MLA is in the state assembly; MP in Parliament
questions.why: An MLA is elected to the state Legislative Assembly. An MP is elected to Parliament, the national legislature. They work at different levels.

questions.q: Case: In a 60-seat assembly, Party X has 28, Party Y 20, Party Z 12. X and Z join to form the government. Total and type?
questions.why: X and Z together have 28 + 12 = 40 seats. A majority in a 60-seat house is 31 or more, so 40 is enough. Because two parties join, it is a coalition.

questions.q: Case: Newspapers report a hospital shortage. An MLA raises it in the Assembly and the Health Minister announces new hospitals. This shows
options: how the Assembly holds the government accountable
questions.why: News reports led an MLA to raise the issue in the Assembly, and the minister then acted. This shows how the Assembly holds the government accountable.

questions.q: Who heads a department like education?
questions.why: A minister heads each government department, such as education or health.

questions.q: Arrange: Governor invites leader; elections; CM sworn in; ministers get departments
options: elections → Governor invites → CM sworn in → ministers get departments
CM sworn in → elections → Governor → ministers
questions.why: First elections are held. Then the Governor invites the leader of the majority party, the Chief Minister is sworn in, and the ministers are given their departments.

questions.q: Why is a strong opposition good for democracy?
options: It questions the government and makes it accountable
questions.why: A strong opposition questions the government and makes it answer for its actions. This is a check on power.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Growing up as Boys and Girls (Civics)
courses.summary: How societies shape different roles and expectations for boys and girls, why household work is undervalued and invisible, the double burden faced by women, and how equal sharing and government support can change this.
outcomes: Learners can explain how gender roles are shaped by society, not by nature
Learners can explain why housework and care work are undervalued
Learners can describe the double burden faced by many women
Learners can suggest ways families and governments can share and support care work
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: In the 1920s, a researcher described life in the Samoan islands of the Pacific, where children of both sexes looked after younger siblings and learnt many tasks early.
In a small town in Madhya Pradesh in the 1960s, girls were expected to walk home quickly and stay in, while boys roamed the streets.
What children are allowed to do depends a lot on what society expects of boys and girls.

steps.title: Society shapes roles
steps.body: Being born a boy or a girl is biological, but **how we grow up** — what we wear, play, which jobs we are encouraged to dream of — is shaped by **society**. Different societies and different times have different ideas. These ideas are called **gender roles**, and they can change.

steps.title: Stereotypes
steps.body: A **stereotype** is a fixed idea about a group: 'boys don't cry', 'girls are not good at maths', 'boys can't cook'. Stereotypes limit both boys and girls and are not based on facts.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Is 'girls should play only with dolls' natural or social? → **Social** — toys are chosen by adults and society; children of any gender can enjoy any toy.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Give an example of how gender roles change over time. → Earlier, few women worked as pilots or engineers; today many do.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating social expectations as biological facts.
- Thinking gender stereotypes harm only girls — they limit boys too.

items.text: Boys should be engineers, girls nurses

quiz.q: Gender roles are mainly shaped by
quiz.why: Gender roles are mostly shaped by society, through family, school and customs. They are not fixed by biology.

quiz.q: "Girls are bad at maths" is a
quiz.why: "Girls are bad at maths" is a stereotype, a fixed idea about a group. It is not a fact or law.
Gender roles are learned from society, so they can change over time, and they differ across places.
Stereotypes limit both boys and girls, for example by telling boys not to show feelings or girls not to play sports.
Choosing toys by gender is a habit that society teaches, not a biological need or a rule.

scenes.text: Arav's mother wakes at 5, cooks, cleans, gets children ready, and goes to her office job.
When asked, Arav says, "My mother doesn't work — only my father works."
His sister points out: all that housework is work too!

steps.title: Invisible work
steps.body: Housework — cooking, cleaning, washing, fetching water, caring for children and elders — is mostly done by women and girls. It is **not paid**, so it is often **not seen as 'work'** and is **undervalued**. Yet it is hard, takes many hours and is essential for the family to function. Many women also do **paid domestic work** in others' homes, often at low wages and with little respect.

steps.title: Double burden
steps.body: Many women work outside the home **and** do most of the housework. This is the **double burden**. Time-use surveys show women spend far more hours per day on unpaid household work than men.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is housework called invisible? → Because it is unpaid and taken for granted, people do not recognise it as work.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What is the double burden? → Women doing both paid work outside and most unpaid work at home.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a homemaker 'doesn't work'.
- Thinking domestic workers' jobs are easy — they are physically demanding and long.

activity.prompt: Make a list of the housework done in your home in one day. Who does each task, and how long does it take?
activity.hint: Notice who does most of it. Which tasks could you or other family members share this week?

quiz.why: Housework is undervalued largely because it is unpaid. People often think only work that earns money counts.

quiz.q: Doing both paid work and most housework is the
quiz.why: Doing paid work as well as most of the housework is called the double burden.
Care work means looking after children, the sick and elders. It is usually unpaid in the home.
Paid domestic workers often get low wages, long hours and little respect.

quiz.q: Who usually does more unpaid housework in India?
quiz.why: Time-use surveys show women and girls do much more unpaid housework than men in India.

story.title: A new chart on the fridge

scenes.text: After a class discussion, Neha's family makes a chart: everyone shares cooking, cleaning and shopping.
Her brother learns to cook dal; her father does the laundry.
Her mother finally has time to rest and read.

steps.title: Families can share
steps.body: Housework and care can be shared equally by all members, regardless of gender. Boys learning to cook and clean is a life skill, not a loss of status.

steps.title: Government support
steps.body:
Governments recognise that caring for children is a burden often borne by women. Laws and schemes help:

- **Anganwadis** (child-care centres) in villages provide care, nutrition and pre-school learning.
- Laws require **crèches** (day-care) at workplaces with many women employees.
- Equal Remuneration (equal pay for equal work) is required by law.

These allow more women to take up jobs outside the home.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How do anganwadis help women? → They look after young children, so mothers can work or study.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Suggest two ways boys can help at home. → Cook simple meals, wash dishes, look after younger siblings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking sharing housework is only a 'women's issue' — it concerns the whole family.
- Thinking crèches are only for rich workplaces — laws require them in many workplaces.

items: List all daily household tasks
Divide tasks fairly among all members, boys and girls alike
Learn one new task this week (e.g. cooking a simple dish)
Thank family members for care work
Review the plan at the end of the week

quiz.why: Anganwadis give child care, nutrition and pre-school education, especially to poor families.
Crèches are day-care centres where young children are looked after while their parents work.

quiz.q: Equal pay for equal work is
quiz.why: Equal pay for equal work is required by law, so men and women doing the same work should be paid the same.
Housework should be shared by all family members, not left to women and girls only.

quiz.q: Government child-care support helps women to
options: take up jobs outside the home
quiz.why: With child-care support from the government, women can take jobs outside the home.

lessons.title: Practice: case studies on gender and work

scenes.text: Case 1: A girl is stopped from joining the school football team. Case 2: A father is mocked for taking leave to care for his baby. Case 3: A domestic worker is not paid for extra hours.
Students discuss what is unfair and what could change.

steps.title: How to analyse a case
steps.body:
1. Identify the stereotype or unfair treatment.
2. Ask who loses and how (dignity, opportunity, money).
3. Suggest action: family, school, workplace, law.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Case 1: stereotype that 'football is for boys'. The girl loses an opportunity. The school should allow mixed or girls' teams; the Constitution forbids discrimination by sex.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Case 3: the worker's labour is undervalued. She should be paid fairly for extra hours; employers must respect labour laws and her dignity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blaming the person facing the stereotype instead of the stereotype.
- Giving only one-word answers in case-based questions — explain the reasoning.

statements.s: Mocking a father for caring for his baby is a gender stereotype.
Girls cannot legally join sports teams.
statements.why: No such law; discrimination by sex is not allowed in public institutions.

statements.s: Unpaid extra work by domestic workers is fair.
Case answers should explain the reasoning.

quiz.q: A girl being kept from football is due to
quiz.why: Keeping a girl from football because she is a girl is based on a stereotype, not on any real biological reason.

quiz.q: A father taking care of his baby is
quiz.why: A father looking after his baby is good and normal. Care is a shared duty, not a woman's job alone.
Domestic workers deserve fair pay, rest and respect, like any other workers.

quiz.q: The first step in analysing a case
options: identify the unfair treatment or stereotype
quiz.why: To analyse a case, first identify the unfair treatment or stereotype in it. Then think about why it happens and what could change.
Gender equality benefits everyone, because it gives all people the freedom to learn, work and care without limits.

questions.q: Gender roles are
questions.why: Gender roles are shaped by society, which is why they vary across places and can change.

questions.q: Unpaid housework is often
questions.why: Unpaid housework is often undervalued, because no wages are paid, though it takes much time and effort.

questions.q: Anganwadis are
questions.why: Anganwadis are child-care centres run under government schemes.

questions.q: "Boys don't cry" is a
questions.why: "Boys don't cry" is a stereotype. Everyone has feelings and can cry.

questions.q: Double burden refers to
questions.why: The double burden is doing paid work outside the home and also most of the housework.

questions.q: Crèches help
questions.why: Crèches look after young children, so working parents can go to work.

questions.q: Equal pay for equal work is
questions.why: Equal pay for equal work is a legal right. A person cannot be paid less for the same work because of gender.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Housework is often not considered "work". Reason (R): It is unpaid.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: housework is often not seen as work. R is true: it is unpaid, and people link work with pay. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Gender roles are the same in every society. Reason (R): They are biologically fixed.
questions.why: Both are false: gender roles differ from society to society, and they are shaped by society, not biologically fixed.

questions.q: Who benefits when housework is shared equally?
questions.why: When housework is shared, the whole family gains. It is fairer and gives everyone more time for school, work and rest.

questions.q: Which is care work?
questions.why: Looking after a sick grandparent is care work. Watching TV, buying a car and playing a game are not.

questions.q: Case: A woman teacher returns home and does all the cooking and cleaning while others rest. This is an example of
questions.why: The teacher works at school and then does all the housework while others rest. This is the double burden.

questions.q: Case: A village gets an anganwadi; more mothers join a self-help group for work. Why?
options: Children are cared for during the day
questions.why: With the anganwadi caring for children in the day, mothers are free to join the group and earn. So child care support helps women work.

questions.q: Which statement is a stereotype?
options: Boys are naturally bad at cooking
questions.why: "Boys are naturally bad at cooking" is a fixed idea about a group. That makes it a stereotype. Cooking is a skill anyone can learn.

questions.q: Why do time-use surveys matter?
options: They show how much unpaid work women do, making it visible
questions.why: Time-use surveys record how people spend their day, so they show how much unpaid work women do. This makes it visible.

questions.q: Which combination best promotes gender equality at home and work?
options: Sharing housework, child-care services, equal pay laws
questions.why: Equality needs several things together: sharing housework, child-care services and equal pay laws. One alone is not enough.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Women Change the World (Civics)
courses.summary: Stereotypes about women's jobs, the struggle of women to learn and study, schooling and literacy today, and how the women's movement has campaigned, raised awareness, protested and shown solidarity to change laws and attitudes.
outcomes: Learners can identify stereotypes about women and work
Learners can describe how women like Rashsundari Devi and Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain fought to learn
Learners can interpret literacy data and reasons children leave school
Learners can describe strategies and achievements of the women's movement
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Asked what they want to be, girls in a class say "doctor", "pilot", "engineer", "scientist".
Some classmates laugh: "Girls can't be pilots!"
Their teacher shows a photo of Indian women fighter pilots. The laughter stops.

steps.title: Stereotypes about work
steps.body: Many people believe women are better suited to certain jobs — teachers, nurses — and that science, technology, engineering or the army are 'for men'. Such **stereotypes** limit choices: girls are discouraged from some careers, and boys are pressured to earn a lot and not take up 'soft' jobs.

steps.title: Breaking barriers
steps.body: Women in India now work as pilots, police officers, scientists, engineers, judges, sportspersons and leaders. In many families, though, girls still have to fight to study and to choose their careers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Give one stereotype about women's work and how it is harmful. → 'Women can't be engineers' — it discourages talented girls and wastes their abilities.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do stereotypes affect boys? → Boys may be pressured to choose high-paying jobs and discouraged from careers like nursing or teaching.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking ability depends on gender.
- Thinking stereotypes are harmless jokes.

statements.s: Women can be pilots and engineers.
Nursing is only for women.
Stereotypes limit career choices.
Ability depends on gender.
statements.why: It depends on interest, effort and training.

options: a fixed idea about a group
quiz.why: A stereotype is a fixed idea about a group of people. It treats everyone in the group as the same.
"Only men can be scientists" is a stereotype. Many women are scientists.
Stereotypes harm both boys and girls, since they limit what each is expected to do.
Women today work in many fields, such as pilots, judges and scientists, so jobs are not limited to nursing or teaching.
The best response to a stereotype is to question it using facts and examples.

scenes.text: Around 200 years ago in Bengal, a girl named Rashsundari Devi was not allowed to learn to read.
She secretly learnt letters by comparing them with a page from a book her son used.
At about 60, she wrote her autobiography, "Amar Jiban" — one of the earliest autobiographies by an Indian woman.

steps.title: Rashsundari Devi
steps.body: **Rashsundari Devi (1800–1890)** was born in West Bengal. In those days, people believed that if a woman learnt to read and write, she would bring bad luck to her husband and become a widow. She taught herself to read in secret. Her autobiography **Amar Jiban** (published **1876**) is the first known autobiography written by an Indian woman, in Bengali.

steps.title: Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain
steps.body: **Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (1880–1932)** learnt to read and write Urdu, Bengali and English with the support of her elder brother and sister. In **1905** she wrote a remarkable story in English, **Sultana's Dream**, imagining a land called Ladyland where women had freedom, travelled, studied and invented things (like flying machines). In **1910** she started a **school for girls in Kolkata**, which still functions.

steps.title: Schooling and literacy today
steps.body: In **1961**, literacy among boys/men was about **40%** and girls/women about **15%**. In **2011**, men's literacy was about **82%** and women's about **65%**. Gaps remain larger among Dalit, Adivasi and Muslim girls. Reasons children leave school include lack of schools nearby, lack of transport, no proper teachers, and families being unable to afford education.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why did Rashsundari Devi learn to read in secret? → People believed a literate woman would bring bad luck to her husband.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What gap remained between men's and women's literacy in 2011? → About 82% − 65% = **17 percentage points**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up Rashsundari Devi (Amar Jiban) and Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (Sultana's Dream, Kolkata school).
- Thinking the literacy gap has closed.

events.text: Amar Jiban by Rashsundari Devi is published
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain writes Sultana's Dream
Rokeya starts a girls' school in Kolkata

quiz.why: Amar Jiban, written by Rashsundari Devi, is considered the first autobiography by an Indian woman.
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain wrote Sultana's Dream in 1905.

quiz.q: Rokeya started a girls' school in
quiz.why: Rokeya started a school for girls in Kolkata in 1910.
Women's literacy was about 65% in 2011, up from about 15% in 1961.

options: no school nearby or no transport
quiz.why: Girls often leave school when there is no school nearby or no safe transport.

scenes.text: Women's groups march against dowry deaths and violence at home.
Years of campaigning lead to new laws and court guidelines.
On 8 March each year, women around the world mark International Women's Day.

steps.title: What the movement is
steps.body: Women individually and collectively have struggled to bring changes. This struggle is the **women's movement**. Many women and men from different parts of the country are part of it; there is diversity, passion and effort.

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Campaigning**: against discrimination and violence. Campaigns led to new laws: the **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (2005)**; in **1997** the Supreme Court issued guidelines (often called the **Vishaka guidelines**) to protect women against **sexual harassment at the workplace** and in educational institutions; campaigns against dowry deaths led to changes in dowry laws in the 1980s.
- **Raising awareness**: street plays, songs, public meetings.
- **Protesting**: rallies, demonstrations to draw attention to injustice.
- **Showing solidarity**: standing with other women and causes, e.g. on **International Women's Day (8 March)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Name two laws or guidelines that resulted from the women's movement. → Domestic Violence Act (2005) and the 1997 Supreme Court guidelines against workplace sexual harassment.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do street plays help? → They raise awareness about issues among ordinary people in an engaging way.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the women's movement is only protests — it also includes campaigns, awareness and solidarity.
- Thinking only women take part; many men support it too.

activity.prompt: Match the strategy with the example.
pairs: Pushing for a law against domestic violence
Standing together on International Women's Day
Against sexual harassment at the workplace

quiz.q: Domestic Violence Act was passed in
quiz.why: The Domestic Violence Act was passed in 2005 to protect women from violence at home.

quiz.q: Supreme Court guidelines on workplace sexual harassment
quiz.why: In 1997 the Supreme Court gave guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace.
International Women's Day is on 8 March.
Street plays, songs and posters are used by the women's movement to raise awareness.

options: women and men working for equality
quiz.why: The women's movement includes both women and men working for equality, in towns and villages.

scenes.text: Read each short case and answer with reasons.
Use facts from the chapter in your answers.

steps.title: Case 1 with model answer
steps.body:
Case: A village girl, the first in her family to finish Class 10, wants to study science, but relatives say girls should only learn sewing.

Answer: This is a stereotype. Education is her right; she can cite women scientists. The family's support (like Rokeya's siblings) can change her future.

steps.title: Case 2 with model answer
steps.body:
Case: An office has no committee to handle sexual harassment complaints.

Answer: Since the 1997 Supreme Court guidelines (and later law), workplaces must have a mechanism to address such complaints; women's groups campaigned for this.

steps.title: If you or someone you know faces violence
steps.body: Speak to a trusted adult or teacher. In an emergency call **112**; for children, **1098 (Childline)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Answers without reasons.
- Mixing dates of laws.

statements.s: Education helped women like Rokeya change society.
Workplaces need not address sexual harassment complaints.
The women's movement has changed laws in India.
Childline number in India is 1098.

quiz.q: Supporting a girl's choice to study science challenges
quiz.why: Supporting a girl's choice to study science goes against the stereotype that science is only for boys.

quiz.q: A workplace complaint mechanism for sexual harassment comes from
options: the 1997 Supreme Court guidelines (and later law)
quiz.why: The 1997 Supreme Court guidelines asked workplaces to set up complaint systems against sexual harassment. A law was passed later.
112 is the all-in-one emergency number in India.
Childline is 1098, a helpline for children in need of help.
