A good case answer gives facts and reasons, not just a yes or no.

questions.q: International Women's Day
questions.why: International Women's Day is observed on 8 March.

questions.q: Amar Jiban is
questions.why: Amar Jiban is the autobiography of Rashsundari Devi, written in Bengali.

questions.q: Sultana's Dream imagines
questions.why: Rokeya's Sultana's Dream imagines Ladyland, where women lead and men stay at home.

questions.q: A stereotype is
options: a fixed belief about a group
questions.why: A stereotype is a fixed belief about a group of people. It may not be true of individuals.

questions.q: Women's literacy in 1961 (approx.)
questions.why: Women's literacy was about 15% in 1961. It rose to about 65% in 2011.

questions.q: Domestic Violence Act
questions.why: The Domestic Violence Act was passed in 2005.

questions.q: Rokeya's school in Kolkata was started in
questions.why: Rokeya started her school for girls in Kolkata in 1910.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Rashsundari Devi learnt to read in secret. Reason (R): People believed educated women would bring bad luck to their husbands.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: Rashsundari Devi learnt to read in secret. R is true: people then believed educated women would bring bad luck to their husbands, so she had to hide it. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The literacy gap between men and women has fully closed. Reason (R): In 2011, women's literacy was about 65%.
questions.why: A is false: the gap has not closed. R is true: women's literacy was about 65% in 2011, while men's was about 82%, a gap of about 17 points.

questions.q: Which strategy uses songs and street plays?
questions.why: Songs and street plays help raise awareness about issues. They reach many people in a simple way.

questions.q: Workplace sexual harassment guidelines were issued by the
questions.why: The Supreme Court issued guidelines on workplace sexual harassment in 1997.

questions.q: Case: Girls in a tribal village drop out because the nearest secondary school is 15 km away with no bus. Best solution?
options: Provide transport or a nearer school
questions.why: The problem is distance and transport. A nearer school or a bus would help the girls continue their studies.

questions.q: Case: Women in a town hold candlelight vigils and join hands with other groups after a crime. This is
questions.why: Candlelight vigils and joining hands with other groups show solidarity and are a form of protest.

questions.q: By how many percentage points did women's literacy rise from 1961 to 2011?
questions.why: Women's literacy rose from about 15% in 1961 to about 65% in 2011. 65 − 15 = 50 percentage points.

questions.q: Why are women like Rokeya important for history?
options: They used education to challenge restrictions and open doors for others
questions.why: Women like Rokeya used education to challenge restrictions and opened doors for other women.

questions.q: Which is NOT a strategy of the women's movement?
questions.why: The women's movement uses campaigning, awareness and protest. Spreading stereotypes is what it works against.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Understanding Media (Civics)
courses.summary: What media is, how technology and money shape it, its role in democracy, balanced reporting, independence and censorship, how media sets the agenda, and how people use local media to tell their own stories.
outcomes: Learners can identify different forms of media and the role of technology
Learners can explain how money and advertising influence media
Learners can explain the role of media in democracy and what balanced reporting is
Learners can analyse how media sets the agenda and evaluate news critically
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Grandpa got news from the radio; Dad reads the newspaper and watches TV.
You watch short videos and news on a phone.
All of these cost money to make — and someone pays for it.

steps.title: What is media?
steps.body: **Media** (plural of 'medium') refers to all the means of communication — **radio, TV, newspapers, magazines, internet**. Media that reach millions of people at once are called **mass media**. **Electronic media**: TV, radio, internet; **print media**: newspapers, magazines.

steps.title: Technology
steps.body: Technology has changed media: printing, radio, TV, satellites, the internet. Media keep changing technology to reach more people and improve quality.

steps.title: Money and media
steps.body: Mass media need a lot of money for staff, equipment and broadcasting. Most media earn through **advertisements**. Because of the need to earn money, media may avoid stories that anger advertisers or the powerful and may focus on stories that attract more viewers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why are many TV channels free to watch? → They earn money from advertisements.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name one print and one electronic medium. → Newspaper (print), TV (electronic).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking media is only TV.
- Thinking free media has no cost — someone (often advertisers) pays.

quiz.why: Mass media reach millions of people at the same time, through TV, radio and newspapers.

quiz.q: Main source of income for many media
quiz.why: Many media earn most of their money from advertisements, which are paid by businesses.
The internet is electronic media. Newspapers and magazines are print media.
Media is the plural of medium, a means of carrying information.

options: reach more people and improve quality
quiz.why: Technology lets media reach many more people and improves the quality of what they show.

scenes.text: Newspaper A headlines: "Shopkeepers' protest disrupts traffic!"
Newspaper B headlines: "Small traders fear losing jobs to big companies."
Same event — very different pictures. Which one is complete?

steps.title: Role in democracy
steps.body: Media plays an important role in providing news and discussing events in the country and the world. Citizens learn how the government works and can take action (write letters, join protests, start campaigns).

steps.title: Balanced reporting
steps.body: A **balanced** report discusses a point of view from **all sides** of a story and lets readers make up their own minds. Media should give **accurate** information. Sometimes reports focus only on one side — readers must notice this.

steps.title: Independent media and censorship
steps.body: Media should be **independent** — no one should control or influence its coverage. But: (1) **Government control** — when the government prevents a news item, scene or song from being shown to the public, it is **censorship**. (2) **Business control** — media owners or advertisers may influence stories. Media can sometimes be biased to protect business interests.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Make the headlines balanced. → 'Traders protest new policy; traffic affected as they demand their concerns be heard.'

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What is censorship? → The government stopping news, scenes or songs from reaching the public.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing every news report is complete and neutral.
- Thinking censorship is only by government — businesses can also influence coverage, though that is not called censorship.

a.text: You are a reporter covering a protest by street vendors against a new market rule. Whom do you interview?

c.text: Your editor asks: "Where are the vendors' voices?"

choices.label: Go back and interview vendors and shoppers

b.text: An advertiser who supports the rule asks you to drop the vendors' views. What do you do?

choices.label: Keep the report balanced and accurate

e.text: Readers would get a one-sided picture. Reconsider?

d.text: Your report shows all sides; readers can decide for themselves. That is the media's role in democracy.

quiz.why: A balanced report presents all sides of an issue. A one-sided report shows only one view.

options: government stops some content from being shown
quiz.why: Censorship is when the government stops some content from being shown or published.

options: it is owned by government only
quiz.why: Independent media means no one controls what it covers, neither the government nor business.

options: informing citizens about government and events
quiz.why: Media helps democracy by informing citizens about the government and about events, so they can decide for themselves.
If business interests control media, they may only report what helps them. That can make it biased.

lessons.title: Setting the agenda and local media

scenes.text: A TV channel spends an hour on a celebrity cricket wedding.
The same day, a few seconds mention that 3 lakh people in the city have no clean water.
By choosing what to show, media decides what we talk about.

steps.title: Setting the agenda
steps.body: Media draws our attention to particular issues and so **sets the agenda** — influencing what we think about. It can highlight important issues (e.g. alcoholism or water problems) and help bring change. But it can also ignore issues affecting ordinary people (like poverty or lack of water) while covering celebrity news in detail.

steps.title: Local media
steps.body: Because mass media may ignore local issues, people use **local media**: community radio, local newspapers, wall newspapers, videos made by local groups, and social media. Examples include community radio stations run by farmers or a women's group, and newsletters by tribal or Dalit communities to share their stories.

steps.title: Being a smart reader
steps.body:
- Ask: Who made this? What is left out? Is it balanced?
- Check facts with more than one reliable source.
- Do not forward unverified messages; fake news can cause harm.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How can media set the agenda? → By choosing which stories to highlight, it decides what people discuss and what seems important.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do communities start local media? → To tell their own stories and raise local issues ignored by mass media.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the most-covered news is always the most important.
- Sharing a message just because it 'looks like news'.

activity.prompt: Before I share a news item, I will:
items: Check the source — is it a reliable outlet?
Look for the same news in two other sources
Read beyond the headline
Check the date — is it old news?
Ask: whose side is missing?
Not forward if I am unsure

options: deciding what issues people focus on
quiz.why: Setting the agenda means the media decide which issues people talk about by what they choose to show.

quiz.q: Community radio is an example of
quiz.why: Community radio serves a local area and local people, so it is local media.
A smart reader checks several reliable sources before believing a message, to avoid being misled.
Stories about poverty attract fewer viewers and advertisers, so media may skip them.
Fake news spreads false information and can cause harm and confusion.

scenes.text: Students compare three reports of the same event: a newspaper, a TV clip and a social media post.
They note what each includes, what each leaves out, and who paid for it.

steps.title: Media analysis checklist
steps.body:
1. Who is speaking? Whose voices are missing?
2. Is the headline fair to the content?
3. Are facts and opinions separated?
4. Who owns the outlet or paid for the ad?
5. What action is the report asking me to take?

steps.title: Model analysis
steps.body: A report on a dam quotes only the company. Missing: villagers who may be displaced, and environmental experts. It is not balanced.

steps.title: Model analysis 2
steps.body: An ad shows only fair-skinned people as 'successful'. This promotes a harmful stereotype; media literacy helps us question such messages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing opinion pieces with news reports.
- Ignoring who benefits from a story.

statements.s: An opinion piece is the same as a news report.
statements.why: Opinion expresses views; news should report facts.

statements.s: Missing voices can make a report unbalanced.
Ownership of media can influence stories.
Headlines are always accurate summaries.

options: who is speaking and who is missing
quiz.why: When analysing media, first ask who is speaking and whose voice is missing. This shows whose view is being shown.

quiz.q: A report quoting only one side is
quiz.why: A report quoting only one side is unbalanced.

quiz.q: Ads promoting only fair skin as success spread
quiz.why: Ads suggesting that only fair skin is success spread stereotypes, which are unfair ideas about people.

options: opinion is a view; fact can be checked
quiz.why: A fact can be checked and proved. An opinion is someone's view, which may differ.
Media literacy helps us question and judge the messages we read, hear and see.

questions.q: Radio, TV and newspapers are
questions.why: Radio, TV and newspapers are forms of media, ways of carrying news and information.

questions.q: Main income of many media
questions.why: Many media earn most of their income from advertisements.

questions.q: Government stopping a news item is
questions.why: When the government stops something from being shown, it is called censorship.

questions.q: A balanced report
questions.why: A balanced report shows all sides of an issue, not just one.

questions.q: Community radio is
questions.why: Community radio serves a local community, so it is local media.

questions.q: Setting the agenda means
questions.why: Setting the agenda means choosing what issues get attention. What media show becomes what people talk about.

questions.q: Internet is
questions.why: The internet is electronic media, as it carries information by electronic means.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Media may avoid stories that anger advertisers. Reason (R): Media earn much of their money from advertisements.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: media may avoid stories that anger advertisers. R is true: media earn much of their money from ads. That is why they hesitate, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mass media always cover issues of poor people in detail. Reason (R): Media sets the agenda.
questions.why: A is false: mass media often ignore the issues of poor people. R is true: media set the agenda, so they choose what to cover.

questions.q: Independent media means
options: free from control of government and business in coverage
questions.why: Independent media is free from the control of government and business in what it reports.

questions.q: Why should we check news with more than one source?
options: To avoid being misled by false or biased news
questions.why: Checking more than one source keeps us from being misled by false or biased news.

questions.q: Case: A channel shows 50 minutes on a film star's party and 30 seconds on a city water crisis. This shows
questions.why: The channel chose a party over a water crisis, which decides what people think is important. That is setting the agenda.

questions.q: Case: A village women's group starts a radio station to discuss farm prices and health. This is
questions.why: A radio station run by the village women for local issues is local, or community, media.

questions.q: Case: A forwarded message claims a school will close tomorrow; no official source mentions it. You should
options: not forward it; check with the school
questions.why: An unverified forwarded message may be false. Check with the school and do not pass it on.

questions.q: Why is media important for democracy?
options: Citizens need accurate, balanced information to make decisions and hold governments accountable
questions.why: In a democracy citizens need accurate, balanced information to choose well and hold the government accountable.

questions.q: Which shows business influence rather than government censorship?
options: A newspaper drops a story that criticises its main advertiser
questions.why: A newspaper dropping a story that criticises its main advertiser is business influence. The other options involve the government or the courts.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Markets Around Us (Civics)
courses.summary: Different kinds of markets — weekly markets, neighbourhood shops, shopping complexes and malls — how goods travel through a chain of wholesale and retail traders, markets everywhere including online, and the question of markets and equality.
outcomes: Learners can compare weekly markets, neighbourhood shops and malls
Learners can explain the chain of markets from producer to consumer
Learners can describe markets everywhere including phone and internet shopping
Learners can explain how markets affect people unequally
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Every Tuesday, an open ground in the town fills with stalls: vegetables, utensils, clothes, toys.
Customers bargain; sellers set up in the morning and leave at night.
On other days people buy from small shops in their lane, often on credit.

steps.title: Weekly markets
steps.body: Held on a **specific day of the week**. No permanent shops — traders set up stalls and shut them in the evening. Things are **cheaper** because traders do not have rent, electricity bills or workers' wages for permanent shops; many sellers compete, so customers can **bargain**. Most things people need are available in one place. Many weekly market traders are small, with little money to invest.

steps.title: Neighbourhood shops
steps.body: Permanent shops near homes: grocery stores, medical shops, stationery. They are useful because they are **close by** and open on all days. Customers often buy on **credit** — the shopkeeper knows them and lets them pay later. Roadside stalls and hawkers also sell goods.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why are things cheaper in a weekly market? → No permanent shop costs (rent, electricity, staff), and competition among many sellers.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do people buy on credit at neighbourhood shops? → The shopkeeper knows them personally and trusts them to pay later.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking cheaper always means poorer quality.
- Forgetting that neighbourhood shops face costs like rent and electricity.

items.text: Held on one fixed day each week
Many sellers of the same goods compete

options: on a fixed day each week
quiz.why: A weekly market is held on a fixed day of the week, in the same place.

quiz.q: Goods are cheaper in weekly markets because
options: no permanent shop costs and competition
quiz.why: Weekly market traders have no permanent shop to pay for, and there is much competition. So prices are lower.

quiz.q: Buying now and paying later is
quiz.why: Buying now and paying later is buying on credit.

options: they are near and open daily
quiz.why: Neighbourhood shops are close to home and open daily, so they are handy for everyday needs.
Bargaining is common in weekly markets. Malls and online stores usually have fixed prices.

scenes.text: In a big city mall, Rahul sees branded shoes priced four times higher than at the haat.
The mall is air-conditioned, with escalators, food courts and cinemas.
Few people buy; many just walk around.

steps.title: Malls and complexes
steps.body: In urban areas there are **shopping complexes** — many shops together — and **malls** — large multi-storey air-conditioned buildings with shops on different floors. They sell both **branded** and **non-branded** goods. **Branded** goods are more expensive, often promoted by advertising and claims of better quality. Few people can afford them.

steps.title: Why prices differ
steps.body: Malls have very high costs — rent, air-conditioning, staff, decoration, advertising — and these are added to prices. Weekly markets and roadside shops have low costs.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why are goods in malls more expensive? → Higher costs (rent, AC, staff, advertising) and branded products.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Who mostly shops in malls? → People who can afford branded goods; many others visit only to look around.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming branded always means better.
- Ignoring that mall prices include high running costs.

activity.prompt: Match the market with its feature.
pairs: Many shops together in urban areas

quiz.why: Malls are large, air-conditioned, multi-storey buildings with many shops.
Branded goods usually cost more, because of advertising and brand image.

quiz.q: A reason for higher mall prices
quiz.why: Mall prices are higher partly because of high rent and running costs, such as electricity and staff.
Branded products are promoted through advertising, to build a brand image.
Malls are mostly found in cities and towns, where many customers can afford them.

lessons.title: Chain of markets: wholesale to retail

scenes.text: A farmer in Nashik grows onions. He sells them in bulk at the mandi to a wholesale trader.
The wholesaler sells sacks to vegetable vendors in Mumbai.
The vendor sells half a kilo to your mother. Each person in the chain earns something.

steps.title: Who is who
steps.body:
- **Producer**: makes or grows goods (farmers, factories).
- **Wholesale trader**: buys goods in **large quantities** from producers. E.g. a vegetable wholesaler buys several quintals of vegetables.
- **Retailer**: sells goods in **small quantities** to the final consumer (vegetable vendors, shopkeepers).
- **Consumer**: the final user who buys for use.

The chain: **producer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer**. Each trader buys and sells goods, adding a margin (profit). Goods change hands many times — this is the **chain of markets**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: A wholesaler buys 1000 kg of tomatoes at ₹10/kg and sells to retailers at ₹14/kg; a retailer sells at ₹20/kg. Who earns how much per kg? → Wholesaler ₹4/kg; retailer ₹6/kg (before their costs). The consumer pays ₹20 while the farmer got ₹10.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do retailers buy from wholesalers instead of farmers directly? → Wholesalers collect goods in bulk from many producers and sell in quantities retailers need.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing wholesale (large quantities) with retail (small quantities).
- Forgetting that every link adds to the final price.

items: Farmer grows vegetables (producer)
Wholesale trader buys in bulk at the mandi
Retailer buys smaller quantities from the wholesaler
Consumer buys a kilo from the retailer

quiz.why: Buying or selling in large quantities, usually to traders, is wholesale.
Selling in small quantities to the final consumer is retail.
Goods usually move from the producer to the wholesaler, then to the retailer, and finally to the consumer.
Each trader in the chain adds a margin to the price so as to earn a profit.

quiz.q: A vegetable vendor in your lane is a
quiz.why: A vegetable vendor in your lane sells small amounts to consumers, so he is a retailer.

scenes.text: Kiran orders medicines on an app; a delivery person brings them in an hour.
Meanwhile, factories buy raw materials through many markets we never see.
But the small hawker and the mall owner do not earn equally.

steps.title: Markets everywhere
steps.body: We do not always go to a market: we can place orders by **phone or internet**, and goods are delivered home. Many markets are **invisible** to us — when factories buy raw materials from traders, or a car factory buys engines and steel. Goods pass through many markets before reaching us.

steps.title: Markets and equality
steps.body: Markets offer people opportunities to work and earn and to buy what they need. But **earnings are unequal**: a weekly market trader or hawker earns little, while big shop owners or mall owners earn much more. Similarly, as **buyers**, people with more money can buy expensive goods; those with less cannot. Markets do not make everyone equal.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Give an example of a market we may not see. → A car factory buying steel, engines and tyres from other companies.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do markets not ensure equality? → Sellers with more money (big shops, malls) earn far more than small traders; richer buyers can afford more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking online shopping has no chain — warehouses, delivery workers and traders are still involved.
- Thinking all sellers in a market earn the same.

statements.s: Markets exist even when we order online.
A hawker earns as much as a mall owner.
Factories buy raw materials through markets we may not see.
Markets make everyone equal.
statements.why: They offer opportunities but outcomes differ.

quiz.q: Ordering goods by phone or internet is
quiz.why: Ordering goods by phone or internet is still a market, since buyers and sellers exchange goods for money.
A mall owner usually earns far more than a hawker, weekly market vendor or cobbler. Markets are unequal.
Markets give people opportunities to earn and to buy what they need. They do not give equal incomes.
A factory buying raw materials is a market we do not usually see. It is behind the scenes.
People with more money can buy more expensive goods. Others must buy cheaper things.

questions.q: A market held on a fixed day of the week
questions.why: A market held on a fixed day each week is a weekly market (haat).

questions.q: Selling in small quantities to consumers
questions.why: Selling in small quantities to consumers is retail.

questions.q: Malls sell
questions.why: Malls sell branded goods as well as non-branded goods.

questions.q: Buying on credit means
questions.why: Buying on credit means getting goods now and paying for them later.

questions.q: Wholesale traders buy
questions.why: Wholesale traders buy in large quantities, then sell to retailers.

questions.q: Weekly markets are cheaper due to
questions.why: Weekly markets are cheaper because sellers have low costs and there is much competition.

questions.q: Branded goods cost more partly because of
questions.why: Branded goods cost more partly because of advertising and brand image.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Neighbourhood shops often give credit. Reason (R): Shopkeepers know their customers.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: neighbourhood shops often give credit. R is true: shopkeepers know their customers and trust them, so they agree to wait for payment. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Markets ensure equal earnings for all sellers. Reason (R): Markets offer opportunities to earn.
questions.why: A is false: sellers do not earn equally. A mall owner earns far more than a hawker. R is true: markets offer chances to earn.

questions.q: Which is the final link of the market chain?
questions.why: The consumer is the final link in the market chain, because the goods end up with them.

questions.q: A shop selling to other shops in bulk is a
questions.why: A shop that sells to other shops in bulk is a wholesaler.

questions.q: Case: A farmer sells onions at ₹12/kg; a consumer pays ₹30/kg in the city. The difference goes to
options: traders' margins and transport costs in the chain
questions.why: The price rises as goods pass from the farmer through traders to the consumer. Each adds a margin, and transport costs are added too.

questions.q: Case: A family buys groceries from the corner shop on credit until salary day. Why not from the mall?
options: The corner shop gives credit and is nearby
questions.why: The corner shop is nearby and gives credit till salary day. A mall usually does not give credit.

questions.q: Case: A tomato wholesaler buys at ₹8/kg, sells at ₹11/kg; the retailer sells at ₹16/kg. Retailer's margin per kg?
questions.why: The retailer buys at ₹11 and sells at ₹16. Margin = 16 − 11 = ₹5 per kg.

questions.q: Why do small traders in weekly markets earn little?
options: They have little money to invest and face competition
questions.why: Small traders have little money to invest and face a lot of competition, so they earn little.

questions.q: Which statement about online shopping is correct?
options: It is part of the market system with traders, warehouses and delivery
questions.why: Online shopping is still part of the market system, with sellers, warehouses and delivery workers. It is not barter.

courses.title: Ch 8 · A Shirt in the Market (Civics)
courses.summary: Following a cotton shirt from a farmer's field to a city shop and abroad: loans from traders, the cloth market, weavers under the putting-out system, garment factories and exporters, foreign buyers — and who gains and who loses in the market.
outcomes: Learners can trace the chain from cotton farmer to consumer
Learners can explain how small farmers and weavers are dependent on traders
Learners can describe the work of garment exporters and factory workers
Learners can analyse how profits are shared unequally and suggest fairer alternatives such as cooperatives
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A small farmer in Andhra Pradesh grows cotton on 1.5 acres.
Before sowing, she borrows money from a local trader for seeds, fertiliser and pesticide.
The trader makes her promise to sell all her cotton to him — at the price he fixes.

steps.title: Dependent on traders
steps.body: Small farmers often need loans for seeds, fertilisers and pesticides. Local traders lend money on the condition that the farmer sells the crop to them. At harvest, the trader may offer a **low price** (blaming low market prices). The farmer has no choice because she owes him money and cannot wait. In the cotton market (e.g. Kurnool in Andhra Pradesh), big traders buy cotton, remove seeds in **ginning mills**, and press it into bales sold to cloth makers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why does the small farmer sell to the trader even at a low price? → She took a loan from him and promised to sell him her crop; she also needs money immediately.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What happens in a ginning mill? → Seeds are removed from cotton and it is pressed into bales.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the farmer freely chooses whom to sell to — debt limits her choice.
- Thinking cotton goes straight from field to factory.

statements.s: Small farmers often borrow from traders before sowing.
The farmer can always demand a high price.
Ginning removes seeds from cotton.
Cotton bales are sold to cloth makers.

quiz.why: Small farmers take loans to buy seeds, fertilisers and pesticides, which they need before the crop is ready.

quiz.q: In return for a loan, the farmer must
options: sell the crop to the trader
quiz.why: The trader who gives the loan makes the farmer sell the crop to him. This keeps the farmer dependent.

options: remove seeds and press cotton into bales
quiz.why: Ginning mills remove the seeds from the cotton and press it into bales.

quiz.q: Why does the farmer get a low price?
options: she is in debt and cannot bargain
quiz.why: The farmer is in debt to the trader and cannot bargain, so she has to accept a low price.
Cotton is a raw material used to make cloth. It is not a finished shirt.

lessons.title: Cloth market and weavers: the putting-out system

scenes.text: In Erode (Tamil Nadu), one of the largest cloth markets, traders give yarn to weavers.
Weavers work on looms at home and return the cloth to the trader.
The trader pays them a small amount for their work and sells the cloth for much more.

steps.title: Putting-out system
steps.body: Cloth merchants supply **yarn** to weavers and get the finished cloth in return. This is the **putting-out system**. Weavers often buy looms on loans; they depend on merchants for raw material and for selling cloth. They get only a **small amount for their labour** and have no idea who they make the cloth for or at what price it will be sold. Merchants decide what kind of cloth is made and get it at low cost.

steps.title: Weavers' cooperatives
steps.body: In a **cooperative**, people with common interests come together and work for their mutual benefit. In a weavers' cooperative, weavers buy yarn together, produce cloth and sell it directly (sometimes to the government, which buys cloth for school uniforms etc.), reducing dependence on merchants and earning a fairer price. For example, the Tamil Nadu government and some co-operative societies help with this.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Explain the putting-out system. → Merchants put out (supply) yarn to weavers; weavers return cloth and are paid for their labour.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do cooperatives help weavers? → They reduce dependence on merchants by buying yarn and selling cloth collectively at fair prices.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking weavers own the cloth they make in the putting-out system — the merchant owns it.
- Confusing cooperatives with companies owned by one person.

pairs: Merchant supplies yarn; weaver returns cloth for a fee
Large cloth market in Tamil Nadu
Group working together for mutual benefit

quiz.q: In the putting-out system, yarn is supplied by
quiz.why: In the putting-out system, the merchant supplies the yarn to the weaver, who weaves it into cloth.
Weavers working under this system get only a small payment for their labour. The merchant keeps most of the gain.

options: people working together for mutual benefit
quiz.why: A cooperative is a group of people who work together for mutual benefit.
Erode is in Tamil Nadu and has a large cloth market.
Cooperatives let weavers buy yarn and sell cloth together, so they depend less on merchants.

lessons.title: Garment exporters, factories and foreign buyers

story.title: A shirt for a foreign shop

scenes.text: In a garment factory near Delhi, rows of workers stitch shirts under tight deadlines.
The exporter must meet the foreign buyer's strict standards on quality, price and delivery.
The shirts are sold in a big store abroad for many times what workers earned.

steps.title: Exporters and buyers
steps.body: Garment exporting factories use cloth to make shirts for **foreign buyers** (large companies, often in the USA and Europe). Buyers demand top quality and timely delivery at the **lowest price**; they can switch to other suppliers if unhappy. To meet these demands and still earn profit, exporters **cut costs** — mainly workers' wages — and hire workers on a temporary basis.

steps.title: Factory workers
steps.body: Many workers are women; they work as helpers, thread cutters, ironers, button stitchers, and get low wages. Tailors may be paid a little more. Jobs are often insecure, with long hours.

steps.title: Who earns what
steps.body: Suppose a shirt is sold abroad for $26 (about ₹1800). The **foreign businessperson** keeps a large share (after advertising, shop costs) as profit. The **exporter** earns a smaller share. **Workers** get a tiny fraction for their labour. **Farmers and weavers** get still less. The gains from the market are **not equally shared**: those with money and power earn the most.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why do exporters keep wages low? → Foreign buyers demand the lowest price; to keep profits, exporters cut wages.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Who earns the most from the shirt? → The foreign buyer/businessperson.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking workers share the profit equally with owners.
- Forgetting the farmer and weaver at the start of the chain.

items: Farmer grows cotton
Trader buys and ginning mill makes bales
Merchant gives yarn to weavers (putting-out)
Cloth goes to a garment exporting factory
Exporter ships shirts to a foreign buyer
Shirt is sold in a store abroad

options: low price, top quality, timely delivery
quiz.why: Foreign buyers demand a low price, top quality and delivery on time.

quiz.q: To cut costs, exporters often lower
quiz.why: To cut costs, exporters often lower workers' wages, as wages are a big part of the cost.

quiz.q: Who earns the largest share from the shirt?
quiz.why: The foreign businessperson who buys and sells the shirt earns the largest share. Farmers, weavers and helpers earn very little.
Many garment factory helpers are women, who are often paid low wages.

quiz.q: The market chain of a shirt shows
quiz.why: The shirt's market chain shows that gains are shared very unequally among those in it.

lessons.title: Market and equality: what can change?

scenes.text: Weavers form a cooperative; farmers form producer groups to sell directly.
Some buyers choose fair-trade products that pay producers better.
Workers organise for fair wages and safe conditions.

steps.title: Why unequal?
steps.body: In the market, those with **money (capital), ownership and power** gain the most; small farmers, weavers and workers with little money and information get the least, are often in debt and have weak bargaining power.

steps.title: Ways to fairness
steps.body:
- **Cooperatives** of farmers and weavers
- Government support: fair prices, cheap credit, buying from cooperatives
- Labour laws: minimum wages, safe workplaces
- Consumers choosing fairly made goods

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Suggest one way a small cotton farmer can get a better price. → Join a farmers' cooperative, get loans from banks instead of traders, and sell collectively.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How can consumers help? → Buy from cooperatives or fair-trade brands and ask brands about workers' conditions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking inequality in markets cannot be changed.
- Thinking only government can act — groups and consumers can too.

activity.prompt: Think of a piece of clothing you are wearing. List all the people who may have worked on it, from the field to the shop.
activity.hint: Who do you think earned the most? The least? What would make it fairer?

quiz.q: Who gains most in the market chain?
quiz.why: Those with money and power gain the most in the market chain. Small farmers and workers gain the least.

quiz.q: Cheap bank loans help farmers by
quiz.why: Cheap bank loans mean farmers need not borrow from traders, so they can sell at better prices.
Minimum wage laws protect workers by making sure they are paid at least a set amount.
Fair-trade products aim to pay producers fairly for their work.
In a cooperative members work together for mutual benefit. This gives them more strength than working alone.

questions.q: Cotton farmers often borrow from
questions.why: Cotton farmers often borrow from local traders, who then buy the crop from them.

questions.q: The putting-out system involves
questions.why: In the putting-out system, merchants give yarn to weavers and collect the cloth.

questions.q: Erode is famous for its
questions.why: Erode in Tamil Nadu is famous for its cloth market.

questions.q: Seeds are removed from cotton in a
questions.why: Seeds are removed from cotton in a ginning mill.

questions.q: A weavers' cooperative
questions.why: A weavers' cooperative lets weavers work together, so they depend less on merchants.

questions.q: Foreign buyers want shirts at
questions.why: Foreign buyers want shirts at the lowest price, so they pressure exporters to cut costs.

questions.q: Who gets the smallest share from a shirt?
questions.why: Farmers and workers get the smallest share of the money from a shirt, though they do much of the work.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Small farmers often sell cotton at low prices. Reason (R): They are in debt to the traders who lend them money.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: small farmers often sell cotton cheaply. R is true: they are in debt to traders, who set the price. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In the putting-out system, weavers decide the price of cloth. Reason (R): Merchants supply yarn.
questions.why: A is false: the merchants decide the price, not the weavers. R is true: merchants supply yarn, which gives them the power.

questions.q: Exporters cut costs mainly by
questions.why: Exporters cut costs mainly by keeping wages low.

questions.q: Correct chain
options: farmer → trader/ginning → weaver → exporter → foreign buyer
questions.why: The cotton goes from the farmer to the trader and ginning mill, then to the weaver. The exporter then sells it to the foreign buyer. The other orders are wrong.

questions.q: Case: A shirt sells abroad for ₹1800; the factory worker who stitched it earned ₹20 for it. This shows
questions.why: The worker who stitched the shirt earned ₹20 while it sold for ₹1800. The gains are shared very unequally.

questions.q: Case: Weavers form a group, buy yarn together and sell cloth to the government for school uniforms. This is a
questions.why: Weavers who group together, buy yarn together and sell cloth jointly form a cooperative.

questions.q: Why can foreign buyers drive down prices?
options: They can switch to other suppliers
questions.why: Foreign buyers can switch to other suppliers if prices are high. This gives them the power to push prices down.

questions.q: Which measure would MOST improve a small farmer's bargaining power?
options: Access to bank credit and joining a cooperative
questions.why: Bank credit frees the farmer from the trader's loan, and a cooperative gives collective strength. Together they improve bargaining power.

questions.q: What does "A Shirt in the Market" teach about markets?
options: Markets are always unfair and should be abolished
People with money and power gain most; small producers and workers gain least
questions.why: The chapter shows that people with money and power gain most from the market, while small producers and workers gain least.

questions.q: A party with more than half the seats in the assembly
questions.why: A party with more than half the seats in the assembly has a majority.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ladakh is a cold desert. Reason (R): It gets very little rainfall and has sparse vegetation.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: Ladakh is a cold desert. R is true: it gets very little rain and has sparse plants, which defines a desert. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mansabdars personally governed their jagirs. Reason (R): Jagirs were revenue assignments.
questions.why: A is false: most mansabdars did not live in their jagirs, and their servants collected the revenue. R is true: jagirs were revenue assignments.

questions.why: Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti's dargah is in Ajmer. Tukaram was from Maharashtra, Shankaradeva from Assam and Basavanna from Karnataka.

questions.q: Spring tides occur when
options: the Moon is in its first quarter
Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line
there is no Moon in the sky at noon
questions.why: Spring tides occur when the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line. Their pulls then add up.

questions.q: Case: A hospital refuses an injured accident victim citing no beds; a court later says this violates his rights. Which right?
questions.why: Denying emergency treatment violates the right to life, which is in Article 21. This was the ruling in the Hakim Sheikh case.

questions.q: Case: A Bengal temple has a two-sloped roof copying a thatched hut. Type?
questions.why: A Bengal temple with a two-sloped roof is a dochala. A four-sloped one is a chauchala.

questions.q: Case: A farmer sells onions at ₹10/kg; the wholesaler sells to retailers at ₹15; the retailer sells at ₹24. Retailer's margin per kg?
questions.why: The retailer buys at ₹15 and sells at ₹24, so the margin is 24 − 15 = ₹9 per kg.

questions.q: Case: A village in the Ganga plains floods often but has very fertile soil. Why fertile?
options: Floods deposit fresh silt on floodplains
questions.why: Floods spread fresh silt over the floodplain, which keeps the soil fertile.

questions.q: Arrange: Khaljis, Lodis, Tughluqs, Sayyids
questions.why: The order of the dynasties is Khaljis, Tughluqs, Sayyids and then Lodis.

questions.q: Which statement links civics and history correctly?
options: Bhakti saints and the Constitution both challenge caste discrimination
questions.why: Bhakti saints spoke against caste discrimination, and so does the Constitution, which bans it. The other options are false.

questions.q: Which combination best describes the stratosphere?
options: Ozone layer, few clouds, good for aeroplanes
questions.why: The stratosphere has the ozone layer and few clouds, so it is good for aeroplanes. Meteors burn in the mesosphere, and weather is in the troposphere.
